articles.title: The NF Data Portal: A Community-Driven Resource to Accelerate Neurofibromatosis and Schwannomatosis Research and Drug Development
articles.authors: Kara Quaid; Belinda B. Garana; Chang In Moon; Aditya Nath; Christina Parry; Efren Munoz; Jineta Banerjee; Alexandra J. Scott; Milen Nikolov; Sang Y. Lee
articles.abstract:
The NF Data Portal (nf.synapse.org) is a free, open-science platform that centralizes data and resources related to neurofibromatosis (NF) and schwannomatosis (SWN), a group of rare genetic tumor predisposition syndromes. The portal hosts a growing collection of NF and SWN multimodal datasets including genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and imaging with links to resources such as patient-derived tumor tissue collections, cell lines and preclinical models. The goal of the portal is to provide the broader academic and commercial research community with well-annotated, trusted datasets that can be used in a variety of ways, including asking new scientific questions, benchmarking new methods or tools, and combining datasets across studies. Ultimately, our mission is to accelerate the discovery of treatments and cures for NF and SWN through maximizing the global usability of high-quality data. . 
The NF Data Portal has a cross-institutional backbone of supporters composed of funding organizations, a data coordination center, and a community of clinicians and scientists. Together, this community has developed reusable building blocks for open science, including shared infrastructure, governance frameworks, metadata standards, and a structured data contribution lifecycle. In this publication, we reflect on over a decade of effort to support the data contributor and data user journeys. We share recent platform features and integrations and highlight newly available datasets. 
Whether longtime NF scientists or those encountering this resource for the first time, the NF Data Portal provides access to one of the largest NF datasets available to advance academic research, industry-driven discovery and therapeutic development. For industry users, the portal serves as a strategic translational research asset that supports target validation, biomarker discovery, patient stratification and data-driven decision making, helping to de-risk development programs and inform clinical strategy. As AI-driven analytical methods transform biomedical research, richly annotated, disease-specific datasets like those housed in the NF Data Portal, will be essential raw material for developing and validating new tools and novel treatments.

articles_hidden.title: An item bank of reporting items and concepts in evidence synthesis reporting guidelines
articles_hidden.authors: Kyle Morrison; Edward R. Ivimey-Cook; Malgorzata Lagisz; Ayumi Mizuno; Manuela Santos Santana; Eduardo S. A. Santos; Alfredo Sánchez-Tójar; Zachary P. Simpson; Matthew James Grainger; Biljana Macura
articles_hidden.abstract: Evidence synthesis integrates findings from multiple research studies, and its value for decision making depends on complete, transparent reporting. Authors often rely on reporting guidelines, checklists, flow diagrams, or structured text guiding manuscript reporting, but they still struggle to implement what counts as clear, complete reporting. A central issue is that many guidelines address the same underlying concepts using different wording, making it unclear whether differences between guidelines are meaningful or merely semantic. To address this, we compiled an item bank of 2,249 reporting items from 59 unique evidence synthesis reporting guidelines (from 83 studies, 68 checklists), using a six-step process: literature searching and screening, item collation, readability analysis, concept extraction, and overlap assessment. Compiled items were relatively verbose (mean words/item = 19.9) and linguistically complex (Moving-Average Type-Token Ratio = 0.959), indicating limited reuse of consistent wording—likely making items harder to interpret and compare. Because items can contain multiple concepts, and concepts can recur across items and guidelines, we identified 403 unique reporting concepts. Guidelines also showed modest conceptual overlap (Jaccard Similarity Index = 0.166, n = 1,830 pairwise comparisons), suggesting some concepts were widely shared across reporting guidelines for different methodologies and disciplines, pointing to clear potential to harmonise reporting guidance and reduce duplicated effort. We provide all reporting items and concepts in the supplementary files. We further discuss trends and gaps in item use and wording across guidelines, outline applications of the collated item bank, and note limitations that point to future research. Together, our findings offer much-needed direction for developing and harmonising future reporting guidelines, an essential step toward more consistent and transparent reporting across evidence synthesis.

articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Messori

articles_hidden.title: How Much Replication Is Enough? Balancing Novelty and Replication in a Truth-Driven Evolutionary Simulation
articles_hidden.authors: Kaitlyn Harper; Felix D. Schönbrodt
articles_hidden.abstract: Scientific progress relies on a balance of original research, which furthers the boundaries of knowledge, and replication, which assures the quality of existing knowledge. In recent years, calls for increased replication have gained momentum, but replication requires resources that could otherwise support novel research. Here, we take a cultural-evolutionary approach to answer the question: what share of limited scientific resources should be allocated to original versus replication studies? We simulated a scientific ecosystem with a “utopian” selection criterion: whether research moves beliefs closer to the truth. Within this ecosystem, researchers differ in their tendency to pursue original or replication work, and more successful strategies (i.e., those which contribute most to truthful Bayesian information gain) are selected for over time. Under broadly realistic parameter assumptions, the model suggests an optimal replicator share of 5-32%, with 7-21% of published studies being replications, and replication success rates of 20-30% (all replications) and 72-88% (only published replications). Stronger publication bias, greater base null rates, and smaller original study sample sizes all increase the optimal replicator share. Our model may underestimate the optimal replicator share, because the model omits biases such as p-hacking that additional replication could help correct, or overestimate, because our model’s simplistic choice of replication targets may be less efficient than more strategic ones. Ultimately, our simulations suggest that replication primarily evolves as a compensatory mechanism in response to distorted research environments, and that overall scientific progress is maximised when underlying issues such as publication bias are resolved, which would largely eliminate the need for replications.

articles_hidden.title: Time for Journals to Claim a Sustainable Future in Scientific Publishing
articles_hidden.authors: yong sik ok
articles_hidden.abstract: Scientific publishing depends on trust, fairness, and transparency. This article argues that publishers should take greater responsibility for how research integrity concerns, investigations, and retractions are handled. It calls for clearer procedures, fair opportunities for authors to respond, stronger editorial involvement, and proportionate decisions based on scientific judgment. Greater accountability and cooperation among publishers, editors, researchers, and institutions are essential for building a more trustworthy and sustainable scientific publishing system.

articles.title: From app open to app close: Function and well-being across TikTok sessions
articles.authors: Sabrina Fay Norwood; Tamás Andrei Földes; Nick Ballou; David Joachim Grüning; Malte Elson; Andrew K Przybylski
articles.abstract: Social media use is often measured in aggregate or characterised by a single motivation, despite individual sessions being temporally bound and potentially dynamic. We used experience sampling to capture behavioural function (entertainment, access, social attention, escape/avoidance) and momentary well-being at both the onset and offset of naturally occurring TikTok sessions. Across seven consecutive days, 161 participants produced 3,943 paired sessions. Exploratory analyses showed that 42% of sessions ended with a different function than they began, with transitions frequently ending in entertainment. In preregistered multilevel analyses, individual escape-oriented sessions were not reliably associated with lower post-session well-being within persons, whereas participants who more frequently used TikTok for escape reported lower post-session well-being under the preregistered model specification. However, the within- and between-person coefficients did not themselves differ significantly, and the between-person association was attenuated to near zero in a sensitivity analysis. Exploratory transition analyses further suggested that well-being change was more closely organised around the function reported at session close than at session onset. Together, these findings suggest that conclusions about social media use and well-being depend on both the analytical level and temporal point at which behaviour is measured, and demonstrate that within-session dynamics can be observed directly by aligning measurement with the natural boundaries of app use.

articles.title: Reimagining Social Media Literacy: A Narrative Review on The Importance of Social Contexts and Peer Relationships
articles.authors: Jolien Trekels; Chiara de Jong; J. Loes Pouwels
articles.abstract: This narrative review explores the convergence of media literacy and adolescent social media use, highlighting the essential role of understanding social context in shaping adolescent behaviors and overall well-being. As young people increasingly navigate through social media platforms, they encounter a multifaceted landscape filled with both opportunities and challenges. We argue that effective media literacy interventions must go beyond individual knowledge and critical awareness to address the social dynamics and peer influences that profoundly impact online behavior. By utilizing social network theory, we propose strategies for integrating these social dynamics into media literacy programs, focusing on the importance of leveraging peer relationships to cultivate positive digital habits. By situating media literacy within broader social contexts, this paper aims to outline an agenda for future research aimed at improving the effectiveness of social media literacy interventions.

articles.title: Liar's Dice: Eye Measures in a Social Deceptive Game
articles.authors: Valentin Foucher; Anke Huckauf
articles.abstract: Eyes have been identified as markers of deception. Yet, most existing research typically relies on instructed deception directed toward screens or confederates, limiting ecological validity. The present study introduced a novel paradigm from the Liar’s Dice game to investigate spontaneous deception in an interactive context. Two players alternated between the roles of “bidder”, who rolled dice and made truthful or deceptive bids, and “challenger”, who evaluated the bid’s veracity. The challenger could either contest, ending the round, or accept, becoming the new bidder who rolled new dice and made a higher bid. The challenger won if the contested bid was false and lost if it was true. Participants played against a computer in Experiment 1 and against another participant in Experiment 2. The study addressed three objectives: to characterise the effects of spontaneous deception, social dynamics, and veracity judgments on response times, fixations and blinks. Across experiments, lying was associated with longer response latencies, fewer and longer fixations, consistent with an increased cognitive load arising from decision complexity. Experiment 2 further showed decreased blink rate, an effect potentially amplified by the social context. Fewer fixations directed at the opponent’s face when lying suggest that deception was attentionally directed toward the social agent. Challengers exhibited longer response latencies, fewer and longer fixations, fewer blinks, but also increased attention on the bidder’s face when contesting a bid. These findings provide new insights into receivers of deception and veracity judgments, indicating that suspicion reduces eye movements but enhances attention toward the opponent.

articles.title: Recognizing strengths in individuals with ADHD: Exploring experiences and applications in clinical practice
articles.authors: Amy De Roubaix; Jennifer de Smidt; Lessa Madelief Schippers; Rob Abels; Patricia van Casteren; Barbara Franke; Corina Greven; Pieter Hoekstra; Petra Hurks; Akke Meilink
articles.abstract:
Background. Growing recognition of strengths associated with ADHD has stimulated interest in strength-based approaches. Highlighting these strengths may promote well-being and self-acceptance and help counter stigma. Although incorporating strengths into ADHD care may enhance positive outcomes, little is known about how ADHD-related strengths are currently recognized, valued, and applied in clinical practice. This study examined whether and how strengths are discussed in Dutch ADHD care, the perceived importance of attention to strengths, factors needed to support flourishing, associations with stigma, and characteristics of adults associated with reporting strengths related to ADHD.

Method. In co-creation with a Dutch ADHD advocacy organization, we conducted a mixed-method study and developed a survey containing open- and closed-ended questions on strengths associated with ADHD, attention to strengths in clinical care, support needs, and stigma. All members with ADHD were invited to participate. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics and tests of associations between experiencing strengths, stigma, and participant characteristics, while qualitative response were analyses thematically. 

Results. Among 224 respondents, 87.1% reported experiencing strengths associated with their ADHD. Participants who reported such strengths had received their diagnosis at a younger age than those who did not. Strengths were discussed more often during treatment (50.4%) than during diagnostic assessment (36.2%), mainly in the context of identifying and utilizing personal strengths. Experiencing strengths was associated with having discussed them in treatment, although the effect size was small. Most participants (78.6%) considered attention to strengths essential. A supportive and understanding environment was most frequently identified as necessary for strengths to flourish (73.2%). No association was found between experiencing strengths and reported stigma.

Conclusion. Most respondents experienced strengths associated with ADHD and considered attention to these strengths important. However, strengths are not systematically addressed in clinical care. Participants emphasize that understanding and acceptance of ADHD are key conditions for enabling strengths to flourish.

articles.title: The popBAT: A New Beat Alignment Task to Assess Beat  Perception Abilities in Children
articles.authors: Francesca Cantoni; Zoé Mandernach; Erika Godde; Anna Fiveash; Barbara Tillmann
articles.abstract:
Beat processing is a fundamental skill for music and speech processing, as well as motor 
coordination. Existing tools testing beat perception, such as the seminal Beat Alignment Test 
(BAT), mostly use beat keepers that are external to the music, and may be too long to be 
engaging for children. We here developed the popBAT: a novel, child-friendly test using 
groovy pop-music excerpts, a musically integrated kick drum as the beat keeper, and a cover 
story, all aiming to enhance ecological validity and children’s engagement. Across four 
experiments, the popBAT was validated in adults (Exp. 1-2) and 7- to 8-year old children (Exp. 
3-4). In adults, the kick drum significantly increased subjective ratings of “pleasure”, “wanting 
to move”, and “pulse clarity”, compared to a triangle timbre playing the beat. In children and 
adults, popBAT performance was significantly above chance level, and popBAT performance 
correlated positively with performance in a previously used BAT implementation (adapted from 
Dalla Bella et al., 2017), confirming its convergent validity. In Experiment 4, popBAT 
performance significantly correlated with chronological age and reading performance, further 
confirming the link between beat perception and reading abilities. The popBAT provides a 
short, engaging, and ecologically valid measure of beat perception in children. Its success in 7- 
and 8-year-old children supports its use for investigating the developmental trajectories of 
rhythm processing and its role in language abilities, offering a promising tool for both research 
and clinical settings.

articles.title: Gestures speed up responses to semantic knowledge questions in a virtual reality interactive quiz
articles.authors: Cecilia Husta; Caitlin Decuyper; JUDITH HOLLER; Eleanor Huizeling; Sharice Clough
articles.abstract: Interlocutors often gesture in conversation. Emerging evidence indicates that gestures can facilitate fast turn-taking. Corpus studies have shown that yes-no questions are answered faster when paired with gestures compared to without. This finding was confirmed in a controlled behavioral experiment in which participants responded to yes-no questions presented with and without gestures with a button press, focusing on iconic gestures in particular (i.e. gestures that depict semantic information, such as objects and actions). However, it is unclear whether iconic gestures also facilitate verbal responding in dialogic, controlled settings, and whether this effect extends to other question types. In a study using a virtual reality setup, we bridge naturalistic and experimental approaches to test whether gestures facilitate verbal responses to both yes-no and wh-questions. Sixty participants took part in this experiment using a Meta Quest 3 head-mounted display. A virtual human asked 112 semantic knowledge questions, which participants answered as quickly as possible. On half of the trials, a critical word in the question was paired with an iconic gesture, with the informative movement (gesture stroke) beginning 227 ms before word onset, informed by analyses of their natural timing. On the remaining trials, the virtual human asked questions without any accompanying gestures. Gestures sped up responses to both yes-no questions and wh-questions, showing that gestures facilitate turn-taking across question types. Thus, the presence of iconic gestures in questions might aid information uptake (e.g. based on prediction or other mechanisms) and, in turn, facilitate simultaneous speech planning processes.

articles.title: Gradual Progress or Breakthrough Moments? Antecedents and Consequences of Sudden Gains in a Digital Neuroticism Intervention
articles.authors: Gabriel Olaru; Peter Haehner; Amanda Jo Wright; Rosalie Andrae; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Sudden gains—large and abrupt improvements in symptoms between consecutive sessions—are a well-documented phenomenon in psychotherapy research and reliably predict better treatment outcomes. Personality trait change, in contrast, is typically seen as a gradual process, and whether such sudden gains also occur and matter in the context of volitional neuroticism change is still unclear. In this preregistered study, we used daily and weekly measures of neuroticism to examine whether sudden gains occur during a 6-week digital neuroticism intervention embedded in an 8-week intensive longitudinal study (N = 427), and tested divergent claims from two theories on sudden gains in psychopathology. Sudden gains occurred in 11.2% (weekly) and 16.9% (daily) of participants, exceeding the rates that would be expected based on gradual change and noise, but far below the rates reported in psychotherapy research. Consistent with findings from psychotherapy, these gains occurred more frequently for participants with stronger state fluctuations overall but occurred equally often across conditions targeting neuroticism at the state, habit, or trait level. While gains coincided with large improvements in self-control, self-efficacy, self-esteem, and self-concept clarity (0.37–0.68 SD), we did not find robust evidence for an effect on neuroticism trait change. In contrast, gradual progress across the days and weeks of the intervention predicted stronger neuroticism trait changes. Our findings suggest that breakthrough moments or sudden shifts are less common and less consequential in volitional personality trait change than in the treatment of psychological disorders.

articles.title: Perceptions of a Foreign Leader: Donald Trump, Democratic Identity, and the Reconfiguration of Traditional Geopolitical Alignment
articles.authors: Marie Kovářová; Martina Klicperová; Eric Shiraev
articles.abstract:
This study focuses on the relationship between attitudes to the American President, democratic identity and cultural identification. The Czech Republic served as a case study because its geography and history placed it at the intersection of Western and Eastern Europe.
A two-wave national quota panel in Czechia (N = 977 matched respondents) was used to assess attitudes toward Donald Trump before (August 2024) and after his re-election (April 2025). A four-point rating scale included positive, neutral or mixed, and negative categories, supplemented by open-ended questions. Stability and change in attitudes were examined along with relationship to democratic identity, cultural identification, perceived geopolitical threats, and religiosity.
The higher order typology based on ratings across both waves comprised six categories: Consistently Negative (n = 326), Positive Shift (n = 178), Negative Shift (n = 125), Consistently Mixed (n = 119), Consistently Positive (n = 63), and Consistently Neutral (n = 63). Negative evaluations were the most common and stable. Positive change typically reflected shifts from negative to mixed evaluations; full reversals were rare (n = 3).
Respondents Consistently Negative toward Trump identified more strongly with Western culture and democratic Europe, placed greater importance on living in a democracy, more likely perceived Russia as a threat, less likely perceived Ukrainian migrants as a threat, and reported lower religiosity. Consistently positive respondents showed a contrasting profile, including weaker identification with the West and with democratic Europe and stronger identification with Eastern civilization/Slavic culture. Respondents whose evaluations of Trump improved did not display coherent profiles, suggesting a pragmatic reconsideration. 
The findings indicate a significant relationship between attitudes toward a foreign leader and broader social identities and geopolitical worldviews. In this Central European case, they suggest a significant reconfiguration of the traditional geopolitical alignment in which an American president represented the democratic West: commitment to democracy was instead associated with negative attitudes toward Trump.

articles.title: Individual Patterns in the Association Between Social Media Use and Adolescent Well-being
articles.authors: Jane Shawcroft; Samantha Vigil; Drew Cingel; Sarah Coyne
articles.abstract: Research on the association between social media use and youth well-being has begun adopting an individualized paradigm by focusing on the within-person associations between social media use and well-being to provide clarity in a literature characterized by inconsistent findings. We provide a more holistic examination of the individualized nature of the effects of social media on youth well-being by using EMA data from 99 adolescents living in the United States to (1) show the between- and within-person variability in social media harms and benefits related to eight dimensions of well-being and (2) create individualized predictive models of youth well-being using fifteen features of youth’s social media experiences. Across both analyses, we found considerable nuance and variability when examining the interplay between social media use and well-being at an individual level, illustrating the challenges an individualized approach poses to researchers seeking to build a generalizable understanding of social media use and well-being.

articles.title: Knowing when to doubt: a measure of epistemic vulnerability to scientific disinformation
articles.authors: José Eduardo Rosales-Trabuco; Jesús Adrián-Ventura; Diego Avendaño; Cornelia Betsch; Lars Korn; Elvis Andy Pinedo Yzaguirre; Juan Manuel Espinoza Nuñez; Maniela Dejo-Vásquez; Carlos Moquillaza Vizarreta; Angelo Fasce
articles.abstract: Scientific disinformation poses a challenge for public understanding of science, yet the psychometric assessment of epistemic dispositions underlying vulnerability to misleading scientific claims remains underdeveloped. This study introduces and validates the Epistemic Vulnerability to Scientific Disinformation Scale across six samples from Peru, Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda, and the United States (total N = 4,932). Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses across samples yielded a 12-item unidimensional scale encompassing source and credibility analysis, evidence evaluation, logical reasoning, and contextualization of scientific information. The final scale showed satisfactory factorial validity, internal consistency, and configural and metric invariance across samples. Construct validity was supported by theoretically consistent associations with epistemic beliefs, attitudes toward science, fake news detection, vaccine hesitancy, climate change denial, familiarity with scientific concepts, and overclaiming. The scale provides a concise and psychometrically robust measure of epistemic vulnerability to scientific disinformation.

articles.title: Beyond WEIRD and White: Building a Globally Inclusive Science of Sport Leadership
articles.authors: Radhika Butalia; Filip Boen; Nicholas de Cruz; S. Alexander Haslam; Rolf van Dick; Katrien Fransen
articles.abstract: Research in the social sciences overwhelmingly relies on participants drawn from Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) societies despite the fact that these populations represent about 12% of the world’s population. Moreover, these samples are disproportionately White. Although this limitation has been widely discussed in the social sciences, its implications for sport science remain underexamined. In this expert statement, we use sport leadership research as a test case to illustrate why moving beyond WEIRD and White dominance is critical to building a more inclusive and representative science of sport. First, we discuss how cultural and social contexts shape leadership expectations, perceptions, and effectiveness, thereby calling into question the appropriateness of applying theories developed in WEIRD samples to other contexts. Second, we synthesise the current state of the literature and highlight recent advances, particularly insights from the Cross-Cultural Research on Leadership in Sport (CROLIS) programme. Drawing on these insights, we provide practical and methodological recommendations and identify priorities for future research that together offer a roadmap for building a science of sport leadership in which diverse populations, cultural contexts, and knowledge systems shape equitable knowledge production.

articles.title: Memories that remain: Image memorability transfers to scene descriptions
articles.authors: Diana Kollenda; Yee Lee Shing; Katharina Dobs; Benjamin de Haas
articles.abstract: Some images remain in memory while others fade quickly. Memorability reflects an observer-independent, intrinsic property of an image, which can be predicted by computational models. While semantic content has been proposed as the critical determinant of memorability, it is challenging to disentangle image content from visual features on display. Here, we find that the memorability of scene images transfers to short textual descriptions of those scenes, whether generated by humans or multimodal large language models. Furthermore, new images produced with generative AI from descriptions alone reproduce the memorability of original images. Together, these findings show that semantic content, including interrelations captured in scene descriptions, accounts for a meaningful portion of the variation in scene memorability, and that language serves as an efficient compression of memory-relevant visual content.

articles.title: Change by Compassion: Introducing moralistic versus compassionate evaluation as a bridge between do-gooder derogation, nonviolent communication, and self-compassion
articles.authors: Daniel Florian Dorji Gratzer; Jana Katharina Köhler
articles.abstract: We introduce the construct of moralistic evaluation—contrasted with compassionate evaluation—as a bridging concept linking do-gooder derogation (DGD) with frameworks of self-compassion and nonviolent communication. We further provide exploratory evidence that moralistic evaluation increases DGD, thereby reducing persuasiveness relative to compassionate evaluation. In a preregistered within-participants online experiment (N = 458 non-vegan German speakers), participants viewed two short videos of a vegan advocating a plant-based diet, presented in moralistic or compassionate evaluation. Manipulation checks confirmed higher perceived judgment in the moralistic condition. Compassionate framing increased likability (reverse DGD) and persuasiveness (r(rb) = .88 and .74, respectively). In a mediation model, likability statistically accounted for the association between framing and persuasiveness (β = 0.69); no direct path was detectable. Interpreted through the lens of self-compassion and nonviolent communication, these findings provide exploratory support for the proposed bridging construct and invite further study.

articles.title: Fast Love in Hard Times: Societal Stress Shapes Romantic Representations Across Five Decades of US Songs and Movies
articles.authors: Markus Foramitti; Daniel Reiter; Mauricio Martins
articles.abstract:
How do cultural representations of romantic relationships respond to societal adversity, and can they anticipate changes in pair-bonding behavior? Behavioral-ecological theories predict that harsh and unpredictable environments reduce investment in long-term relationships in favor of immediate attraction. To test this hypothesis, we used large language models to quantify slow love (emotional attachment and long-term partner investment) and fast love (passion and immediate attraction) across three corpora spanning five decades of US popular culture: 266,086 Billboard Hot 100 chart appearances (1973-2023), 1,180 highest-grossing US movies within 1977-2018, and 14,505 US movies produced within 1950-2018. We examined long-term historical trajectories, responses to major societal shocks, and associations with psychological distress, political instability, and pair-bonding.
Representations of romantic relationships evolved through distinct historical phases rather than continuous linear trends. Across media, romanticism declined during the decades surrounding the sexual revolution, increased throughout the late twentieth century, and subsequently diverged, with song lyrics showing a pronounced decline between 2001 and 2016, before rising again. In movies, romanticism generally increased after 2000. Across datasets, periods of greater psychological distress and political instability consistently showed a relative shift toward immediate attraction and away from long-term emotional investment. The 2008 financial crisis provided suggestive evidence of accelerating this trend in song lyrics, whereas the COVID-19 pandemic produced no comparable effect. Temporal analyses further suggested that greater cultural romanticism preceded lower future political instability and, in movie production, higher future marriage-to-divorce ratios. Conversely, psychological distress preceded a stronger focus on sexual attraction.
Together, these findings suggest that modern romantic culture is neither historically linear nor socially autonomous. Instead, it evolves through successive historical phases that systematically covary with broader psychological and societal conditions. Overall, the findings are consistent with behavioral-ecological accounts proposing that societal adversity reduces the psychological romantic tendencies essential to invest in long-term pair bonding.

articles.title: Similarity or Cumulative Load? A Response Surface Analysis of Autistic Traits and Parental Stress in Mother-Child Dyads
articles.authors: Jan Łabędź; Julia; Alicja Niedźwiecka; Joanna Ludwika Beck; Ewa Pisula; Gianluca Esposito; Agnieszka Pluta
articles.abstract: Phenotypic overlap in autistic traits between parents and children may have contrasting implications for caregiving. Greater similarity may promote mutual understanding, predictability, and shared communication styles, potentially facilitating parent–child interactions. Conversely, when both parent and child show elevated autistic traits, their combined characteristics may increase caregiving demands and reduce the parent's capacity to respond effectively to the child's needs.We examined 115 mother-child dyads to determine whether congruence or mismatch in autistic trait levels was associated with maternal parenting stress. Mothers’ and children’s autistic traits were assessed using age-appropriate forms of the Social Responsiveness Scale, Second Edition (SRS-2). Response surface analysis was used to evaluate two competing hypotheses. The Congruence Hypothesis proposed that maternal parenting stress would be lower when mothers and children showed similar levels of autistic traits, whereas the Discrepancy Hypothesis proposed that parenting stress would increase as the difference in autistic trait levels between mothers and children became greater. Finally, the Directionality of Mismatch Hypothesis predicted higher parenting stress when children’s autistic trait levels exceeded those of their mothers. None of these hypotheses was supported. Instead, higher autistic trait levels in both dyad members were associated with greater maternal parenting stress, with children’s traits showing the stronger association.

articles.title: Tracing uncertainty in mind perception: Examining the role of affirming versus denying mental capacities in robots.
articles.authors: Yasmina Giebeler; Nueud Kassaye; Basil Wahn; Eva Wiese
articles.abstract:
Mind perception, the capacity to infer others’ intentions and affective states, is central to social
cognition. Its two dimensions, agency (act and plan) and experience (sense and feel), shape
perceived responsibility and empathy, structure moral behavior, and determine perceived social
relevance. Robots are less readily perceived as “having a mind”, which can negatively impact
human-robot interaction. Although it is well established that an agent’s appearance impacts mind
perception, it remains unclear how body and face cues selectively promote perceptions of agency
and experience. Moreover, prior research strongly relies on explicit ratings, offering limited
insight into decision-making processes and potential uncertainties associated with judging a
robot’s mind. Mouse-tracking provides a promising approach capturing both explicit mind
perception judgments and associated uncertainties. As uncertainty is linked to negative affective
responses and cognitive conflict, the present study uses mouse tracking to examine whether
explicit agency and experience ratings, associated with robotic face and body features variations,
trigger uncertainty. Explicit ratings showed distinct effects of appearance: body features were
associated with variations in agency perception, whereas facial features explained variations in
both agency and experience. Mouse-tracking parameters did not differ as a function of physical
features (body vs. face) or mind perception dimensions (agency vs. experience). Interestingly
though, overall greater uncertainty was observed when participants affirmed versus denied
mental capacities, which was particularly pronounced for agency assessments. These findings
demonstrate that face and body cues reliably shape mind perception, while also being linked to
intrinsic uncertainty associated with affirming mental capacities in artificial agents.

articles.title: Reducing belief in conspiracy theories as they unfold using large language models
articles.authors: Thomas H Costello; Nathaniel Rabb; Michael Nicholas Stagnaro; Gordon Pennycook; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: The emergence of conspiracy theories in the wake of major events is a significant societal challenge. Here we test whether conversational dialogues with a large language model (LLM) can reduce belief in immediately unfolding conspiracies. In experiments conducted in the days following the July 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump and the September 2025 assassination of Charlie Kirk, U.S. adults (Experiment 1: N = 472; Experiment 2: N = 1035) holding conspiratorial views about the crisis event engaged in a multi-turn conversation with an LLM prompted to reduce their conspiracy belief. Compared to control participants who either discussed an irrelevant topic with an LLM or viewed a static fact sheet, participants in the LLM treatment showed significantly reduced conspiracy beliefs in both experiments. We also found evidence of downstream effects of the LLM treatment, observing reduced belief in different conspiracies one to two months later in the wake of subsequent crisis events. These results shed light on the psychology of emerging conspiracies and highlight the potential for scalable, cognitively-focused interventions to counteract misinformation in the immediate aftermath of high-profile societal events.

articles.title: The Morality-Effectiveness Disconnect of Pro-environmental Behaviors
articles.authors: Jareef Martuza; Hege Landsvik
articles.abstract: Not all pro-environmental behaviors are created equal—some are vastly more effective at mitigating climate change than others. Do people judge the more effective behaviors as proportionally more moral? Five main and six supplemental studies (N = 9,247) across five countries reveal a robust morality-effectiveness disconnect: pro-environmental behaviors that rank better on objective climate-mitigation potential rank worse on individual moral judgments. Laypeople fail to predict this pattern, believing that a positive relationship exists. Further, labeling behaviors by climate impact category reduces the morality-effectiveness disconnect, and detailed impact information reverses it and increases policy endorsement of more effective behaviors over less effective behaviors. While the disconnect primarily stems from effectiveness misperceptions that accurate information can mitigate, we find that personal support for less effective behaviors plays an additional role. Thus, people's moral intuition for climate action appears miscalibrated: moral cognition can undermine the collective welfare that such cognition should presumably promote.

articles.title: Identifying effective misperception correction messages to increase public support for biodiversity policies
articles.authors: Sandra Jeanette Geiger; Jeffrey Martin Lees; Mathew P. White
articles.abstract: People often underestimate support for pro-environmental policies. While correcting such misperceptions should, in theory, boost policy support, the evidence remains mixed. To improve message effectiveness, we develop and test a systematic process titration approach based on three stepwise, theoretically informed criteria: messages that target (1) substantial misperceptions of (2) majority positions, which are (3) conceptually close (statistically related) to policy support. Across three preregistered studies in the US (n = 21,600)—a survey, single-message experiments, and a tournament of ten corrective messages—we apply this approach to 32 perceptions of others’ beliefs, emotions, values, policy preferences, and behaviors, to increase support for the UN Convention on Biological Diversity. Criteria 1 and 2 most reliably distinguish effective from ineffective messages (δ = 0.24, 95% CrI [0.11, 0.36]). Contrary to theory and existing research practices, Criterion 3—statistical associations between misperceptions and the outcome—provides no predictive value in identifying effective interventions beyond Criteria 1 and 2. Overall, a two-step titration process approach offers a practical and effective way to identify misperception targets before large-scale implementations.

articles.title: HOW ARE INVISIBLE RELIGIOUS LONGINGS AND HOPES TRIGGERED BY SOCIAL MEDIA AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE?
articles.authors: Bojan Godina
articles.abstract:
This article examines the activation of invisible religious longings and hopes in the
modern digital media landscape. Building on research from 2003–2007, which identified
elements of transcendence in films, video games, and advertising, this study analyzes a
paradigm shift. Whereas offers of transcendence were previously conveyed sporadically
through specific media content, today their activation occurs continuously and in a
highly individualized manner through the algorithmic architecture of social media and
artificial intelligence. Using a proven three-part explanatory model – consisting of the
needs for transcendent identity, perfection, and salvation – this work illustrates how
modern recommender systems exploit human vulnerabilities to lead users into so-called
“rabbit holes.” Drawing on current phenomena such as the digital cult of beauty, the
trend of “Looksmaxxing,” extremist promises of salvation, and the perception of AI as an
omniscient authority (“GPTheology”), the study demonstrates how algorithmic processes
operationalize religious longings.
The article concludes that social media and AI should be viewed as hybrid systems
that form functional equivalents of religious structures, thereby generating a new form of
“implicit transcendence.” The findings call for greater integration of ethical issues and
human rights into the media discourse.

articles.title: The Functional Role of Eye Movements in Episodic Remembering Depends on the Individual and the Memory: Evidence Across the Phantasia Spectrum
articles.authors: Sylvana Brewer; Mikael Johansson; Roger Johansson
articles.abstract:
Eye movements are thought to support episodic remembering by reinstating aspects of the content and relational structure of previous experiences. However, it remains unclear whether this functional role differs across mental imagery phenotypes spanning the spectrum from aphantasia to hyperphantasia. To address this question, we experimentally manipulated eye movements during retrieval in participants sampled broadly across the imagery spectrum.
Gaze reinstatement occurred reliably during free viewing and predicted recollection. Restricting eye movements significantly impaired recollection, providing experimental evidence that the opportunity to move the eyes contributes functionally to episodic remembering. Critically, the benefit of free viewing depended on imagery ability, showing a nonlinear relationship with imagery vividness that was greatest at intermediate levels and reduced toward both ends of the imagery spectrum. Imagery vividness did not systematically predict gaze reinstatement itself, indicating a distinction between spontaneous oculomotor behaviour and its functional contribution to remembering. This relationship became increasingly pronounced with greater visual exploration during encoding: memories with a more extensive visual sampling history showed greater subsequent dependence on eye movements during retrieval. Spatial imagery provided an additional independent source of variation, with individuals high in spatial imagery exhibiting greater impairment when eye movements were restricted.
These findings demonstrate that the functional role of eye movements in episodic remembering is not uniform across mental imagery phenotypes but depends jointly on imagery ability and the extent of visual exploration during encoding. More broadly, they suggest that eye movements constitute a flexible retrieval mechanism whose contribution varies across individuals and memories.

articles.title: Context Matters: Within-Person Effects of Smartphone Use on Momentary Well-Being
articles.authors: Katherine Roehrick; Mahnaz Roshanaei; Serena Jimyn Soh; Sumer Sumeet Vaid; Joanne M. Chung; Joseph Bayer; Gabriella M. Harari
articles.abstract: We adopt a contextual framework to examine the within-person associations between smartphone use and subsequent momentary well-being. In a large intensive mobile sensing and experience sampling study (N = 1,003 young adult; 36,949 observations), we examined the relationship between five broad indicators of well-being (loneliness, stress, sadness, contentment, and energy level), two indicators of smartphone use (frequency and duration of use), and two contextual factors (social and spatial). We found that frequent “check-ins” had a small positive association with momentary well-being: when people unlocked their phones more often than usual, they reported feeling less lonely, less sad, more content, and more energetic. On the other hand, long sessions had a small negative association with momentary well-being: when people spent longer periods of time on their phones than usual, they reported feeling more lonely and more sad, while also feeling less content and less energetic. Moreover, we found that contextual factors were (a) a more important predictor of momentary well-being, and (b) moderated the within-person associations between smartphone use and well-being. Frequent and prolonged smartphone use was more detrimental to momentary well-being when occurring in social settings (around strong or weak ties vs. when alone) and in public or work environments (vs. at home). Overall, we find a relationship between smartphone use and momentary well-being exists, but the direction of this effect is sensitive to context—underscoring the value of a situational approach to media effects research.

articles.title: Too Much, Too Little, or Just Right? Identity Processes and Motivations Explain  Everyday Perceptions of Time Spent on Social Media
articles.authors: Gabriella M. Harari; Serena Jimyn Soh; Zhenchao Hu; Sanaz Talaifar; Alan Meca; Noah Vinoya; Rui Pei; Samantha Jo Grayson; Sumer Sumeet Vaid; Nilam Ram
articles.abstract: Emerging adults use social media—and evaluate their use—while navigating the critical task of identity development. We investigate how evaluations of time spent on social media are associated with (a) individual differences in identity development and (b) situational fluctuations in identity-relevant social media motivations. In our longitudinal field study (N = 2,251; 87,283 observations), emerging adults forming their identity tended to evaluate their social media time as balanced (i.e., the right amount), whereas those evaluating their identity tended to perceive imbalance (i.e., too much or too little time spent). Using social media to connect with others was associated with momentary perceptions of balanced use, whereas doing so to explore personal and professional goals was associated with imbalance. These findings suggest that emerging adults’ evaluations of their time spent on social media may depend on how well use aligns with identity-relevant needs. We discuss implications for psychological and digital well-being.

articles.title: Nothing “Evaluative“ about Evaluative Priming?  Semantic Relatedness Beyond Evaluation Is Not Necessary for a Facilitation of Evaluative Judgements
articles.authors: Manuel Becker; Marie Jakob; Karl Christoph Klauer
articles.abstract: Ever since Zajonc proposed that preferences need no inferences, psychologists have debated whether evaluations can be conceptualized and measured independently of co-activated semantic content. One prominent arena for this debate has been the Evaluative Priming Task, which tracks the effects of conflicting or congruent evaluative relationships between stimuli. Surprisingly, two prior lines of research found that effects of evaluative congruency in the task do not emerge in the absence of additional semantic relationships. This not only conflicts with other findings, but also challenges dominant theoretical accounts of the task, whose assumptions entail that congruency effects should arise irrespectively. In Studies 1 and 2 (Ns=81, 85), we re-examine these two lines of research and show that when vulnerabilities in the original experimental and analytical designs are rectified, evaluative congruency effects do reliably occur (even in the absence of strong semantic relationships). A third study (N=80), that implements strong semantic relationships under especially controlled conditions, also yields reliable congruency effects. In Study 4 (N=81), the trials with low semantic relatedness from the first three studies are combined, replicating consistent and reliable, but small congruency effects. Our results thereby strengthen models that accommodate an independent role of evaluations, and we illustrate how these models might be modified to account for an augmenting influence of semantic relatedness. Currently, in domains for which evaluations and their measurement are integral (like the measurement of race-based evaluations, consumer or health behavior), the pronounced and potentially biasing effects of semantic relatedness remain largely unrecognized as a serious confound.

articles.title: Change in Adaptive Identity Processes and Well-Being Supported by  Self-Reflection and AI-Mediated Reflection in Digital Intervention
articles.authors: Serena Jimyn Soh; Subigya Nepal; Noah Vinoya; Gabriella M. Harari
articles.abstract: Young people are increasingly turning to conversational AI agents for support in figuring out what they want to do with their lives. Reflecting on career goals is characteristic of emerging adulthood (ages 18 to late twenties), a critical time for exploration and commitment to one’s personal and vocational identity. Yet it is unclear whether and how conversational AI agents benefit or hinder the development of positive and coherent identities, which has potential consequences for well-being. Our two pre-registered field experiments (Study 1: N= 165; Study 2: N = 248) tested the efficacy of digital intervention treatments designed to promote adaptive identity processes via career-focused reflection activities. Using an active-controlled RCT design, we assigned participants to either a Self-Reflection or an AI-Mediated Reflection condition. We found that both conditions promoted within-person adaptive change in daily identity exploration and commitment processes on treatment days, compared to no treatment days. However, when comparing the relative efficacy of the two treatments, we found that self-reflection may better facilitate adaptive changes (e.g., increasing identity commitment, decreasing ruminative exploration), compared to AI-mediated reflection. Exploratory analyses also showed that the intervention had positive effects on daily affect and post-intervention eudaimonic well-being, although AI-mediated reflection was less beneficial. Linguistic analysis of the reflection content suggest that the conditions may shape the cognitive and affective experience of reflection in meaningfully different ways. Our discussion contextualizes these findings within the literature on conversational AI agents as a tool for self-development and highlights future directions for research on human-AI interactions.

articles.title: Computational and neural signatures of volatility learning in infancy: Links with temperament and the early caregiving environment
articles.authors: Dimana V. Atanassova; Nemes Zsuzsanna; Marlene Meyer; Sabine Hunnius
articles.abstract:
Infants demonstrate a remarkable ability to learn from statistical patterns. Yet, in probabilistic environments, successful learning requires distinguishing random variability from true changes in the underlying contingency (i.e. volatility). However, the extent to which successful volatility learning in infancy is modulated by environmental and temperamental differences is still unclear, as well as the extent to which infant neural processing reflects learning from changes. To answer these questions, we investigated the computational and neural basis of volatility learning in 11-month-old infants and examined how temperament (Infant Behavior Questionnaire-Revised; Very Short Form) and features of the early caregiving environment (Comprehensive Early Childhood Parenting Questionnaire) shape individual differences in this process.
Infants (N=77, Mage=331.13±15.25 days; 32 girls, 45 boys) observed a probabilistic environment in which the most likely location of a target periodically changed. Infants learned these contingencies, as reflected in their anticipatory looking, demonstrating sensitivity to environmental volatility. To characterize the computational processes underlying this learning, we used a Hierarchical Gaussian Filter model, which captures how learners update their beliefs about both the current state of the environment and its volatility. Prediction errors derived from this model, in combination with anticipation accuracy, predicted EEG activity 588–714 ms after feedback across a broad fronto-central region, providing evidence that the cognitive mechanisms captured by the model are represented in the infant brain. 
Additionally, we found that individual differences in volatility learning were primarily captured by model-derived change sensitivity: infants with a stronger change sensitivity detected reversals in the volatile environment better and adapted their behavior more rapidly. Change sensitivity was positively related to IBQ Effortful Control, suggesting infants with stronger regulatory capacities also updated their beliefs about volatility in a more optimal fashion. 
infants with higher Effortful Control detected environmental reversals more rapidly and showed more optimal belief updating. Finally, Positive Discipline was associated with higher Effortful Control, although its indirect association with change sensitivity was not significant. Finally, in a Structural Equation Model, we found that higher Effortful Control was predicted by stronger Positive Discipline, although the indirect pathway to change sensitivity was not significant. 
Together, these findings identify early computational and neural signatures of hierarchical volatility learning and highlight emerging temperament and caregiving influences on adaptive learning in infancy.

articles.title: Virtual Empathy Scale (VES): Development and Psychometric Validation Among Indian Young Adults
articles.authors: Aishu S Gowda; Akash Nethravathi Raju; Dhiksha J
articles.abstract:
This research was targeted at constructing and testing the virtual empathy scale (VES) that is intended to assess the empathy that is realized in the online communication between young college-going adults. It is based on multidimensional empathy models and is composed of three: empathic expression, cognitive empathy, and affective empathy. There was a generation of a pool of 49 items, and it underwent the face and content validity examination by experts reducing the pool to 41 items. Then we performed EFA on a sample of 421 college going students. This gave a 32-item scale, and good factor loading. We subsequently applied CFA to another sample of 331 students, and this supported the three-factor model, with reasonable fit statistics (CFI= .90, TLI=.899, RMSEA=.061). To conduct the reliability analysis, it was demonstrated that the results had high internal consistency (α > 0.87, ω > 0.87) in all three factors. The scale demonstrated convergent validity as demonstrated in high factor loading and composite reliability, however, the average variance extracted was a little below the optimal thresholds. And lastly, discriminant validity with some factor correlation approaching upper limits was determined with the use of HTMT. This scale has demonstrated high psychometric characteristics and is a potentially useful instrument to measure empathy in digital communication and can be used in a variety of psychological studies, online learning, and digital wellbeing intervention.
Keywords: virtual empathy, digital communication, psychometric validation, exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, young adults.

articles.title: Digital media intervention research for young people across geo-cultural contexts: A critical review of bias and representation
articles.authors: I. Chaplinska; Peter Nikken; Sophie Mary; Carlo Schuengel
articles.abstract: Children's digital wellbeing develops within unequal conditions of access, skills, support, and institutional response, which shape which digital needs are recognised, evaluated, and made actionable. Evaluated digital media interventions may inform policy; yet when evaluations concentrate in particular regions, dimensions of wellbeing, and delivery settings, the evidence base offers a structurally partial view, leaving some children, contexts, and experiences outside the scope of institutional action. This paper examines what the evaluated evidence base reveals about whose digital wellbeing becomes institutionally visible and actionable across geo-cultural contexts. Drawing on 120 publications reporting 131 intervention instances across 38 countries (2006–2024), we apply the Global Kids Online risks-and-opportunities framework and treat the literature as a selective record of institutional legibility. Four findings stand out. Evaluative visibility is geographically concentrated: nearly half of all country-linked observations come from five countries, with Africa and South America minimally represented. Risk-oriented interventions consistently outnumber opportunity-focused ones, positioning children as users to be protected rather than as participants, creators, and rights-bearing subjects. Three-quarters were delivered through schools, while family, peer, community, and platform-proximate contexts remain marginal. Participant characteristics – including ethnicity (14%) and neurodivergence (4%) – are rarely specified, rendering some groups analytically invisible and digital inequalities largely unexamined. The evaluated field is thus shaped by what is institutionally feasible rather than by socially needed responses. Policy built on it, therefore, risks reproducing the same partiality. Strengthening evaluation capacity in under-represented regions, broadening opportunity-oriented agendas, and developing non-school-based models are necessary steps towards a more equitable and child-centred evidence base.

articles.title: The Conflict Device: A Control Theory Model of Problematic Digital Media Use
articles.authors: Warren mansell; Amy Mowle; Louis Trouchet; Mehdi Zemestani; Jason Sharbanee; Tauseef Gulrez; Danielle Einstein
articles.abstract: Digital media refers to smartphone use, social media, video-gaming and artificial intelligence among other forms, which are becoming increasingly integrated across platforms. Whilst there are widely recognised benefits, their documented harms, especially pre-adulthood, are leading to statutory restrictions across the world. For most adult users exempt from any bans, it is critical to understand the contexts and vulnerabilities within which digital media use is experienced as problematic, to inform individual, community and device-focused interventions. We critically review contemporary research and theories to develop an integrative model across digital media based on perceptual control theory. Through conceptualising digital media as a closed-loop extension of the self via hyper-efficient, dynamically adaptive and digitally amplified feedback pathways, we illustrate the mechanisms through which restricted attention utilises neural reorganisation to entrench habitual control. This entails a range of additional vicious cycles maintaining distress. As an exit from this state, we specify the factors that support the development and maintenance of a mindset of metacontrol flexibility (MCF) associated with tolerance of goal conflict and the effective use of fringe consciousness. The seeds of the MCF are the diverse opportunities to attend to, and meet, basic needs via restorative factors in the offline world.

articles.title: From TikTok Keeps Me Going to TikTok Keeps Me Unknowing: Profiling Adolescents Based on Their Online Short Video Use for Mental Health Information and Support
articles.authors: Marie Geertrude Oldeman; Bram Orobio de Castro; Melanie de Looper; Eva van Reijmersdal; Eline Suzanne Smit
articles.abstract:
Introduction: There is much debate on how online short videos (OSVs) on social media (e.g. TikToks) may interact with adolescent mental health. For example, there is concern about adolescents using these videos for mental health information and support. The goal of this study was to identify groups of adolescents based on their OSV use for mental health information and support, and to examine differences between these groups.

Methods: We conducted an online cross-sectional survey in 2024 among Dutch adolescents with and without mental health complaints (general sample: N = 1532; Mage = 14.20; 53.92% female, 44.97% male, .85% other; clinical subsample: N = 239; Mage = 15.70; 65.69% female, 34.31% male, 0.00% other). We inquired them about their OSV use, mental health, mental health literacy and attachment representations. 

Results: In both samples, we identified three profiles: Regular users, Occasional users, and Non-users. In the clinical subsample, we additionally identified two groups: Intermittent users and Support seekers. In both samples, profiles characterized by higher consumption of mental health information and/or support via OSVs experienced more severe mental health concerns, more insecure attachment representations, and greater mental health literacy. 

Conclusions: These results show that different adolescents use online short videos differently. There is a need for targeted research and interventions, as not all adolescents use OSVs equally and may thus ultimately experience different positive and negative effects.

articles.title: Effects of Shot Size on Social Impressions in Humans and Multimodal AI
articles.authors: Hua Hwang; Dahyeon Kang; Sung Park
articles.abstract: The same person can be judged differently depending on how tightly they are framed. As image- and video-based evaluations become increasingly common in settings such as hiring, screening, and interviews, this raises a practical question: does shot size change social-impression ratings in human observers and a multimodal large language model (GPT-4o)? From one master photograph of each of eight adults with neutral expressions, we created medium-shot (MS), close-up (CU), and extreme-close-up (ECU) versions while holding expression, pose, lighting, perspective, and output size constant. Sixty participants rated all eight identities in a balanced design, and a fixed GPT-4o configuration evaluated each of the 24 images in ten stateless repetitions. Both evaluators rated the same five outcomes: Trust, Competence, Likeability, Discomfort, and Approachability. In human crossed linear mixed models, tighter framing increased Discomfort and decreased the other four outcomes; all five MS–ECU contrasts remained significant after Holm correction. Discomfort showed the largest human MS–ECU change (b = +0.600), whereas Competence showed the smallest (b = −0.221) and decreased in 5 of 8 identities. GPT-4o showed the same overall direction of change across all five outcomes, and all five identity-level MS–ECU sign-flip tests remained significant after Holm correction. The predicted larger CU–ECU change was not supported in humans, and no GPT-4o outcome showed a significant transition difference. For Discomfort, the larger observed change occurred from MS to CU in humans but from CU to ECU in GPT-4o. Across both evaluators, tighter framing produced less favorable social impressions and greater Discomfort for the same neutral identities.

articles.title: A Bayesian Psychometric Item-Level Resource for Korean Early Vocabulary and Developmental Measurement
articles.authors: Jun Ho Chai; Eon-Suk Ko
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Parent-report vocabulary measures are widely used to study early language development, but CDI-based analyses typically summarize children’s responses using total vocabulary scores. This approach provides limited information about how individual words differ in developmental timing and psychometric function. This study develops a Korean item-level vocabulary resource that jointly characterizes developmental emergence, item response theory parameters, and input frequency.
Method: Using Korean Words & Gestures comprehension and Words & Sentences production data from Wordbank, we estimated Bayesian age of acquisition (AoA) at the 50% response threshold. We then examined associations between Bayesian AoA estimates, Bayesian two-parameter item response theory item difficulty and discrimination parameters, and corpus-derived Korean input frequency. The stability of Bayesian AoA and item response theory estimates was evaluated through repeated child-level resampling.
Results: Bayesian AoA and item response theory estimates were stable across repeated resampling. Words that emerged earlier also tended to be psychometrically easier, and more frequent words tended to emerge earlier and show lower latent difficulty. However, AoA and input frequency were only weakly associated with item discrimination, indicating that developmental timing and input frequency do not fully explain how informative a word is for distinguishing children along the latent vocabulary scale.
Conclusion: Early Korean vocabulary items vary along partially distinct developmental and psychometric dimensions. The resource characterizes Korean CDI words by AoA, latent difficulty, discrimination, and input frequency, providing a foundation for item-level analyses of Korean early vocabulary development to relate measurement properties to theories of lexical development.

articles.title: Toward Personalizing a Digital Intervention for Co-Occurring Cannabis Use and Binge Eating: An Idiographic Network Analysis
articles.authors: Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Sukriti Ghosh; Benjamin Kaveladze; Jacob Borodovsky; Alan Budney; Nicholas C. Jacobson
articles.abstract: Cannabis use (CU) and binge eating (BE) frequently co-occur, yet existing interventions treat each behavior in isolation. This pilot study evaluated whether individually tailored (idiographic) symptom network models better characterize momentary risk for CU and BE than a single group-level (nomothetic) model, as a first step toward a personalized just-in-time adaptive intervention (JITAI) for co-occurring cannabis use disorder and binge-spectrum eating disorders. Thirty adults with clinically significant CU and BE completed 28 days of ecological momentary assessment surveys four times daily, assessing CU, BE, and shared risk factors (e.g., emotion dysregulation, distress intolerance). Nomothetic and idiographic networks were estimated using multilevel and graphical vector autoregression, respectively, and compared on model fit and structural similarity. Idiographic models fit participants' own data better than the nomothetic model for every participant with an estimable person-specific network (n = 29) and for every symptom node. Correspondence between idiographic and nomothetic temporal pathways was, on average, weak (Mean r = .06; range: −.17 to .37). The nomothetic model nonetheless identified plausible bridge pathways linking urges for CU, loss-of-control over CU, and cognitive restraint over CU to subsequent BE. Person-to-person variability was greatest for pathways connecting shared regulatory processes to eating-disorder-specific outcomes. These findings support a personalized, network-informed approach to intervention development for co-occurring CU and BE, suggesting that idiographic assessment may be most valuable at the specific junctures where transdiagnostic risk factors intersect with disorder-specific behavior.

articles.title: Measuring the effective polarity and level along the excitation patterns produced by focussed cochlear-implant stimulation
articles.authors: Robert P. Carlyon; Francois Guerit; John M. Deeks
articles.abstract:
Three experiments estimated the effective polarity and level of neural activation
produced by trains of “baseline” symmetric biphasic pulses, where the order of the phases
of each pulse was anodic-cathodic (AC) or cathodic-anodic (CA). Detection thresholds were
measured for trains of quadrupolar-mode anodic-leading pseudomonophasic probe pulses,
where each pulse was presented immediately after a baseline pulse or in quiet. Thresholds
were substantially lower in the presence than in the absence of the baseline in several
conditions, including for monopolar baselines in CA order. This unmasking was also
observed with wide-bipolar (BP+10) and wide-tripolar (TP=3, TP+5) baselines, whenever
the probe was presented to an electrode where the second phases of the baseline pulses
were anodic. Because the polarity of the baseline varied across the electrode array for BP
and TP stimuli, this allowed us to measure reversals in the effective polarity of the
baseline stimulus along its excitation pattern. The unmasking is attributed to constructive
charge interactions between the first (anodic) phase of each probe pulse with the second
phase of the preceding baseline pulse. The results are compared to voltage profiles for
each baseline measured along the electrode array, and are discussed in terms of potential
implications for the development of improved cochlear-implant stimulation methods.

articles.title: Prospective associations between depressive symptoms and cognitive function remain uncertain: A reanalysis of Wang et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Wang et al. reported longitudinal findings that were interpreted as evidence that depressive symptoms contribute to subsequent deterioration in cognitive function. However, statistically significant cross-lagged coefficients are not, by themselves, sufficient evidence for a genuine prospective effect because similar estimates can arise through alternative statistical processes. Using simulated data constructed to reproduce the sample size and correlation structure reported by Wang et al., we assessed the stability of the reported conclusions across several defensible analytical specifications. Results differed markedly depending on the model employed. Some specifications suggested positive prospective associations, whereas others indicated negative or statistically non-significant relationships. When estimates from all specifications were synthesized using meta-analytic procedures, no significant overall effects emerged. These findings indicate that the evidence presented by Wang et al. does not provide a stable foundation for concluding that depressive symptoms prospectively influence cognitive function. Consistent with recommendations from the multiverse-analysis literature, conclusions should be based on evidence aggregated across reasonable analytical alternatives rather than on the results of a single model.

articles.title: Acculturation as a Situated Transactional Process
articles.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu
articles.abstract: Acculturation research commonly links broad preferences for heritage-culture maintenance and participation in the receiving society to psychological and sociocultural adjustment. Yet meta-analytic and longitudinal evidence shows that these associations are often weak, heterogeneous, and limited over time, suggesting that broad preferences alone cannot explain why cultural engagement leads to different outcomes across situations. This conceptual article develops a situated transactional framework within a broader complex dynamic systems account. Building on established work showing that acculturation is contextual, domain-specific, and interactional, the framework specifies how these influences come together within concrete encounters. It proposes a process in which locally relevant conditions shape appraisal, the mobilization of culturally patterned resources, response, relational and institutional reception, multidimensional outcomes, and feedback into later encounters. The article also distinguishes the adaptation process, understood as the continuing person-environment transaction, from adaptation outcomes, including psychological, sociocultural, relational, and externally observed consequences. By organizing these elements into an explicit recursive architecture, the framework generates testable predictions about context-specific responses, reception, multidimensional outcomes, learned response patterns, and structural change. It thereby provides a concrete empirical agenda for testing whether these mechanisms improve explanation and prediction beyond broad-orientation and contextual-moderation accounts.

articles.title: Reframing Acculturation:  When (and Why) Acculturation Science Warrants a Systems Explanation
articles.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu; Karen Phalet
articles.abstract: Acculturation has always been understood as a process of change, and contemporary research examines that change from several complementary perspectives, including developmental trajectories, reciprocal intergroup relations, ecological contexts, situated cultural processes, and multilevel social change. The field therefore contains many elements of a systems account without a shared architecture for relating them. This article offers a selective integrative review and metatheoretical synthesis using complex dynamic systems theory (CDST). CDST provides a coordinating framework that complements existing acculturation theories and encounter-level models of adaptation. It distinguishes five explanatory questions distributed across different traditions: what form change takes, who or what influences whom, how change moves across levels of organisation, where broader conditions become relevant, and how processes unfolding at different rates become linked. We organise these questions through five dimensions: nonlinear dynamism, relational reciprocity, multilevel emergence, situated adaptation, and multiscale temporality. Together, they provide a way to examine how patterns of acculturative change depend on prior experience, relationships, local conditions, levels of organisation, and processes unfolding at different rates. For each type of systems claim, we specify a linear-additive alternative and the evidence needed to distinguish between them. Power differences and prior history are treated as conditions that can shape how the system operates and changes. The framework therefore shifts attention from average associations between acculturation variables and outcomes toward explaining how acculturative change is organised, when different processes become connected, and when a systems explanation adds value beyond conventional models.

articles.title: Apparent kindling in a washboard potential model of mood dynamics
articles.authors: Jihwan Myung
articles.abstract: The kindling hypothesis proposes that repeated stressors or mood episodes leave persistent sensitizing traces that lower the threshold for subsequent episodes. Evidence in bipolar disorder is mixed, and recurrence alone does not establish such persistent change. Here I propose a phenomenological landscape in which progression can appear causally linked without being so. Mood state moves on a multi-well washboard potential landscape. Kindling would persistently change the geometry of the landscape, and circadian and sleep-related inputs reversibly tilt it. In an illustrative four-well landscape, two inner wells represent normal daily mood variation, while two outer wells represent depression-like and mania-like states. The circadian phase then changes the accessibility of existing states without altering the landscape itself. This distinction provides a complementary account of two clinical observations: the diurnal direction of mood switches reported in rapid-cycling bipolar disorder, and the rapid but transient remission of depression during wake therapy. Circadian organization should add predictive information beyond episode history, and the tilted washboard model suggests chronotherapeutic interventions timed to internal circadian phase.

articles.title: Interactional dynamics in online spoken conversations with people who do and do not stutter
articles.authors: Lotte Eijk; Emilia Horn; Buhan Guo; Sophie Meekings
articles.abstract:
Everyday conversation involves precise co-ordination between speakers as they take turns, a collaborative effort that is necessarily affected by motor speech difficulties such as stuttering. People who stutter (PWS) report difficulties in conversational interaction that have a significant impact on quality of life. However, relatively little research exists on turn-taking in this population.
This study examines sixty conversations between ten pairs of people who do not stutter (PWNS), and ten PWNS-PWS pairs. Conversations were analysed for turn-taking speed, utterance length, number of backchannels, interruptions and completions - factoring in speaker disfluency and the fluency of the utterance being responded to. The pitch profile of interruptions and completions was also analysed.
Across groups, talkers responded most to disfluent utterances and more disfluent speakers had conversations with longer gap durations. PWNS with a higher stuttering severity score had conversations with longer turns, and PWS with a higher stuttering severity score had conversations with more interruptions compared to more fluent speakers. Interruptions were produced with higher pitch than completions, but this difference narrowed as stuttering severity increased. Overall, results suggest that disfluency affects interactional dynamics regardless of whether talkers have a motor speech disability, but there are additional challenges in interaction for PWS.

articles.title: Using Text Embedding Models to Quantify Strategies in Multilingual Verbal Fluency: Evidence from Young and Older Adults
articles.authors: Huitian Chen; Chin Tung Wu; Zhengyuan Liu; Haoyun Zhang
articles.abstract: Verbal fluency tasks, particularly semantic fluency, assess language and executive functions, yet conventional measures may not fully capture cross-language retrieval dynamics or their cognitive correlates in multilingual speakers. We developed an automated approach that represents consecutive responses as vectors and derives Mean Semantic Distance (MSD), the average distance between adjacent responses, and the Standard Deviation of Semantic Distance (SD), reflecting variability in those distances. Experiment 1 evaluated four candidate models.
