BGE-M3 was selected for strong agreement with human semantic judgments, convergence with another psychologically plausible model, and less compressed distance geometry. Experiment 2 examined 45 young Cantonese, Mandarin, and English multilingual adults. Conventional fluency measures showed the strongest performance in Cantonese and the weakest in English. In contrast, MSD was highest in Mandarin and lowest in English, whereas SD was lower in English than in Cantonese and Mandarin. Proactive control was differentially associated with Mean Cluster Size across languages, while processing speed–MSD associations differed between Cantonese and Mandarin. Stroop interference showed no reliable language-specific modulation. Experiment 3 compared the young adults with 26 older Cantonese and Mandarin bilingual adults. Older adults produced fewer words, but the cross-language MSD and SD patterns were broadly similar across age groups. Proactive control showed selective age- and language-dependent associations with Total Number of Words and Mean Cluster Size, whereas processing speed showed no reliable three-way interaction with MSD. Together, these findings show that continuous semantic distance measures complement traditional fluency scores by revealing retrieval patterns and cognitive associations that conventional measures may miss.

articles.title: Care Versus Friction: Water Sustainability Attitudes, Conservation Behaviour and the Intention–Action Gap Among Young Singaporeans
articles.authors: Gemma Anne Calvert; Krishnan Menon; Steven Graham; James Breeze; Zakhran Khan; Ganesh Honnur
articles.abstract: Singapore is among the most water-stressed nations in the world, yet has engineered a resilient supply through its Four National Taps strategy and its reclaimed water programme, NEWater. That system depends not only on infrastructure but on a population willing to value, conserve and accept unconventional water. Using an artificial-intelligence powered conversational interviewing platform, we conducted 498 semi-structured interviews with Singapore residents aged 15 to 35, of which 497 were analysable, covering conservation habits, tap and recycled water attitudes, smart monitoring technology, shopping behaviour, embodied water footprints, and the ethics of transboundary water consumption. Pro-environmental belief approached saturation: 92% reported a recent water-saving action, 64% were comfortable drinking recycled water, and 77% were interested in smart water meters. What constrained further action was not indifference but the accumulation of small frictions: an unfamiliar word, an inconvenient routine, an unclear price differential, a perceived trade-off with comfort. The pattern was sharpest in the ethical domain, where 78% judged overseas water shortages unfair yet only 34% said this would definitely change their purchasing. Coding cost, environmental value and comfort independently, we find these considerations co-occur within individuals rather than distinguishing between them: 322 of 497 respondents held all three, and only 30 held one alone. Message targeting therefore cannot resolve a tension respondents hold within themselves. We further identify a sequencing effect, whereby household effort is judged negligible until larger consumers act, and a verification gap, in which willingness to credit environmental claims is limited by the absence of checkable evidence rather than by distrust. We propose that the operative tension for this cohort is care versus friction rather than care versus apathy, and derive design principles accordingly.

articles.title: The pitfalls of pay-to-play morality
articles.authors: Ryan W. Carlson; Molly Crockett
articles.abstract: Morality is often measured in dollars and cents. Economic games and charitable giving tasks frame giving money to strangers as moral and keeping money as selfish. This ‘pay-to-play’ paradigm has grown popular with the rise of online experiments, yet its underlying assumptions often go untested. Here, we present data that complicate the interpretation of this paradigm. We invited US crowdworkers (N=1384) to make charitable decisions and measured not just their choices, but the motives and meanings they ascribed to those choices. We found that crowdworkers’ most common motive for keeping money was acute financial need (e.g., struggling to pay for medical care or groceries). These individuals reported significantly lower incomes, and did not view their decisions to keep money as selfish. Third-party judges (N=140) agreed that keeping money in economic tasks out of financial need was not selfish, and considered such tasks to be an unreasonable measure of altruism and selfishness. Finally, we found that crowdworkers reporting financial need were unresponsive to standard interventions designed to motivate generosity. Overall, these findings challenge the assumption that keeping money uniformly reflects selfishness, and raise ethical and practical questions about how experimenters should define, measure, and motivate moral behavior.

articles.title: Word Familiarity Norms as a Test Case:  Improving Methodological Standards in Word Norming Research
articles.authors: Maria Montefinese; Erin Michelle Buchanan; Irene Di Pietro; Giada Viviani; Begum Ulku; Silvia Benavides-Varela; Ettore Ambrosini
articles.abstract: Normative databases of word properties are essential for experimental psycholinguistics, yet methodological heterogeneity limits their reproducibility and comparability. Subjective word experience, particularly familiarity and subjective frequency, is inconsistently operationalized across studies. Here, we reviewed 61 studies spanning 15 languages, analyzing construct definitions, rating instructions, sampling, data cleaning, validation, and data accessibility. We found substantial conceptual and methodological inconsistencies, including frequent use of familiarity labels for frequency-based judgments, reliance on homogeneous student samples, and limited data transparency. At the same time, recent studies show improvements in methodological rigor and open science practices. Building on these findings, we propose evidence-based recommendations and a practical checklist for improving transparency, comparability, and representativeness in word norming research. We also introduce a scalable framework integrating AI-generated estimates with targeted human validation to enhance lexical coverage while preserving interpretability. These contributions support more cumulative, reproducible, and methodologically transparent advances in psycholinguistics.

articles.title: Updating rigor in psychological mixed methods research: A systematic methodological guidance review
articles.authors: Tamarinde Laura Haven; Martina S Isaksen Duque; Amirali Rezazadeh; Adira Daniel
articles.abstract: Mixed methods research (MMR) is increasingly used in psychology, yet strengthening rigor remains challenging because of fragmented guidance and new approaches in MMR practice such as co-creation, open science, and emerging technologies. We conducted a preregistered systematic methodological review to investigate (1) how rigor is defined and conceptualised in the context of MMR and (2) what strategies are used to ensure or demonstrate rigor in MMR? Searches of databases, preprint archives, leading mixed methods journals, citation networks, reporting guidelines, journal instructions to authors, empirical psychology articles, and methodological textbooks yielded 345 included sources. From these sources, we extracted 236 interpretations of rigor definitions and 1,698 rigor strategies. The definitions were synthesized into four interdependent components: critical reflection, consistent set-up within and across study strands, grounding in paradigmatic and theoretical foundations, and meaningful integration. The extracted strategies were consolidated into 90 unique practices organized across 10 research-lifecycle categories: assembling, framing, reflecting, co-creating, designing, collecting, analysing, integrating, concluding, and reporting. Findings indicate that rigor in MMR cannot be reduced to applying separate quantitative and qualitative quality criteria or to compliance with a universal checklist. Instead, rigor depends on coherent, context-sensitive methodological decision-making. The definition and strategies provide psychologists with a flexible blueprint for designing, conducting, evaluating, and reporting rigorous MMR.

articles.title: Shared research materials in psychology are widely downloaded but often difficult to reuse
articles.authors: Daniel S Quintana
articles.abstract: Open science reforms have made posting data and code common, but are shared materials actually used, and easily reused? Treating download counts of Open Science Framework (OSF) supplements as a usage index, I analysed 1,660 articles from four psychology journals (Cognition, Psychological Science, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, Journal of Memory and Language) across three years (2015, 2020, 2025). OSF sharing rose from 9% in 2015 to 52% in 2025. Among 392 papers with download data, materials were downloaded a median of 152 times; only 1% went undownloaded. Download volume was associated with citation count and altmetric attention. Availability did not ensure easy reuse: only 40% of repositories provided documentation, 34% were flagged for a hard-coded file path, and 42% referenced a missing file — shortcomings that did not improve as sharing grew. Altogether, shared materials are being used, but often not easily reusable.

articles.title: Beauty Care as a Self-Compassion Intervention for Family Caregivers of Care Recipients with Dementia: A Preliminary Community-Based Study
articles.authors: Hana Sakurai; Tomoko Wakui; Fumiko Miyamae; Riko Nakayama; Mutsuko Okamura; Kumiko Fukasawa; Chiaki Ura; Tsuyoshi Okamura
articles.abstract:
Background: Family caregivers of care recipients with dementia often experience substantial stress. Self-compassion and self-efficacy have been identified as modifiable factors that may help caregivers cope with stress more adaptively. Beauty care, which encourages self-attention, may offer a practical and accessible approach to fostering self-compassion and self-efficacy; however, empirical evidence in caregiving contexts remains limited.
Objective: This preliminary study examined the psychological effects of a community-based beauty care programme on self-compassion and caregiving self-efficacy and subjective health status among family caregivers of care recipients with dementia.
Methods: A single-group pre–post design was employed. The programme consisted of a single-session beauty care intervention, including stretching, facial massage, skin care, and makeup, delivered collaboratively by Shiseido, Urban Renaissance Agency, and Tokyo Metropolitan Institute for Geriatrics and Gerontology. Self-compassion was assessed using the Self-Kindness subscale of the Japanese version of the Self-Compassion Scale, and caregiving self-efficacy was measured using the Self-Efficacy for Obtaining Respite subscale of the Revised Scale for Caregiving Self-Efficacy. Subjective health status was measured with a single item. Pre- and post-intervention scores were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
Results: The final analysis included 8 participants. A marginally significant increase in self-kindness was observed after programme participation. No significant change was found in caregiving self-efficacy for obtaining respite and subjective health status.
Discussion: The absence of significant change in caregiving self-efficacy and subjective health status may reflect the brief, single-session nature of the programme, which may be insufficient to affect skill- or health-based outcomes. In contrast, the marginally significant increase in self-kindness suggests that emotionally oriented outcomes may be more responsive to short-term interventions. Future programmes might incorporate more targeted, skill-based components alongside beauty care to address both the emotional and practical dimensions of caregiver well-being.

articles.title: Shared Dimensions, Divergent Patterns: Multidimensional Well-Being Among Cultural Majority and Minoritized Adolescents
articles.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu; Jozefien De Leersnyder
articles.abstract: Adolescents adapt constantly to their social environments, which can support certain functions while limiting others. In intercultural contexts, adolescents share institutions but hold different social positions and cultural references. Consequently, similar overall well-being scores can mask entirely different combinations of health, relationships, and material conditions—a limitation of single total scores. Well-being and acculturation research approach this problem differently. Well-being research provides broad theories but typically focuses on global indicators within Western majority samples, while acculturation research studies adaptation in intercultural contexts but primarily examines minorities and separates psychological adjustment from sociocultural competence. Researchers currently lack a common multidimensional framework to capture well-being variations among adolescents sharing an intercultural environment. We addressed this gap in 1,385 Belgian-majority and Turkish–Moroccan minoritized adolescents using exploratory and multigroup factor analyses, which supported a broadly comparable five-domain structure. This demonstrates that a common framework can apply across groups while accommodating meaningful differences in how well-being is experienced and organized. Item-level differences formed a mixed profile rather than a consistent advantage for either group. Cross-sectional Gaussian graphical models revealed differences in overall edge-weight structure and global strength, with greater aggregate connectivity in the Turkish–Moroccan network, though no individual edge difference survived correction. Across both groups, the strongest associations clustered within domains alongside cross-domain links. These findings suggest that adolescent well-being is better understood as a multidimensional system than as a single score: shared dimensions can coexist with different profiles and relational organization. Longitudinal research is needed to determine whether these patterns reflect contextual conditions, cultural orientations, or their interplay.

articles.title: Numerical resolution can exceed measurement precision in psychometric score reporting
articles.authors: Takenari Fujio; Hiromi Fujio
articles.abstract: Scores are routinely reported at a numerical resolution finer than the precision supported by the underlying measurement process. We develop a framework linking this display–measurement mismatch to the psychometric conditions required to sustain fine distinctions and to a testable behavioural account of overadaptation to uncertain evaluation metrics. Using classical test theory and item response theory, we quantify the conditions under which distinctions at the 0.01-standard-deviation scale—equivalent to 0.1 points on the Japanese hensachi scale—could be measured rather than merely printed. Under classical test theory, reliability must approach unity: about 0.9999 for the standard error of measurement to equal 0.1 hensachi points, and about 0.999993 for the full 95% interval width to fall within 0.1 points. Idealized item-response calculations require thousands of highly informative, locally targeted items, while finite-bank simulations show that 0.01-SD precision, where attained at all, is strongly ability-dependent. These results distinguish numerical resolution from psychometric precision and motivate a preregistered behavioural programme, supported by formal operating characteristics, to test whether fine display resolution inflates perceived certainty and alters decisions. The framework provides a quantitative basis both for score reporting and for studying how people adapt to uncertain scores.

articles.title: Perceptual adaptation to human-likeness in voices
articles.authors: Christine Nussbaum; Sebastian Goerke; Ibrahim Vefa Arslan; Stefan R. Schweinberger
articles.abstract: With synthetic voices now being a part of everyday life, it is important to understand how the perception of synthetic voices is shaped and modified through exposure. Therefore, we employed an adaptation paradigm to test whether perception of human-likeness is amenable to short-term perceptual encounters. In three experiments, we presented morphed target voices on a human-synthetic-continuum in three conditions: without prior adaptation, and after repeated exposure to adaptor voices that all were either synthetic or human. Experiment 1 (N = 26) was conducted online, Experiment 2 (N = 31) was a full replication in the lab, and Experiment 3 (N = 36) employed an adjusted procedure with blocked and reduced adaptor exposure to test the robustness of effects. In all experiments, we observed consistent contrastive aftereffects: After adaptation to synthetic voices, ambiguous voices were more often classified as human. After adaptation to human voices, the same ambiguous voices were more often classified as synthetic. Intriguingly, in Experiment 1 and 2, contrastive aftereffects were even larger in trials which employed digital caricatures (i.e., 25%-exaggerated human or synthetic voices) as adaptors, even though caricatures themselves were not consistently rated as more human (or synthetic, respectively) compared to original voices. While the adaptation effect survived the adjusted procedure (Experiment 3), substantial modulations by caricatured adaptors were no longer observed. Together, these findings provide robust evidence that impressions of vocal human-likeness are not only determined by the acoustic features but are the result of a complex interplay with listeners and their recent perceptual experiences.

articles.title: Cracking the Code: Grant Writing for Health Psychology Scholars
articles.authors: Tugce Varol; Thomas Gültzow; Sanne Raghoebar; Kristina Pfeffer; Patrick Stefan Höhener; Rory Coyne; James A Green; Katie Newby; Benjamin Schüz; Eline Suzanne Smit
articles.abstract: Research grants form a cornerstone for enabling research, providing researchers with the funding and support necessary to perform research, purchase tools, and form teams. Most post-PhD early- and mid-career scholars will be required to develop research grant writing as a core professional competency, and will be — at least partly — evaluated on their ability to successfully obtain research funding by employers and academic promotion committees. Drawing on insights from an EHPS EMPOWER 2025 pre-conference workshop and a subsequent webinar on the topic, this piece serves as a practical guide designed to help health psychology scholars navigate the funding landscape and write highly competitive research proposals, covering key areas such as idea generation, aligning ideas with funding opportunities and grant writing.

articles.title: Partisans are more likely to entrench their beliefs in misinformation when political outgroup members correct claims
articles.authors: Diego A. Reinero; Elizabeth Ann Harris; Steve Rathje; Annie Duke; Jay Joseph Van Bavel
articles.abstract:
Misinformation has become a global issue with potentially dire consequences (e.g., election
results, COVID-19 vaccines, international conflicts). The most common strategy to reduce
beliefs in misinformation is to issue corrections or fact-checks. However, fact-checks are often
ineffective for polarized issues and there has been debate over whether misinformation
corrections sometimes "backfire," causing people to become more entrenched in misinformation.
Across three experiments (N = 1,217) we identify a key feature – the partisan identity of the
source – that explains when corrections will be effective and when they will be most likely to
backfire. We found that while corrections work on average, backfires still occurred 23% of the
time and were 52% more likely to occur when the correction came from a political outgroup vs.
ingroup member – leaving people with more entrenched beliefs in misinformation. Indeed, the
effect of partisan bias on initial belief in misinformation was 5x larger than the effect of
corrections. Partisan bias was most prominent and corrections were least effective when famous
politicians were involved. In sum, corrections have small effects compared to partisan identity
congruence, and sometimes backfire–especially if they come from a political outgroup member.

articles.title: Negative Urgency, Not Negative Affect, Mediates the Association Between Sleep Problems and Eating Disorder Symptoms
articles.authors: Victoria Franco; Emily R. Linn; Noa A. Bregmann; Stacey M. Schaefer; Richard Davidson; James I. Hudson; Kristin Javaras
articles.abstract:
Objective: There is increasing evidence suggesting that sleep problems may cause alterations in
eating behavior (e.g., poor sleep quality is linked to eating disorders (EDs) and ED symptoms).
However, little is known about the mechanisms by which sleep problems may increase ED
symptoms. Sleep deprivation has been linked to elevated negative urgency (NU; the tendency to
act rashly in response to extreme negative affect [NA]), and NA. Both are consistently linked to
higher ED symptoms and potentially mediate the association between sleep problems and ED
symptoms. This study examined whether NU and NA mediate the relationship between sleep
problems and ED symptoms. Method: Female-identifying introductory psychology students at a
midwestern university (n = 119) completed self-report measures of impulsivity (UPPS-P), ED
symptoms (Eating Disorder Diagnostic Scale), and sleep problems (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality
Index), and a task-based measure of NU (total commission errors for negatively-valenced
distractors in the CANTAB Affective Go/No-go Task). Mediation analyses included bias-
corrected and accelerated confidence intervals estimated via non-parametric bootstrap. Results:
Sleep problems were significantly associated with (Box-Cox-transformed) ED symptoms
(B=0.26, p<0.01). Self-reported NU mediated a significant proportion of the association between
PSQI sleep problems and transformed ED symptoms (Proportion = 61%; p<0.01), but task-based
NU (Proportion = 4%; p=0.73) and NA (Proportion = 23%; p=0.74) did not. Discussion: Poor
sleep may increase ED symptoms partly due to increasing trait-like NU, but not via task-based
NU nor NA. Trait-like NU may be an important mechanism linking sleep problems and eating
disturbances.

articles.title: Does Person-First Language Reduce Stigma? Evidence Across Health Condition Labels From Two Experimental Studies
articles.authors: Elizabeth Kruse; Paige Amormino; David Dodell-Feder
articles.abstract: The stigmatization of mental health conditions remains a widespread problem. One proposed intervention involves reforming the language used to describe people with mental health conditions by using terminology that separates the individual from the label (i.e., person-first language) rather than language that defines the individual by the label (i.e., identity-first or identity-only language). Across two studies, we tested whether manipulating the language used to describe an individual alters multiple dimensions of stigma, including attitudinal stigma, trait-based stereotype judgments, and dehumanization, across a broad and intentionally heterogeneous set of labels spanning mental health and related conditions. In Study 1, language framing did not consistently influence attitudinal stigma across labels, with the exception of responses to psychopathy. In Study 2, language framing did not significantly influence perceived stereotype judgments or dehumanization for any label examined. Instead, the specific label used and, to a lesser extent, personal familiarity with mental health conditions showed the most consistent associations with stigma across both studies. These findings suggest that individual labels are embedded in distinct social schemas that shape perceptions independent of language framing, and that social or personal contact may be a more reliable pathway to reducing stigma than terminology reform.

articles.title: Auswirkungen von Künstlicher Intelligenz auf psychische Belastung in der Arbeitswelt – ein Überblick
articles.authors: Markus Langer; Annette Kluge
articles.abstract:
Der vorliegende Beitrag arbeitet den Forschungsstand zu den Auswirkungen des KI-Einsatzes auf psychische Belastungen und Ressourcen am Arbeitsplatz auf. Ein Leitgedanke ist die Ambivalenz: KI-Systeme können auf nahezu jeder Dimension gleichzeitig als Ressource und als Belastung wirken – als Produktivitätsgewinn und Überforderung, als Autonomiezuwachs und Kontrollverlust, als Kompetenzerweiterung und Dequalifizierung. Ob im Einzelfall das eine oder das andere überwiegt, hängt maßgeblich davon ab, wie ein KI-System gestaltet ist und genutzt wird und wie es in Arbeitsprozesse eingebettet und organisational begleitet wird.
Im Beitrag bestimmen wir den Neuheitswert aktueller KI-Systeme. Vieles ist eine quantitative Fortschreibung bekannter Automatisierungstechnologien; qualitativ neu sind jedoch Eigenschaften wie die eigenständige Generierung von Inhalten, die Einsetzbarkeit als Allzweck-Werkzeug, nahezu autonome Aufgabenbearbeitung, probabilistisches und lernendes Verhalten, menschenähnliche Interaktion, engmaschige Entscheidungen über Menschen, schnelle Update-Zyklen sowie die verbreitete informelle Nutzung. Für jede dieser Eigenschaften lassen sich konkrete Chancen und Risiken für die psychische Gesundheit ableiten.
Die empirische Synopse (Stand Frühjahr 2026) ordnet die Befunde in einer soziotechnischen Kontext ein: Einflussfaktoren auf organisationaler, arbeits- und technologiegestalterischer sowie personenbezogener Ebene wirken – vermittelt über Moderatoren und Mediatoren auf verschiedene Ergebnisgrößen. Als belastungskritisch erweisen sich beispielsweise unrealistische Erwartungen und fehlendes Change Management, algorithmisches Management mit Autonomie- und Kontrollverlust, Arbeitsverdichtung statt Entlastung, der Verlust sozialer Einbindung sowie Sorgen um Arbeitsplatz und berufliche Identität. Als Gelingensbedingungen werden beispielsweise KI-Kompetenzen und ausreichende Zeit- und Trainingsressourcen beschrieben.
Daraus leiten wir Handlungsempfehlungen auf drei Ebenen ab. Organisational sollte beispielsweise die KI-Einführung konsequent als menschzentrierter Veränderungsprozess verstanden werden;. Auf der Arbeits- und Technologiegestaltungsebene sind Autonomie und Kontrolle zu sichern, Arbeitsverdichtung zu überwachen, Tätigkeitszuschnitte im Sinne der SMART-Kriterien zu prüfen und Technologien so zu gestalten, dass menschliche Aufsicht gelingt. Auf Personenebene rücken KI- und metakognitive Kompetenzen, der Erhalt arbeitsfachlicher Fertigkeiten sowie die neue Kernaufgabe der effektiven menschlichen Aufsicht von KI-Systemen in den Vordergrund.
Dieser Beitrag zeigt, dass eine menschzentrierte, soziotechnisch gedachte Gestaltung und Einführung von KI-Systemen den technischen Fortschritt nicht ausbremst, sondern Arbeit reichhaltiger, gesünder und nachhaltiger macht – und ist die entscheidende Stellschraube dafür, dass KI zur Ressource statt zur Belastung wird.

articles.title: Media Selectivity Research in Light of Self-Defeating Tendencies: Towards a Novel Understanding of Media Effects on Well-Being
articles.authors: Nicole Bizzotto; Tobias Dienlin; Silvia Knobloch-Westerwick
articles.abstract: A critical gap persists in media uses and effects research: while existing work has predominantly focused on self-serving motivations for media selection, an expanding body of evidence suggests that individuals—including those with psychological vulnerabilities—may seek out online content that aggravates, rather than alleviates, distress. Drawing on scholarship on self-defeating tendencies in offline contexts, we argue that the same process may unfold in mediated environments, especially on social media: when negative self-concepts are salient, users may gravitate toward content that validates these self-views, even at the expense of their well-being. We focus on mental health content as an illustrative case in which these dynamics become particularly visible and harmful, while arguing that similar processes apply to other domains. To guide this line of inquiry and offer a more comprehensive account of media selection processes and their implications for well-being, we extend the established Selective Exposure Self- and Affect-Management (SESAM) model by incorporating self-defeating motivations and outline a research agenda.

articles.title: Dyadic Social Dynamics in Separation-Related Anxiety: Multimodal Arousal Synchrony Between 4-Year-Olds and Their Mothers
articles.authors: Leonard Konstantin Kulisch; Laurin Plank; Anna Exner; Silvia Schneider; Sabine Seehagen; Armin Zlomuzica; Babett Voigt
articles.abstract: Separation anxiety disorder (SAD) is an early-onset disorder linked to adverse outcomes into adulthood. To advance SAD etiology, this study examined how parental risk factors relate to dyadic social dynamics. Seventy-two four-year-olds (50% girls, 93% primarily German-speaking) and their mothers (74% holding a Bachelor’s degree) participated in a standardized separation paradigm. Parental reports, heart rate, and machine-learning-based measures of facial and vocal arousal were assessed. The announcement of separation increased children’s physiological (ꞵ=.17) and vocal arousal (ꞵ=.13). Within individuals, physiological and vocal arousal were coordinated (r=.18–.20), while across dyads, facial (r=.15) and vocal arousal (r=.09) showed consistent synchrony. Physiological synchrony emerged selectively in dyads with higher maternal anxiety (r=.31) but was unrelated to absolute arousal or SAD symptoms. Anticipatory physiological synchrony was negatively associated with child vocal arousal during separation (r=-.44). Early separation-related anxiety appears embedded in dyadic processes, shaped by vocal arousal transmission and maternal anxiety symptoms.

articles.title: KUAI-Kids: Developing a Measurement Instrument for Children’s Knowledge, Use, and Attitudes Toward Generative AI Chatbots
articles.authors: Sarah Malone; Carmen Koehler; Kristin Altmeyer; Dominik Thüs; Marina Dombrovskaia; Johannes Hartig
articles.abstract: The increasing presence of generative artificial intelligence in children’s lives highlights the need for age-appropriate measurement instruments to assess their knowledge, use, and atti-tudes toward these technologies. This study introduces and validates KUAI-Kids, a question-naire on ChatGPT knowledge, use, and attitudes for children in middle childhood and early adolescence (ages 7 to 14; N = 310), based on a previously validated adult scale but with sub-stantially revised and extended items for children. Confirmatory factor analyses supported uni-dimensional structures for the Knowledge and Use scales, both showing good model fit and internal consistency. For the Attitude scale, the originally assumed unidimensional structure was not supported. Instead, factor analyses identified two distinct dimensions, Enthusiastic and Cautious Attitudes toward ChatGPT. Both Attitude subscales demonstrated good model fit and reliability. Latent correlations revealed expected associations: Knowledge and Use were mod-erately positively correlated; Enthusiastic Attitudes were strongly associated with Use, while a moderately strong correlation was observed between Cautious Attitudes and Knowledge. Ex-ploratory analyses indicated higher Enthusiastic Attitudes in boys and higher Knowledge, Use, and Cautious Attitudes scores in older students. The KUAI-Kids offers a psychometrically sound tool to study children’s engagement with AI chatbots and to support AI literacy assess-ment, the evaluation of educational interventions, and evidence-based development of AI-related educational policies. Limitations include the rapidly evolving nature of generative AI technologies and the fact that many children in the sample had little or no direct experience with ChatGPT.

articles.title: How Childhood Adversity Alters Social Information Processing and its Effect on Social Functioning: A Systematic Review
articles.authors: Hannah Dorsman; Elizabeth E. L. Buimer; Antoinette Haverhals; Pauline Wessels; Peter Bos; Eamon McCrory; Anne-Laura Van Harmelen
articles.abstract:
Background: Childhood adversity (CA) affects millions of children worldwide and may change how children perceive and respond to social cues in ways that are adaptive in adverse environments but maladaptive later in life. These maladaptive effects may be particularly pronounced during adolescence, a sensitive period of social reorientation and neurodevelopment. This pre-registered systematic review examined whether CA shapes the way young people process social information, and whether these changes are linked to difficulties in social functioning during adolescence.
Methods: We searched Web of Science, PsycINFO, and PubMed for studies assessing CA before age 18, social information processing across five domains, and social functioning in youth aged 10-24.
Results: Although 6657 studies were identified, only 11 met inclusion criteria. These examined threat-related processing (n=5), emotional reactivity and regulation (n=5), and reward processing and learning (n=3). CA was associated with alterations in social information processing across most domains. If associations between social information processing and social functioning were directly tested, they were generally supported. Evidence spanned different stages of adolescence, but associations with social functioning were tested almost exclusively in early-to-mid adolescent samples.
Conclusions: We find preliminary support for a model where CA is associated with alterations in social information processing which then leads to poorer social functioning. These findings were based mostly on longitudinal samples in early-to-mid adolescent samples, however, prospective examinations of this model were rare. These findings suggest that interventions targeting social information processing may be a promising avenue for supporting adolescents with experiences of CA.

articles.title: Dynamic coordination of speech and gesture in the brain
articles.authors: Jiachen Yao; Cecilia Husta; Linda Drijvers
articles.abstract: Face-to-face communication relies on the continuous integration of auditory signals, such as speech, and visual signals, such as co-speech gestures. Rather than serving as an add-on to spoken language, gestural information has been shown to actively shape how the brain constructs meaning. A central question is how the brain achieves integrating gestures with speech. This is not a trivial problem, as auditory and visual signals are often noisy, temporally misaligned, variable in length, and ambiguous, yet interlocutors still seem to understand each other effortlessly. This chapter will review evidence from neuroimaging (e.g., fMRI, MEG, (dual-)EEG, fNIRS) and brain stimulation (e.g., TMS, tDCS, tACS) methods, both from a within- and a between-brain perspective. Together, these methods have begun to outline a distributed and flexible brain network that supports the integration of speech and gestures. We will discuss how these brain networks coordinate the integration of speech and gestures, and how speech-gesture integration unfolds over time, in both clear and adverse listening conditions.

articles.title: Humans learn to distinguish imagination from reality with age
articles.authors: Andre Sahakian; Stefan van der Stigchel; Nadine Dijkstra; Surya Gayet; Christoph Strauch
articles.abstract: Telling apart what is the product of one's imagination and what is a true sensory experience (i.e., reality monitoring) might feel trivial to most. Yet it remains unclear whether reality monitoring is an innate ability (like breathing, or aversion to pain) or whether it is a learned skill (like speaking, or walking). Here we extend the age range of participants tested by Dijkstra and Fleming (2023) with young children from the age of 5. In a close replication we tested how likely participants were to report actually seeing a faint left or right tilted grating in dynamic noise, depending on whether they were concurrently imagining the same or an orthogonal grating. We found clear evidence that confusion of imagery and perception steadily declined to none with age - independent of perceptual ability or (subjective) imagery vividness. We empirically show that the ability to tell apart imagination from reality develops over age. These findings provide new insights on how we learn to keep apart imagination from reality, which has important implications for the development of psychopathology.

articles.title: ChirPing: A Social Media Simulation Platform Developed for Scientific Research
articles.authors: Nadia Said; Lena Plötz; Nicole Antes
articles.abstract: Experimental research on behavior on social media platforms typically relies on two methodological approaches, each with advantages but also limitations. Experimental studies, while having the advantage of giving researchers full control over the content presented and allowing for direct assessment of other variables of interest, often lack ecological validity, as behavioral intentions are only weakly predictive of actual sharing behavior. Studies conducted directly on live platforms, by contrast, offer ecological validity. However, the lack of control over the experimental environment makes it difficult to draw causal inferences. To address those issues, social media simulation platforms have gained increasing popularity in research. However, these platforms vary widely in usability and flexibility: some require more advanced programming skills, while others are fairly easy to use but may be limited in their use cases. Here we present our social media simulation platform, ChirPing, a new tool embedded within the widely used experimental research platform SoSci Survey. The main advantage of our platform is that it is part of an established platform; thus, researchers can easily integrate it into their surveys and adjust it within a familiar tool environment. Furthermore, our platform is highly customizable, allowing researchers to systematically manipulate experimental parameters (e.g., content presentation and post order). Allowing researchers to examine, for example, causal effects on behavioral outcomes such as sharing, engagement, and decision-making.

articles.title: Do trait and state empathy facilitate interpersonal synchrony in musical interactions?
articles.authors: Persefoni Tzanaki; Lieke Perik; Cagri Erdem; Jonna Katariina Vuoskoski
articles.abstract: Recent research suggests that cognitive empathy facilitates interpersonal synchrony, yet the role of affective empathy and its impact when experimentally induced remain less explored. We investigated how empathy, both as a trait characteristic and the result of induction, influences synchrony in a musical context. Thirty-three dyads completed two synchrony tasks, one before and one after an empathy induction session. In Task 1, participants tapped in time with a metronome before synchronising with their partner’s tapping, whereas in Task 2, they synchronised melodic sequences. To induce empathy, participants shared personal events while their partners were instructed either to empathise (empathy induction) or memorise factual details (control condition). Trait empathy was measured using the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI). Emotional engagement and behavioural mirroring during empathy induction were assessed using self-report and motion-capture measures. Results showed that both cognitive and affective trait empathy contributed to synchrony: higher Empathic Concern (an affective IRI subscale) predicted better alignment with a metronome in Task 1, while higher Fantasy (cognitive IRI) predicted greater synchrony in Task 2, suggesting that empathy’s role may rely on the type of coordination required by the task. Induced empathy showed no main effects; however, high-Fantasy participants who reported greater emotional engagement with partners’ stories synchronised better in Task 2 than those who engaged less. Moreover, high-Fantasy dyads showed greater mirroring of narrators’ head movements in the control condition, whereas this association became weakly negative when empathy was induced. The findings indicate a multifaceted role of empathy in joint action, and future directions to fully understand this role are discussed.

articles.title: Shared research materials in psychology are widely downloaded but often difficult to reuse
articles.authors: Daniel S Quintana
articles.abstract: Open science reforms have made posting data and code common, but are shared materials actually used, and easily reused? Treating download counts of Open Science Framework (OSF) supplements as a usage index, I analysed 1,660 articles from four psychology journals (Cognition, Psychological Science, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, Journal of Memory and Language) across three years (2015, 2020, 2025). OSF sharing rose from 9% in 2015 to 52% in 2025. Among 392 papers with download data, materials were downloaded a median of 152 times; only 1% went undownloaded. Download volume was associated with citation count and altmetric attention. Availability did not ensure easy reuse: only 40% of repositories provided documentation, 34% were flagged for a hard-coded file path, and 42% referenced a missing file — shortcomings that did not improve as sharing grew. Altogether, shared materials are being used, but often not easily reusable.

articles.title: Embodied Emotions in Natural Language
articles.authors: Lauri Nummenmaa; Aatu Liimatta; Eleanor Bennett; Birgitta Paranko; Heidi Jauhiainen; Mikko Sams; Saana Svärd; Juha M. Lahnakoski
articles.abstract: Emotions are often felt in the body, and embodiment is a prominent mechanism supporting language processing. Here we utilized computational linguistics to map embodied representations of emotions in an English text corpus. The data revealed consistent embodied patterns for emotion categories. Comparison between semantics-derived and self-reported bodily maps of emotions revealed similar, discrete bodily representations of different emotions in texts and self-reports. Hierarchical clustering revealed three clusters: positive emotions within the head and chest, negative emotions within the torso and legs, and negative social emotions mostly within the head. Replication in a Finnish corpus yielded consistent results. These findings show that the bodily organization of emotional experience is reflected in the statistical structure of language, linking linguistic meaning to the subjective bodily experience of emotion.

articles.title: The Missing Quadrant: Population Health in the Conversation About AI and Mental Health
articles.authors: Emily E Haroz; Peter P. Zandi; Roy Adams
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence now occupies two roles in mental health that call for different sciences. As an intervention it is deliberately deployed to improve care or to improve understanding. As an exposure it is not deployed for those purposes at all but encountered, largely through consumer products outside any clinical setting. Crossing these two roles with a clinical lens focused on individual patients and a population lens focused on whole communities yields four domains of work, three of which have active research, while the fourth, the population view of AI as an exposure, has comparatively little attention. Public health's tools are the natural starting point for that fourth domain: measurement, surveillance, epidemiologic design, and the study of social, structural, and commercial determinants. But this exposure has features that mean those methods cannot simply be imported, and adapting them is the work now in front of the field. The exposure is already at population scale, but the science that would study it as one is not.

articles.title: No convincing evidence of longitudinal effects linking neuroticism, gaming disorder, and future time perspective: A reanalysis of Guo et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Guo et al. investigated longitudinal associations among neuroticism, internet gaming disorder, and future time perspective, concluding that the findings supported reciprocal influences over time. However, statistically significant cross-lagged parameters do not necessarily indicate genuine prospective effects because such estimates can emerge from alternative statistical mechanisms. Using simulated data that reproduced the sample size and correlation structure reported by Guo et al., we evaluated the consistency of the reported findings across several plausible analytic approaches. The conclusions varied considerably across model specifications. Some approaches yielded positive longitudinal associations, whereas others produced negative or non-significant estimates. When all results were integrated using meta-analytic methods, none of the overall effects reached statistical significance. These findings suggest that the evidence presented by Guo et al. does not provide a robust basis for claims of prospective influence. In line with recommendations from the multiverse-analysis framework, investigators should examine multiple defensible analytic specifications and base conclusions on the aggregated evidence rather than on a single model.

articles.title: Consciousness and emotions in non-human animals: Are laypeople more or less skeptical than experts?
articles.authors: Bastian Jaeger; Stefan Leach; Matthew Zipple
articles.abstract: Consciousness and the capacity to experience affective states, such as pain, pleasure, fear, and hunger (i.e., sentience) are seen as key determinants of an individual’s moral status, a view that is shared by scientists, philosophers, and laypeople. Whether (and which) non-human animals are believed to possess these capacities can therefore have important consequences for how they are treated. In this registered report (study design registration: https://doi.org/10.71240/lcyc.238674), we measured people’s attributions of consciousness and emotions to a diverse set of animals, testing whether laypeople overattribute (as suggested by research on anthropomorphizing) or underattribute these mental capacities to animals (as suggested by research on motivated mind denial). Animal consciousness and emotions are famously challenging to study. In the absence of an unambiguous benchmark against which people’s beliefs could be compared, we tested whether laypeople, a nationally representative sample of 600 U.S. participants, are more or less skeptical about animal consciousness and emotions than scientific experts, a sample of 100 behavioral ecologists, evolutionary biologists, and other animal researchers. We find that, compared to scientific experts, laypeople were less likely to attribute consciousness (-8 percentage points), and substantially less likely to attribute emotions (-21 percentage points) to non-human animals. Laypeople were on average more confident in their beliefs than scientific experts.

articles.title: The partner as reader: recognition, disclosure risk, and the unit of analysis in dyadic reflexive thematic analysis
articles.authors: Vince Jacques de Blauwe; Alina Gheorghita; Antonio Fidalgo
articles.abstract:
Thirty widening-participation students in 15 stranger dyads wrote five probe re-sponses after a 14-minute belonging encounter. Reflexive thematic analysis of 150 im-mediate written micro-accounts generated four interpretive themes: calm-as-distance, vocabulary-as-bridge, masking under instruction, and provisional we-ness. A subse-quent dialogue-informed dyad-level configurational reading of paired texts extended, complicated, and bounded selected individual-level interpretations; it was not used as independent corroboration. Participants sometimes described calm or competent partici-pation alongside relational distance, evaluative effort, or uncertainty about mutuality; composure was therefore not treated as evidence of relational arrival.
This methodological case study develops the Partner-Recognition Framework for dyad-ic qualitative research. The framework addresses a risk that conventional de-identification may leave unresolved: a partner who shared an encounter may recognise an account from shared memory even when external identifiers have been removed. The four substantive themes provide the empirical case through which the framework is de-veloped; the disclosure-cost and recursive-risk analyses show what implementation re-quires. Four rules follow: naming partner recognition in consent, prospective specifica-tion of dyadic provenance, default pair separation in public reporting, and screening of derived artefacts. These are prospective design and reporting rules, not a validated risk-assessment instrument, a guarantee of anonymity, or a substitute for case-specific ethi-cal and legal review.

articles.title: Revisiting Assurance: Theoretical Refinement, Scale Development, and Future Research
articles.authors: Atsuki Ito; Matthias S Gobel; Kosuke TAKEMURA
articles.abstract: Expectations that others will cooperate are critical for sustaining intragroup cooperation. Although extensive research has emphasized trust—expectations of cooperation based on others’ traits and intentions—as a strong predictor of cooperation, assurance—expectations grounded in incentive structures—has received little empirical attention. The present research aims to establish a theoretical and methodological foundation for assurance research. First, we propose that assurance can be understood as a process through which perceived incentive structure gives rise to expectations of others’ cooperation and ultimately promotes cooperation. Second, across three studies using American and Japanese samples (total N = 1,589), we developed the Perceived Assurability Scale, a reliable measure of perceived incentive structure underlying assurance and demonstrated that perceived assurability predicts workplace cooperation independently of perceived trustworthiness. Third, we propose future research directions regarding how group contexts are translated into cooperation through psychological processes captured by the concepts of trust and assurance.

articles.title: The Australian under-16 social media ban: Early influences on access and its relationship with reading
articles.authors: Signy Wegener; Jasmine Spencer; Andrea Salins; Serje Robidoux; Robert Savage; Anne Castles
articles.abstract: Concerns abound that time spent on social media might displace more developmentally adaptive activities, such as reading. In December 2025, the Australian government introduced a world-first social media ban for young people under the age of 16, providing an opportunity to explore whether social media use and the efficacy of the ban are associated with current reading behaviours. In this study, Australians aged 12 to 15 years completed a cross-sectional self-report online survey between March and June 2026. Prior to the ban, 81.55% of the sample used social media. Users of social media reported reading less frequently, for shorter periods and had lower reading motivation than non-users of social media. For users, the initial effect of the ban was often incomplete or transient, with many users subsequently able to regain access to lost accounts. Post-ban, time spent on social media reduced for those who lost access to some or all of their accounts. Although there were differences in reading times by the effect of the ban in the predicted direction, they were not significant. Further, there were no differences in the strength of the association between reading motivation and reading duration by the effect of the ban. These findings suggest that social media use is associated with lower levels of reading engagement than non-use. The early implementation of the social media ban has only been partially effective and there is presently insufficient evidence that the effect of the ban is associated with differences in current reading engagement.

articles.title: Mapping the Content and Consistency of Suicidal Thoughts with Large Language Models: A Two-Study Longitudinal Investigation Among Adolescents and Young Adults
articles.authors: Leily Marieh Behbehani; Ruben van Genugten; Frances Grace Hart; Sharina Hamm; Kathryn Fox; Shirley B Wang
articles.abstract: Suicide is a leading cause of death. Measurement of suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STBs) relies on self-report (e.g., “How strong is your urge to kill yourself right now?”), yet little is known about how individuals translate internal experiences into numerical ratings. We used large language models (LLMs) to examine the content and consistency of suicide urges across severity ratings, between people, and over time. Participants with past-year STBs (Study 1: N=158 adolescents, Study 2: N=202 young adults) completed open-ended questions at baseline and follow-ups. We developed a two-stage topic-modeling pipeline and identified 13 (Study 1) and 14 (Study 2) topics reflecting suicidal thought content (e.g., Family/Friends Reactions, Depressed & Exhausted). Within- and between-person consistency were U-shaped, with highest agreement at endpoints of the scale. These findings highlight the potential of LLMs for advancing measurement of suicide risk and our understanding of how people interpret and respond to self-report rating scales.

articles.title: Wise Empathy Improves Well-being on Instagram
articles.authors: Gregory John Depow; Christopher Oveis; Emily Zohar; Michael Inzlicht
articles.abstract: Most of the global population spends significant time browsing social media making it critical to understand how to improve experiences online to support well-being. Here, we test whether a brief intervention training individuals to use wise empathy on Instagram can improve users’ well-being. In an ecological momentary intervention, we trained half our sample (N = 260) to wisely regulate empathy for positive and negative posts. Using experience sampling (Nobs. = 5,902), we tracked empathy and well-being in daily life. The intervention increased wise empathy online—boosting appreciative joy, positive emotion sharing, and compassion for negative emotions—while reducing negative emotion sharing, upward social comparisons, and personal distress. When participants had recently browsed Instagram, those in the wise empathy condition reported higher well-being than controls, an effect mediated by changes in wise empathy. These findings position wise empathy as a scalable, trainable skill that can enhance well-being on social media.

articles.title: Phonological changes facilitate pragmatic inference during lexical access in Bengali verbs
articles.authors: Pijush Kanti Gayen; Monsija Mitra; Samar Husain
articles.abstract: How do listeners map fine-grained phonological variation onto a speaker’s communicative intention during lexical access? We address this question using a restricted set of Bengali imperative verb forms in which stem-vowel height alternation is associated with different directive speech acts. Native speakers of Bengali (N=176) completed (i) an intention-scaling task to assess perceived illocutionary force and (ii) a cross-modal lexical decision task with auditory verb primes and visual speech-act targets. The lexical decision experiment manipulated prime--target stimulus onset asynchrony (SOA: 30 ms, 60 ms, 240 ms) to test the time course of phonological-to-pragmatic activation. Intention-scaling results showed that participants reliably distinguished the two intended speech acts. In the lexical decision task, congruent speech-act targets were recognised substantially faster than controls at the 60ms SOA (approximately 100ms facilitation for both order and request), whereas effects were small and not reliable at 30ms and 240ms. Request trials also showed slightly longer latencies than order trials, consistent with a higher inferential load for requests. Together, the results provide behavioural evidence that phonological cues can rapidly bias speech-act interpretation, with a temporally constrained window for lexical-pragmatic integration.

articles.title: Voice Can Help and Hurt AI Empathy: How Context Shapes the Effects of Vocal Delivery
articles.authors: Joshua D Wenger; Daryl Cameron; Reza Hadi Mogavi; Michael Inzlicht
articles.abstract: As people increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) for empathy, new modes of human–AI empathic interaction have emerged. While prior research on empathic AI has focused almost exclusively on text-based empathy, we explored how vocal delivery of empathetic messages might enhance or undermine AI versus human empathy. Across five studies (N = 1,584) we examined how the mode of expression (voice vs. text) and the empathy source (human vs. AI) jointly shape perceptions of empathic quality and experiences of feeling heard across different interaction contexts. In interactions involving pre-recorded empathic messages, vocal delivery reduced perceptions of quality and experiences of feeling heard for both human and AI empathizers, though the reduction was stronger for AI. This reduction was eliminated for human empathizers by giving empathy recipients the option to first opt in or consent to receiving empathy from a human empathizer, though the reduction remained for AI voices in this pre-recorded context. The reduction for AI voices also disappeared, and sometimes reversed into a benefit, in more immersive and personally relevant interaction contexts such as extended, live interaction with an AI chatbot. We further explored how the mode of expression impacts feelings of uncanniness, and the mediating role uncanniness plays in shaping feelings of being empathized with and feeling heard. Together, these findings demonstrate that whether voice helps or hurts AI empathy critically depends on the interaction context, and highlight uncanniness as one factor that can undercut spoken empathy in some contexts.

articles.title: Evaluating the Credibility of Human and AI Forecasters: Receivers Discriminate Performance More Finely for Humans
articles.authors: Robert N. Collins; David R. Mandel
articles.abstract: Decision-makers in high-stakes forecasting domains are increasingly asked to weigh probabilistic judgments from human experts alongside those from artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Whether source attribution alters how forecasts are received has been largely unexamined. Three accounts make competing predictions. Algorithm aversion and algorithm appreciation predict a source dependent bias in favor of humans and AI, respectively: both assume that source attribution may affect forecaster evaluation. By contrast, responsibility-attribution research predicts differential discrimination, with credibility ratings distinguishing performance levels more finely for human than AI sources. We tested these accounts in two experiments (N1 = 667; N2 = 1,170). Participants translated verbal probability expressions communicated by either a human expert or an AI system into numeric point estimates and ranges. Separately, participants evaluated source credibility after reviewing a forecaster’s performance record, with accuracy manipulated between subjects. Interpretation was largely unaffected by source: numerical point estimates were similar and ranges equivalent for both human and AI sourced forecasts. In contrast, credibility ratings depended on source: receivers discriminated performance more finely for human than AI forecasters: human forecasters were rated as more credible than equally accurate AI when accuracy was high and less credible when accuracy was low. This differential discrimination is inconsistent with algorithm aversion and appreciation accounts, but consistent with the responsibility-attribution research, according to which people hold human advisors more accountable for outcomes than algorithms. We discuss implications for integrating AI-assisted forecasts into decision support roles.

articles.title: Positive Emotion Displays Support Preschoolers’ and Adults’ Word Learning
articles.authors: Mira L Nencheva; Michael C. Frank
articles.abstract: Emotion displays are one of the most salient features of early social interactions - caregivers often smile, change their vocal register to convey positive emotions to their children. Despite the fact that these emotion displays often accompany the moments in which children learn language, prior work on the role of emotion in word learning has been sparse and has resulted in conflicting findings. The present investigation examines how emotion displays that vary in valence (positive vs. negative) and arousal (high vs. low) influence word learning in preschoolers and adults. Across five experiments, participants completed a word learning task in which novel object-label pairs were introduced by a character displaying one of four emotional states: high-arousal positive, low-arousal positive, high-arousal negative, or low-arousal negative. Results consistently showed that positive emotion displays facilitated word learning relative to negative displays in adults and preschoolers alike, with web-based eye tracking indicating that high-arousal negative displays modestly pull attention away from the labeled object. Following the study, preschoolers preferentially chose stickers depicting objects that had been paired with positive displays as a prize, suggesting that emotion signals shape not only which words children learn but also how they value the objects paired with emotion displays. Together, these findings establish that emotional signals are not merely a backdrop to early language input but an active ingredient in word learning. Specifically, positive emotion in caregivers’ communication to young children may serve a functional role in supporting language development.

articles.title: Simple heuristics structure and bias fairness judgements about climate change
articles.authors: Lucas Woodley; Arthur Le Pargneux; Fiery Andrews Cushman
articles.abstract: Establishing a fair global carbon budget is crucial for mitigating climate change, yet little is known about what shapes citizens' fairness perceptions. In a pre-registered experiment across five countries (N=3,043), we examine how simple informational cues affect what people propose as fair carbon budgets. We find that people’s judgements are structured around proportionality or nominal equality heuristics, yet they are easily biased and frequently contradict all main climate justice principles.

articles.title: “More research being done is so validating”: Insights from transgender and gender-diverse participants on a psychophysiological study with deception
articles.authors: Nina Micanovic; Camden Trepanier; Maddie Katz; Vera Vine
articles.abstract: Laboratory-based research methods (e.g., psychophysiology, stress induction paradigms) are insightful for understanding the mechanisms underlying health disparities experienced by transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) people. Among this population, fear and mistrust of research remain due to historical mistreatment, and TGD people remain under-represented in experimental research. Researchers sensitive to these issues may hesitate to recruit TGD participants in fear of causing discomfort associated with more invasive laboratory-based research methods. Inclusive study design efforts exist, but it is unclear how they are received by TGD people. We explored TGD participants’ experiences in a study involving social exclusion and psychophysiological measurements (electrocardiogram and impedance cardiography) to understand how inclusive study design efforts were perceived. We conducted interviews with the first 10 TGD participants in a study where participants completed a social exclusion manipulation involving deception (i.e., Cyberball; Williams, 2000) while providing psychophysiological data (larger study N = 105). Informed by interpretive description (Thorne, 2016), we coded interview transcriptions to identify commonalities and patterns of participant experiences across each study phase. Overall, participants appreciated research efforts to increase transparency and encourage participant agency. Despite some discomforts, participants report that inclusive efforts fostered a sense of trust and safety throughout the study. During deception (and debriefing) and psychophysiological measurement, participant experiences in the study were positive or neutral. Participants provided constructive feedback about several study design elements. These findings provide researchers with tangible recommendations for inclusive experimental research for TGD participants that may help build trust and mutual respect between minoritized groups and researchers.

articles.title: Measuring audience experience across 20 showings of the same theatre performance using customer feedback kiosks and a questionnaire
articles.authors: Mikko Sams; Einat Amir-Ahola; Enrico Glerean; Sirpa Kähkönen; Taru Mäkelä; Reetta Ristimäki; Antti Ruotoistenmäki; Veli-Matti Saarinen
articles.abstract:
Audience experiences can vary both between performances and among spectators, but little is
known about how different methods capture this variation across repeated showings of the
same production. We therefore examined audience experience across twenty live performances
of the same music theatre production. We combined two complementary methods: immediate
audience ratings collected through customer feedback kiosks and more detailed postperformance
questionnaires. The kiosks recorded 1,887 responses, corresponding to 67% of
total attendance, and 458 audience members (16%) completed questionnaires. Overall, the
reception was positive, but kiosk ratings varied significantly across performances, indicating
that audience-level enjoyment ratings differed from one showing to another. Kiosk and
questionnaire responses to the same enjoyment question did not differ significantly at the
aggregate level, suggesting that brief kiosk feedback may provide a practical, low-burden
measure of audience-level enjoyment. Cluster analysis of questionnaire data identified three
descriptive response profiles that differed primarily in overall engagement and ratings of
specific artistic elements. These profiles illustrate heterogeneity within the audience of a single
production. Qualitative responses from participants whose quantitative ratings were closest to
each cluster centroid provided illustrative accounts of the experiences associated with these
profiles. These narratives added context to the quantitative findings by showing differences in
emotional tone, interpretive emphasis, and personal connection to the performance.
Supplementary interviews with the director, artistic director, and an external playwright
illustrated both interest in and reservations about incorporating audience data into creative
work. Their comments emphasised the potential of empirical findings to support artistic
reflection, while also underscoring the importance of how and when feedback is communicated
within production teams.

articles.title: Naming variation across languages is shaped by shared histories, semantics and familiarity
articles.authors: Alzbeta Kucerova; Carlo Y. Meloni; Johann-Mattis List
articles.abstract: Speakers all around the world use words to name the objects around them. While they often agree on a common word, this is not always the case. Certain concepts seem to attract many different words, while others remain fairly stable in their naming patterns. It is still unclear where these naming differences stem from, which factors trigger the variation, and to which degree this variation results from universal linguistic tendencies, contact, inheritance or concept-level properties. Here, we analyze naming variation patterns in an open dataset that elicits naming responses for 500 unique concepts across 34 languages from 8 distinct families. Our results show that cross-linguistic similarities in naming variation are systematically associated with genetic relatedness, geographical proximity between languages, concept basic-ness, semantic categories, and object familiarity. Although the magnitude of semantic category effects varies across languages, several semantic categories display broadly consistent tendencies toward higher or lower naming diversity across most languages in the sample. These findings indicate that naming variation reflects both concept-level properties, as well as cross-linguistic historical and spatial relationships, while also exhibiting meaningful language-specific heterogeneity.

articles.title: People want human and AI social partners to follow different relational norms despite similar roles
articles.authors: Madeline G. Reinecke; Yueying Chu; Ivar Rodríguez Hannikainen; Andreas Kappes; Sebastian Porsdam Mann; Ilina Singh; Julian Savulescu; Brian D. Earp
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly assuming social roles traditionally held by humans—but do people want human-AI relationships to be governed by the same behavioral norms as human-human relationships? In three pre-registered studies using demographically representative samples in the United Kingdom (N = 910) and United States (N = 862), including a US pilot study (N = 432), we assessed public preferences across four cooperative domains—care, hierarchy, transaction, and mating—within seven relationship types (e.g., romantic partners, close friends, coworkers). Participants rated their ideal norms for each domain and relationship type, either in a human-human or human-AI context. Contrary to a common assumption in alignment research, participants reported systematically different ideals for human-AI versus human-human relationships: across all seven types, they distinguished ideal AI from ideal human behavior in at least one cooperative domain, with the direction and size of differences also varying by relationship type. Specifically, these included preferences for AI assistants and sellers to show greater care than humans in identical positions; AI teachers and mental health providers to express lesser authority; and AI romantic partners, friends, and coworkers to behave more platonically. Participants also preferred humans to show lesser care and greater authority toward AIs across several roles. These findings suggest public expectations for social AIs are shaped by relational context rather than a simple human-to-AI transfer rule, with implications for social AI design.

articles.title: Effects of Anthropomorphic Characteristics of Chat Agents on Perceptions of Bad Advice: An Exploratory Study
articles.authors: Kate Alberga; Michael A. Nees
articles.abstract: Anthropomorphic form is an inherent characteristic of artificial intelligence chatbots driven by large language models and appears to have profound effects on user perceptions of chatbots.  The proliferation of anthropomorphized chatbots has raised concerns about miscalibrated trust and misplaced attributions of responsibility for chatbot mistakes. An exploratory experiment examined the potential effects of anthropomorphic design in both the user interface and the linguistic output of a chatbot that provided bad advice about an everyday medical situation.  In a simulated chatbot interaction, participants experienced either humanlike or machinelike language output.  Additionally, the user interface either simulated typing (i.e., the typewriter effect) or presented a static text response all at once.  Humanlike language increased perceived anthropomorphism and social presence but had no effect on perceived competence and trust.  There were no significant effects of the typewriter effect user interface. More frequent AI usage was associated with higher chatbot trust and perceived social presence. Perceived anthropomorphism, social presence, trust, and competence were all highly intercorrelated. Interestingly, participants who were apparently unaware of the obviously bad advice tended to show considerably higher levels of chatbot perceived anthropomorphism, social presence, trust, and competence.  Finally, we found some evidence that higher perceived anthropomorphism is associated with greater perceived responsibility of the chatbot itself for the advice it gave, whereas higher perceived chatbot trust and competence were associated with lesser perceived responsibility of the developing company for the chatbot’s output. Potential future research directions are discussed.

articles.title: The Flattening Effect: A Comparative Study of Sociopragmatic Erasure and Identity Loss in Translated Vietnamese-English Cyber-Discourse
articles.authors: Ming Ze Tang; Phan Quynh Thu Nguyen; Thi Hong Nhung Nguyen
articles.abstract: This study investigates the "flattening effect" in translated Vietnamese-English code-mixed discourse, a phenomenon where semantic content is preserved while sociopragmatic nuances are erased. Utilizing a subset of the VietMix corpus, an "LLM-as-a-Judge" framework was employed to evaluate four dimensions: Structural Hybridity, Emotional Buffering, Status Signaling, and In-group Identity. While the model demonstrated moderate reliability in binary feature detection (inclusive $\kappa = 0.416$), its alignment with human consensus collapsed when quantifying erasure severity (expressive $\kappa = 0.141$). Qualitative analysis revealed that the model frequently over-interprets functional jargon while failing to recognize localized subcultural markers. These findings highlight a critical capability gap in current models, which prioritize global linguistic patterns over localized sociopragmatic functions. Consequently, future developments should move beyond semantic equivalence to incorporate localized cultural awareness within automated computer-mediated communication (CMC) analysis.

articles.title: Weak language abilities are associated with increased within-individual variability in both response times and rhythm tapping: Support for the intra-individual variability hypothesis from the Steps Study
articles.authors: Anna Kautto; Mira Karrasch; Viveka Lyberg Åhlander; Annette Nylund
articles.abstract:
First language acquisition varies substantially between children. A recent hypothesis suggests that intra-individual variability (IIV) in cognitive processing, which is reflected by response time (RT) IIV, underlies individual differences in language acquisition. In this study, we test this hypothesis by investigating associations between different measures of short-time IIV and language abilities in 15-year-old adolescents.

The participants (n=239) were recruited from the Steps cohort study. Our aim was to investigate whether IIV would be associated with language abilities, and whether the possible association is observed in different IIV measures. The participants completed three different tasks measuring IIV: a simple RT task, as well as externally paced metronome tapping and self-paced rhythm tapping. We were interested in whether IIV in tasks that require aligning to temporal patterns of external, sensory information (metronome tapping) or producing temporal patterns without external cues (self-paced tapping) would be differentially associated with language abilities.

In line with the IIV hypothesis of language, we found that pronounced IIV in all task types (metronome and self-paced rhythm tapping, as well as RTs) was related to weak language abilities.  Some differences in the associations between task types and language abilities emerged; RT IIV was a stronger predictor for language abilities than IIV in rhythm tapping tasks. Our sample consisted of adolescents, at which age language abilities are no longer in an active stage of development. If we assume that IIV reflects cognitive instability that underlies individual differences in language acquisition, this instability seems to be a persistent individual trait and could thus potentially be a helpful marker for identifying children at-risk for language learning difficulties.

articles.title: Two Paths, Two Fates: The Differential Democratic Outcomes of Disappointment-Based and Hatred-Based Affective Polarization
articles.authors: Mabelle Kretchner; Julia Elad-Strenger; Eran Halperin; Daan Vandermeulen; Sivan hirsch hoefler
articles.abstract: Does affective polarization (AP) threaten democratic life? Findings on democratic erosion and political violence remain mixed. We argue this reflects treating AP as unidimensional, when its democratic implications may differ by which emotions dominate. We propose an emotional dual-path model for AP. The more prevalent disappointment-based path (dominated by disappointment and anger) reflects perceptions of opponents as fellow citizens who have failed to meet shared expectations and associated with continued investment in democratic processes. The less prevalent hatred-based path (dominated by hatred, disgust, and contempt) reflects perceptions of opponents as total enemies and is associated with willingness to undermine democratic norms and support political violence. We tested this model in two surveys of Jewish Israelis (Study 1a: N = 1,120; Study 1b: N = 690) conducted during a period of political instability. Across ideological camps and time, disappointment-path emotions dominated, while hatred-path emotions remained low, extending prior single-emotion findings to the path level.  Latent profile and regression analyses showed that, consistent with the model, AP's democratic implications differed by emotional path: while the disappointment path was linked to greater support for democratic norms, the hatred path was linked to lower support for democratic norms and greater support for political violence.

articles.title: Immediate effects of body talk on body image in daily life: An experience sampling study
articles.authors: Nahori Ito; Akira Hasegawa; Asami Beppu; Yuko Matsuda; Ayano Kichinaka; Tetsuya Yamamoto
articles.abstract: This experience sampling study investigated whether momentary changes in state body talk were associated with concurrent and subsequent changes in state body image variables, including body fat dissatisfaction and body appreciation, providing insight into their short-term temporal dynamics. Overall, 118 female university students younger than 30 years completed baseline trait body talk and body image measures, followed by six assessments per day for seven days. Multilevel analyses showed that trait negative fat talk was significantly but weakly associated with a higher average level of state negative fat talk, whereas no such association was observed for positive body talk. Multilevel path analyses showed that state negative fat talk was concurrently associated with higher state body fat dissatisfaction and lower state body appreciation but not with either outcome at the subsequent assessment. These findings provided no evidence for a causal effect, although it remains possible that state negative fat talk had short-lived effects. The concurrent associations of state positive body talk with both body image variables were nonsignificant but in the same direction as those for state negative fat talk. Both forms of state body talk were concurrently associated with higher state appearance comparison.
