In contrast, trait negative fat talk was significantly associated with higher state body fat dissatisfaction and lower state body appreciation, and these associations appeared stronger than those observed for state negative fat talk. Future research should employ assessment methods that can adequately capture the occurrence of state body talk and study designs capable of detecting its immediate effects.

articles.title: Screening for DLD: Reliability and validity of the Screening Tool for Adults with Non-Diagnosed DLD (STAND).
articles.authors: Michelle St Clair; Jenny Louise Gibson; Suze Leitao; Emily Jackson; Ellie Barker; Mia Travlos; Jiayi Liang; Amy Bennett; Iris Edwards; Nicola Botting
articles.abstract: Interest in diagnosis of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD) in adulthood is increasing, but there is no validated screening tool to identify adulthood Developmental Language Disorder (DLD). DLD affects 7% of the population with lifelong impacts on education, employment, and mental-health. This paper evaluates a new screening tool to identify undiagnosed DLD in adulthood: the Screening Tool for Adults with Non-Diagnosed DLD (STAND). Study 1 investigated endorsement rate for STAND items, internal reliability, and test-retest reliability in adults with no NDD and with self-identified DLD. Study 2 (general population sample) and 3 (Student sample) evaluated internal reliability and validity. Study 4 evaluated the STAND’s acceptability by consulting adults with DLD. Internal reliability ranged from excellent to acceptable for current, lifetime, and total scores, and test-retest reliability was good. Adults self-identifying as having DLD endorsed all items more frequently, with significantly higher STAND scores. Studies 2 and 3 demonstrated good construct validity, with family history of language/literacy difficulties and personal NDD history associated with higher scores.  The Language Structure subscale on the Communication Checklist-Self Report (CC-SR) related to more Current and Total Difficulties in Study 2, establishing convergent validity. Study 3 further established convergent validity with the CC-SR Language Structure and Social Engagement subscales predicting STAND scores and the CELF-5 Core Language Score predicting lifetime language difficulties. Study 4 demonstrated broad acceptability of the STAND, leading to minor changes to create a revised STAND. The STAND offers a first step in creating an acceptable, reliable, and valid tool for DLD diagnosis in adults.

articles.title: Combining Psychedelics with Religion or Spirituality: Spiritual Bypassing, Receptivity to Pseudo-Profound Bullshit, Subclinical Psychotic Experiences and Well-Being.
articles.authors: Baptiste Fauvel; Myriam Ichchou; Chérine Elhssaini; Joy Zogheib; Ewen Kervadec; Bruno Roméo; Antoine Bioy; Pascale Piolino
articles.abstract:
Abstract: Psychedelics have been used for spiritual purposes for centuries. However, concerns have been raised regarding spiritual bypassing, maladaptive meaning-making, and increased suggestibility when psychedelics are combined with religious or spiritual beliefs. We examined spiritual bypassing, receptivity to pseudo-profound bullshit, subclinical psychotic experiences, well-being, and mystical and challenging intensity of the most significant psychedelic experience in 147 Western psychedelic users with different motives (religious: n = 21; spiritual but not religious: n = 79; neither religious nor spiritual: n = 47). Religious users were predominantly Christians, whereas spiritual and secular users primarily identified themselves as mindfulness-based practitioners and philosophers or existential meaning seekers. Groups did not differ in education level, psychiatric diagnoses, or receptivity to pseudo-profound bullshit. Religious and spiritual users reported more intense mystical experiences and higher well-being compared with secular users. Religious users reported fewer subclinical psychotic experiences. They also scored higher on spiritual bypassing, which was positively associated with well-being. No association were found between pseudo-profound bullshit receptivity and either mystical experience or spiritual bypassing. Overall, these findings do not support concerns that psychedelic use with religious or spiritual intentions is associated with increased cognitive or psychological vulnerabilities. 
Keywords: psychedelics, spirituality, religion, spiritual bypassing, suggestibility, well-being

articles.title: Short-term prior knowledge improves speech-in-noise perception independently of autistic imagination subtrait
articles.authors: Yurika Tsuji; Shu Imaizumi
articles.abstract: Autistic individuals often experience difficulties using prior knowledge and perceiving speech in noisy environments. Imagination difficulties associated with autistic traits have been linked to difficulty perceiving high-familiarity words, suggesting that this association may reflect difficulty using prior lexical knowledge. The present study aimed to directly examine the effects of prior knowledge on speech perception in noise in relation to imagination difficulties. We hypothesized that greater imagination difficulties would be related to poorer performance in perceiving learned words, but not unlearned words. Seventy-three participants from the general population identified unlearned and learned low-familiarity words presented in noise. In the learned conditions, participants learned the target words through written and spoken presentations and then identified them in noise. The results suggested that learning improved subsequent speech-in-noise perception. However, imagination difficulties were not associated with performance, regardless of whether the words had been learned. Therefore, imagination difficulties may not be associated with the ability to use short-term prior knowledge. Exploratory analyses suggested that attention-to-detail traits and communication difficulties may be associated with better perception of learned words, whereas attention-switching difficulties may be associated with poorer perception. Future studies should replicate these exploratory findings and investigate the role of other types of prior knowledge, such as long-term and semantic priors.

articles.title: How Restorative Justice may Create Social Change: A Contact-to-Change Model
articles.authors: Kimberley Aspinall; Michael Wenzel; Blake Quinney
articles.abstract: Restorative justice is a legal philosophy and practice focused on the repair of harm resulting from wrongdoing; as such, it has the transformative potential to facilitate change at individual, interpersonal and societal levels. Yet, restorative justice practices have diverged from their original social justice goals towards an individual-focused model of repair. The question is: how can we return restorative justice processes to their roots of addressing social injustices that underlie crime, and harness their power to mobilise communities for change? How can restorative justice processes speak to the wider community and promote their support for, or engagement in, collective action to address social injustices? To answer these questions, we propose the Restorative Contact-to-Change (RC2C) model, which draws from collective action, allyship and intergroup contact and dialogue literatures. The RC2C model proposes that community involvement in or, at a minimum, observation of restorative justice can be analysed as an instance of indirect intergroup contact, which—through perspective-taking, problem abstraction, and value consensus—can promote collective action and allyship behaviours for social change. The RC2C model may help understand how restorative justice processes can be transformative for individuals and society.

articles.title: Do Youth Offending Labels Matter? The Impact of the Label “Young Serious Offender” on Public Attitudes Toward Youth Justice
articles.authors: Julia Yesberg; Clare-Ann Fortune; Hasi Kolongahapitiya
articles.abstract: Research on the impact of crime-first labels on public attitudes has focused almost exclusively on sexual offending. This pre-registered conceptual replication of Harris and Socia (2016) examined the effect of the label 'young serious offender' on support for punitive youth justice policies and beliefs about rehabilitation. Using an experimental design, 393 adult residents of New Zealand and Australia were randomly allocated to receive statements using either 'young serious offender' or the person-first alternative 'young people who have committed serious offences'. Contrary to our hypotheses, we found no evidence the label influenced attitudes relative to the person-first alternative, and no consistent moderation effects were observed. Exploratory analyses identified political orientation, ethnicity, and educational attainment as significant predictors of both punitive attitudes and belief in rehabilitation. These findings suggest crime-first labelling effects may only appear where strong stigma and well-established stereotypes already exist (e.g., sexual offending). However, this null result reflects only a single, one-off exposure in a survey context. The introduction of the Young Serious Offender designation in New Zealand embeds crime-first language into policy, with potentially cumulative effects that a one-off exposure cannot capture. Future research should use longitudinal designs to examine repeated exposure to labels over time.

articles.title: Cultural Values Shape Acceptance of Electronic Performance Monitoring
articles.authors: Christine M Cairoli; David L Tomczak; Mauren S. Wolff; Tara S. Behrend
articles.abstract: Employee reactions to electronic performance monitoring (EPM) are mixed and depend on both the characteristics of the monitoring and the individual differences of those being monitored. Using information boundary theory as a foundation, our study investigates how horizontal-vertical individualism-collectivism dimensions affect acceptance of EPM practices that vary in invasiveness. Data from 501 participants showed that horizontal and vertical individualism and collectivism are positively associated with EPM acceptance. Furthermore, verticality is a predictor of acceptance for invasive EPM, such that people with strongly positive vertical individualism values are more likely to accept EPM. Our study demonstrates the need for organizations to consider both cultural values and the invasiveness of EPM methods when implementing monitoring policy. Further research is needed to understand how cultural values shape attitudes toward EPM in various geographic and legal settings. An awareness of cultural differences is crucial for policy makers and organizations aiming to implement EPM in ways that align with people’s norms and expectations.

articles.title: Bilateral continuous theta-burst stimulation of the anterior prefrontal cortex impairs emotional change detection and facial mimicry while enhancing metacognition of facial identity: a TMS–EMG study.
articles.authors: Luis Carlo Bulnes; Axel Cleeremans; Chotiga Pattamadilok; carmen De Vos; Marie Vandekerckhove
articles.abstract: The anterior prefrontal cortex (aPFC/BA10) is causally implicated in visual metacognition, including low-level perceptual judgments about faces. Whether it similarly contributes to the perception and metacognition of facial emotion, and also contributes to embodied facial responses, remains unclear. Facial electromyography (EMG) and skin conductance level responses were recorded while participants performed a change detection task of gradually evolving emotional (anger, happiness) facial changes from neutral (ON condition). A non-emotional change (identity) served as control. Subsequently, participants performed the reverse condition on emotional changes only, by reporting the end of an emotional expression (OFF condition). Confidence was assessed on each trial. Inhibitory continuous theta burst transcranial magnetic stimulation (cTB) was delivered bilaterally over the anterior prefrontal cortex (aPFC) using a pre-post treatment design, with Sham and NoTMS (no-stimulation) control groups. cTB did not alter confidence ratings for emotional changes. Instead, it enhanced relative metacognitive accuracy for changes in facial identity. Crucially, Sham and NoTMS groups became faster at detecting facial changes overall, as expected, whereas the cTB group did not, most clearly for happiness in the ON condition. In the OFF condition, cTB increased reaction times for anger offset detection. EMG results converged with behavioral data and showed reduced happiness-related zygomaticus activity, indicating disrupted congruent facial mimicry. These results suggest that aPFC causally contributes to distinct processing of emotional and non-emotional facial changes and exerts a downstream regulatory effect on embodied responses.

articles.title: Do Large Language Models see the world with rose-colored glasses? Prompting GPT-4o to associate color terms with emotion terms in Spanish and Chinese
articles.authors: Mingshan Xu; Antonio Benítez-Burraco
articles.abstract: Color terms and emotion terms frequently intertwine in language. In this paper, we compare the performance of humans and GPT-4o in an association task involving 13 color terms and 20 emotion terms (and 5 intensities of emotion) in two languages, Spanish and Chinese. Overall, we found that GPT-4o associates color terms with emotion terms similarly to humans. This is true for several main dimensions of emotions: valence, arousal, and power. At the same time, in cases where responses by human subjects differ cross-linguistically (such as intensity of emotion in our study with Spanish vs Chinese speakers), GPT-4o tends to reduce the differences between languages. In conclusion, although GPT-4o is a reliable model of human emotional language, it can contribute to eroding its diversity.

articles.title: Scroll and Snack: Daily Life Exposure to Healthy Food Content on Instagram Boosts Cravings for Healthy Snacks
articles.authors: Monique Caroline Alblas; Matthias Burkard Aulbach; Lena Jeremias; Veronika Pavlovova; Leonardo Pimpini
articles.abstract: Background: Food content pervades social media, yet how everyday exposure shapes momentary craving and snacking in daily life remains unclear. We tested whether experimentally adding unhealthy (H1) vs. healthy (H2) food content on top of participants’ Instagram feeds increased craving for and intake of unhealthy and healthy snacks, relative to adding art content (control). Method: In this preregistered randomized controlled field trial, 116 healthy-weight young adults (Mage = 22.46 years, 79.3% female) completed a 10-day smartphone ecological momentary assessment protocol (five prompts/day; five baseline, five manipulation days). Participants were randomly assigned to follow existing preselected Instagram accounts featuring unhealthy food, healthy food, or art (control); the number of additional accounts was 5% of those already followed. Outcomes (craving, consumption) were modeled using multilevel linear mixed models. Results: Manipulation checks confirmed expected shifts in food-related Instagram content. Against H1, added unhealthy content increased neither craving for (p = .194) nor intake of (p = .867) unhealthy snacks. Supporting H2, healthy food content increased craving for healthy snacks relative to both the control and the unhealthy condition (p < .001), but not healthy snack intake (p = .061). Conclusions: Curating a healthier Instagram feed may increase the desire for healthy snacks, but this effect, possibly due to the short duration of the manipulation, did not extend to intentions and/or intake. In conclusion, food craving may thus be used as early intervention target in future weight loss intervention, whereas changing actual intake likely requires longer or personalized exposure.

articles.title: My better half? Predicting self-esteem using appraisals of oneself, real others, and fictional characters
articles.authors: Eliott K. Doyle; Sara D. Hodges
articles.abstract: In what ways do perceptions of fictional characters supplement and differ from perceptions of real people in the context of self-esteem? The present study investigates differences between appraisals of the self, favorite fictional characters, and close real others, and the relationship between these appraisals and self-esteem. Participants (N = 265) rated themselves and their chosen real and fictional targets on likable and unlikable traits, then completed a measure of self-esteem. Appraisals of self and close real others were more favorable than appraisals of favorite fictional characters. Self-esteem was more strongly associated with self-appraisals than with appraisals of non-self targets. Differences between unlikable self and real other appraisals interacted with unlikable self and character appraisal differences in predicting self-esteem: Less unlikable appraisals of close real others compared to self-appraisals were predictive of lower self-esteem. Results suggest that fictional characters offer opportunities for self-enhancement not always afforded by real others.

articles.title: Consciousness and emotions in non-human animals: Are laypeople more or less skeptical than experts?
articles.authors: Bastian Jaeger; Stefan Leach; Matthew Zipple
articles.abstract: Consciousness and the capacity to experience affective states, such as pain, pleasure, fear, and hunger (i.e., sentience) are seen as key determinants of an individual’s moral status, a view that is shared by scientists, philosophers, and laypeople. Whether (and which) non-human animals are believed to possess these capacities can therefore have important consequences for how they are treated. In this registered report (study design registration: https://doi.org/10.71240/lcyc.238674), we measured people’s attributions of consciousness and emotions to a diverse set of animals, testing whether laypeople overattribute (as suggested by research on anthropomorphizing) or underattribute these mental capacities to animals (as suggested by research on motivated mind denial). Animal consciousness and emotions are famously challenging to study. In the absence of an unambiguous benchmark against which people’s beliefs could be compared, we tested whether laypeople, a nationally representative sample of 600 U.S. participants, are more or less skeptical about animal consciousness and emotions than scientific experts, a sample of 100 behavioral ecologists, evolutionary biologists, and other animal researchers. We find that, compared to scientific experts, laypeople were less likely to attribute consciousness (-8 percentage points), and substantially less likely to attribute emotions (-21 percentage points) to non-human animals. Laypeople were on average more confident in their beliefs than scientific experts.

articles.title: Which gambling harm prevention messages appear the most effective? Results of an online experiment comparing self-appraisal, positive emotional, loss-based, and counter-industry approaches
articles.authors: Philip Newall; William George Chapman; Simon Thomas van Baal; Jamie Torrance; Maira ANDRADE; Leonardo Weiss-Cohen
articles.abstract: Gambling harm prevention messages are increasingly catching up with best practices from tobacco of utilizing independently-designed warnings. Australia was the first country to impose this policy, using messages from three persuasion strategies: “loss-based” messages warn of the likelihood of losing money, “self-appraisal” messages prompt self-reflection of gambling behaviors, and a “positive emotional” message highlights the benefits of not gambling. In the present online experiment (N=3,486) we compared four well-performing messages from each of these classes against four well-performing “counter-industry” messages, which highlight the industry’s role in gambling harms. Messages were compared across six self-report outcomes (e.g., “this message makes me want to gamble less”), and based on the sentiment of optional free-text comments via a natural language processing analysis. Messages were ranked based on the overall sample and the high-risk sub-sample according to the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI). Overall, one message of each class appeared best, with positive emotional and self-appraisal messages appearing better suited to high-PGSI audiences, and loss-based messages to low-PGSI audiences. Counter-industry messages performed similarly among all audiences, but with longer counter-industry messages performing worse in sentiment-based analysis. These findings inform future theory-informed message development and campaign implementation.

articles.title: Zürich Voice Super-Recognizer Test (ZVSRT): Normative Data from Law Enforcement Personnel on Voice Discrimination and Sorting
articles.authors: Andrea Fröhlich; Volker Dellwo; John Peter French; Meike Ramon
articles.abstract: In 2009, Russell et al. identified four “Super-Recognizers” (SRs) with exceptional face processing abilities. The potential existence of voice Super-Recognizers (VSRs) has been discussed both scientifically and related to high-stakes areas like law enforcement, which they could in principle support. Existing methods to formally assess voice identity processing (VIP) are both limited, and oftentimes lack the sensitivity required to reveal superior performance. Moreover, their de facto applied value, e.g. for forensic speaker comparison remains empirically unaddressed. To fill this gap, and drawing on findings from research on (face) SRs, we propose a preliminary working definition for VSRs and report normative data for a novel test battery designed to assess superior VIP: the Zürich Voice Super-Recognizer Test (ZVSRT). Modelling potential VSR deployment scenarios, the ZVSRT involves three difficult perceptual tasks. Its stimuli – derived from a forensic corpus – were selected using a deep learning–based open-source automatic speaker recognition system to ensure the creation of challenging trials befitting its intended purpose. The reported ZVSRT normative data was obtained from a cohort of Swiss law enforcement personnel (N = 204), who completed its constituent components: a voice discrimination, and two voice sorting tasks. These data demonstrate the ZVSRT sensitivity towards capturing the full range of VIP ability – from very low to high performance levels. We discuss future directions, including the utility of the ZVSRT and VSRs’ potential relevance for forensic applications.

articles.title: Expectation-management cues modify delayed processing of unexpected words
articles.authors: Benjamin Adam Menashe; Oren Kadosh; Yoram Bonneh; Michal Ben-Shachar
articles.abstract: Mirative markers, linguistic elements that encode surprise (e.g., “surprisingly”), are widely used to manage readers’ expectations during sentence processing. In theory, mirative markers should prepare readers for an upcoming expectation violation, mitigating the additional processing costs of unexpected words. However, empirical evidence regarding their real-time efficacy remains limited and contradictory. To test whether these cues modulate real-time processing of subsequent unexpected words, we implemented a simultaneous eye-tracking and EEG paradigm. Thirty native Hebrew speakers read sentences containing an expected or unexpected target word, preceded by a mirative marker or a neutral marker. Processing effort was measured using oculomotor inhibition (OMI) duration and N400 amplitude. OMI is the involuntary suppression of microsaccades and eye blinks following stimulus presentation. Results revealed a clear predictability effect at the target word, with unexpected items eliciting longer OMI duration and greater N400 amplitude than expected items. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first known demonstration that OMI duration is sensitive to word predictability during reading. Additionally, results show that the presence of a mirative marker did not modify the response at the target word, but it did eliminate the “spillover” predictability effect at the subsequent word (T+1). These findings support a delayed modulation account of expectation management, where mirative markers modify delayed, but not immediate, processing costs of unexpected words. The results reconcile previous discrepancies regarding real-time and offline effects of expectation management and support a flexible version of the Uniform Information Density (UID) framework.

articles.title: Capturing the temporal dynamics of personality in daily life: The Personality and Contextualized Experiences (PACE) Study
articles.authors: Anabel Büchner; Friedrich Martin Götz; Emorie D Beck; Lisa Shi Yun Li; Andrew Kwok Leung Yeung; Jessie Sun; Benjamin Hardin; Kai Tobias Horstmann
articles.abstract: Thoughts, feelings, and behaviors constantly change in everyday life. Dynamic personality approaches emphasize that these short-term changes are not only relevant for understanding how enduring personality patterns arise but are themselves central to what personality is. Although the growing use of the experience sampling method (ESM) has made it more feasible to apply such approaches, methodological challenges limit the inferences that can be drawn about temporal personality dynamics. This paper describes the rationale, procedure, and dataset of the Personality and Contextualized Experiences (PACE) Study, a large, multi- site ESM study that comprises 1,908 undergraduates (130,402 observations) across Canada, Germany, and the United States. Of these, 714 participants completed the entire study (baseline survey, ≥ 100 ESM surveys, and follow-up survey). The PACE Study aims to advance the study of personality dynamics by combining a large sample with several methodological features targeting key design and measurement aspects for accurately capturing and interpreting these dynamics. The features encompass an experimental comparison of two sampling designs, retrospective assessments of missed states, and a personalized assessment of situational information. The study further includes a newly developed global self-report questionnaire intended to capture aspects of people’s dynamic patterns of states without requiring ESM data.

articles.title: Informed Voting Through Incidental News Exposure? –  Reconceptualizing the O-S-R-O-R Model for Social Media
articles.authors: Jana H Dreston; German Neubaum
articles.abstract: The O-S-R-O-R framework posits that news exposure affects political participation by promoting political discussion and increasing political knowledge. However, due to the widespread adoption of social media as news platforms, this model requires revision for three reasons. First, the level of intentionality of news exposure should be considered because intentional versus incidental exposure to news on social media was found to affect learning and discussion differently. Second, subjective knowledge must be considered alongside objective knowledge because accumulating evidence suggests that the actual and perceived learning effects of social media news use differ. Third, prior work has largely neglected qualitative distinctions of different forms of participation. We address this issue by incorporating “aligned voting” as an outcome. To test these model refinements, we conducted a pre-registered, two-wave panel survey surrounding the 2025 German federal election (N = 697). The results showed that the intentionality of social media news exposure is key in shaping subsequent knowledge gains and political actions, such as voting. Consistent with the O-S-R-O-R framework, exposure to news on social media can enhance the subjective sense of political knowledge. When individuals are incidentally exposed to news on social media and recognize its relevance, this can enhance their objective knowledge. This, in turn, helps them vote in line with their personal stances. These findings support a reconceptualization of the  O-S-R-O-R framework to account for learning and participation in algorithmically curated social media news environments.

articles.title: Errors in social network knowledge predict how ties evolve in the future
articles.authors: Alice Xia; Yi Yang Teoh; Apoorva Bhandari; Oriel FeldmanHall
articles.abstract: A striking feature of people’s social knowledge is that it is riddled with errors. These errors—e.g., making mistakes about who are actually friends in a social network—has typically been attributed to cognitive limitations or heuristics that prioritize knowledge of general social patterns over details about specific ties. Here, we demonstrate that such errors instead reflect an adaptive link prediction process that anticipates how the network will evolve far into the future. By longitudinally following a large, real-world social network (N=196) and tracking the formation and dissolution of social ties over the course of a year, we show that judgments that are wrong in the moment accurately forecast which relationships will emerge or dissolve up to six months later. On average, participants’ errors predicted tie formation nearly 3x, and tie loss more than 1.2x above chance levels. Beyond the use of simple heuristics like triadic closure and homophily, computational modeling reveals that successful link prediction relies on mental representations of the social network that integrates information about both direct and indirect, long-range ties between individuals. Having a social network representation that is future-oriented yields distinct social advantages: those who are better able to predict changes in the network become more centrally positioned over time, contingent on their initial position.

articles.title: Instrumentalising gender conspiracy theories: how narratives about gender ideology may both reflect and fuel general institutional distrust
articles.authors: Peter Teličák; Jakub Šrol; Eva Ballova Mikuskova; Magdalena Adamus
articles.abstract: In two cross-sectional and one longitudinal study conducted in Slovakia and Czechia (total N = 2339, 50,7% women; aged between 18 and 89 years), we tested whether gender ideology narratives are linked with conspiratorial thinking - operationalised as either specific conspiracy beliefs or conspiracy mentality - and pinpointed their most pronounced correlates as political ideologies and institutional distrust. The cross-sectional results show that support for gender ideology narratives is associated with conspiratorial thinking and, albeit unrelated to sociodemographic variables, shows systematic associations with institutional distrust and political stances as expressed by either collective narcissism or conservative political orientation. The preregistered Study 3 fine-tunes the findings by revealing some bidirectional temporal patterns at the within-participants level only with institutional distrust. The results point to a mutually reinforcing nexus between the gender ideology narratives and distrust thereby fostering the understanding of the narratives as embedded within a wider context of power challenging conspiracy theories. Finally, the paper offers insights into how–by exploiting and instilling the sense of distrust–gender ideology narratives can be instrumentalised to tilt political preferences towards anti-establishment, non-mainstream parties that present themselves as beacons of traditional values.

articles.title: Subject Preference as a Flexible Interpretive Heuristic in Thematic Role Assignment
articles.authors: Qingwei Xue; Yi Liu; Mingzhu Yuan; Zhurui Zhang; Tilo Kircher; Luyao Chen; Yifei He
articles.abstract: Sentence-initial arguments often receive interpretive priority during thematic role assignment, reflecting a tendency commonly referred to as “subject preference”. However, whether this preference reflects a stable commitment to a subject-first structural analysis in the final interpretation of the sentence remains unclear. To address this question, we manipulated the availability of verb-based semantic cues in a Mandarin NP1–NP2–Verb paradigm, such that they either provided sufficient information to determine the actor in subject–object and object–subject orders (cue-determined conditions) or remained insufficient to uniquely determine the actor (cue-underdetermined, ambiguous condition). One hundred and twenty native Mandarin speakers completed an actor-choice task, with response times and confidence ratings recorded. Our results showed no evidence of an NP1 advantage under cue-determined conditions. When semantic cues are underdetermined, we observed a modest NP1 preference emerged, accompanied by faster but lower-confidence responses. These findings suggest that subject preference is characterized as a flexible, cue-sensitive heuristic rather than a fixed structural default.

articles.title: Embodied visitor experience in a festival attraction: A mixed-methods evaluation of Art of Perception in Pune, India
articles.authors: Kohinoor Monish Darda; Hansika Mangwani; Sanjana Edwankar; Sakina Bharmal; Tanvi Raghuram; Siyona Varghese; Samrddhee Pathare; Amisha Keshan; Ritika Deshpande; Sakshi Kharbanda
articles.abstract: This study evaluates Art of Perception, a seven-zone attraction presented at Creative Lab Festival 2026 in Pune, India. A convergent mixed-methods design combined matched pre-post surveys from 200 visitors (166 complete cases) with learning statements, 1,339 face-judgment votes, and 65 post-workshop drawings. Five of six self-report outcomes showed positive paired differences after Holm correction. Bodily relaxation showed the largest difference (22.9 points on a 0-100 scale; standardised difference = 0.69); trust in perception did not differ reliably. Data indicated learning about perception, neuroplasticity, art-brain relations, and nature connection. The observational, immediate, and self-reported design does not establish causation or durability. The paper proposes a public laboratory of perception as a provisional framework for construct-aligned attraction design and evaluation.

articles.title: An Expressivist Account of Moral Responsibility
articles.authors: Kiichi INARIMORI; Yugo MAEDA; Shintaro Takahashi; Kengo Miyazono
articles.abstract: Moral expressivism holds that moral statements fundamentally express non-doxastic attitudes (e.g., emotions or desires) rather than doxastic attitudes (e.g., beliefs) that correspond to objective and descriptive contents. This paper applies expressivism to responsibility statements and proposes Retributive Responsibility Expressivism. According to this account, responsibility statements such as “X deserves to be punished for doing Y” fundamentally express a non-doxastic attitude—specifically, our retributive desire for X to be punished. Across two empirical studies focusing on laypeople’s linguistic intuitions, we adopt the methodology of Moorean absurdities to evaluate this expressivist account. In line with expressivist predictions, participants systematically judged first-person Moorean responsibility sentences (e.g., “X deserves to be punished, but I do not want X to be punished”) as semantically infelicitous, whereas third-person versions were judged as making sense. Furthermore, restricting sentences to an autocentric interpretation markedly strengthened this perceived infelicity. These results provide novel empirical support for an expressivist semantics of moral responsibility. Finally, we argue that accepting an expressivist account of moral responsibility—depending on the specific version (e.g., pure vs. hybrid)—calls for reconsidering the traditional role of responsibility judgments in the free will debate.

articles.title: The Australian under-16 social media ban: Early influences on access and its relationship with reading
articles.authors: Signy Wegener; Jasmine Spencer; Andrea Salins; Serje Robidoux; Robert Savage; Anne Castles
articles.abstract: Concerns abound that time spent on social media might displace more developmentally adaptive activities, such as reading. In December 2025, the Australian government introduced a world-first social media ban for young people under the age of 16, providing an opportunity to explore whether social media use and the efficacy of the ban are associated with current reading behaviours. In this study, Australians aged 12 to 15 years completed a cross-sectional self-report online survey between March and June 2026. Prior to the ban, 81.55% of the sample used social media. Users of social media reported reading less frequently, for shorter periods and had lower reading motivation than non-users of social media. For users, the initial effect of the ban was often incomplete or transient, with many users subsequently able to regain access to lost accounts. Post-ban, time spent on social media reduced for those who lost access to some or all of their accounts. Although there were differences in reading times by the effect of the ban in the predicted direction, they were not significant. Further, there were no differences in the strength of the association between reading motivation and reading duration by the effect of the ban. These findings suggest that social media use is associated with lower levels of reading engagement than non-use. The early implementation of the social media ban has only been partially effective and there is presently insufficient evidence that the effect of the ban is associated with differences in current reading engagement.

articles.title: Phonological changes facilitate pragmatic inference during lexical access in Bengali verbs
articles.authors: Pijush Kanti Gayen; Monsija Mitra; Samar Husain
articles.abstract: How do listeners map fine-grained phonological variation onto a speaker’s communicative intention during lexical access? We address this question using a restricted set of Bengali imperative verb forms in which stem-vowel height alternation is associated with different directive speech acts. Native speakers of Bengali (N=176) completed (i) an intention-scaling task to assess perceived illocutionary force and (ii) a cross-modal lexical decision task with auditory verb primes and visual speech-act targets. The lexical decision experiment manipulated prime--target stimulus onset asynchrony (SOA: 30 ms, 60 ms, 240 ms) to test the time course of phonological-to-pragmatic activation. Intention-scaling results showed that participants reliably distinguished the two intended speech acts. In the lexical decision task, congruent speech-act targets were recognised substantially faster than controls at the 60ms SOA (approximately 100ms facilitation for both order and request), whereas effects were small and not reliable at 30ms and 240ms. Request trials also showed slightly longer latencies than order trials, consistent with a higher inferential load for requests. Together, the results provide behavioural evidence that phonological cues can rapidly bias speech-act interpretation, with a temporally constrained window for lexical-pragmatic integration.

articles.title: Feminized Perceptions of Care Work Create Unique Barriers to Labor Organizing
articles.authors: Grace Flores-Robles; Ana Gantman
articles.abstract: Care work (e.g., nursing) is critical to a functioning society, yet workers in these occupations (predominantly women) often experience low pay, and face opposition when they organize for better wages. In the current research, we examined whether care workers face gendered barriers in labor organizing. Using historical data of work stoppages in the United States, Study 1 established differences in the frequency and duration of work stoppages for care and non-care unions. Study 2 found that jobs higher in perceived care were less likely to receive support for their labor organizing. Study 3 experimentally found differences in the preferred length of strikes for care and non-care workers and separately found that gender ideologies were related to how long participants wanted workers to go on strike. Together, these findings demonstrate that care workers face unique barriers to organizing partly because the work they do is feminized.

articles_hidden.title: Toward a Layered Framework of Environmental Experience: Integrating Sensory, Perceptual, and Semantic Processes
articles_hidden.authors: Dylan Chau Huynh; Aja Khalid Hussein; Farzaneh Behzadi; Amir Kalantarifard; Lars Brorson Fich; Andreas Møgelmose; Simone Kühn; Klaus Gramann; Zakaria Djebbara
articles_hidden.abstract: Environmental experience is shaped by sensory stimulation, perceptual organization, and semantic meaning, yet these dimensions are often studied in isolation or reduced to broad environmental categories. This fragmentation limits our ability to explain how environments are experienced, how bottom-up and top-down processes interact, and how person-environment relations can be studied in a mechanistically informative way. Here, we provide an integrative review of work spanning embodied cognition, predictive processing, environmental psychology, and related traditions, and use this synthesis to develop a human-centered framework of environmental experience. In this framework, environmental experience unfolds across three analytically separable but experientially intertwined dimensions: sensory, perceptual, and semantic. The sensory dimension concerns immediate stimulation and salience; the perceptual dimension concerns the organization of environmental input into coherent, action-relevant structure; and the semantic dimension concerns learned meaning, cultural interpretation, familiarity, and contextual relevance. We argue that these dimensions are not sequential stages, but parallel, co-active, and mutually constraining aspects of lived environmental engagement. We then outline methodological implications for studying both dimension-specific contributions and their interaction, emphasizing convergent, multimethod, and temporally sensitive designs spanning behavioral, physiological, neurocognitive, and computational approaches. The framework provides an integrative basis for moving beyond static or overly coarse descriptions of environments and toward a more precise account of how environmental experience emerges across brain, body, and world.

articles_hidden.title: Optimizing Behavioral Strategy Selection during Cognitive Behavior Therapy for Procrastination using Machine Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Devon LoParo; Magdalena Pietruch; Weronika Maria Browarczyk; Joachim Kowalski; Jarosław M. Michałowski; Marek Wypych
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: To determine whether machine-learning models using baseline self-report data could
personalize selection between two behavioral strategies embedded within cognitive-behavioral
therapy (CBT) for procrastination.

Methods: Participants were 256 Polish-speaking university students aged 18–26 years (M=22.4;
73.0% women) who completed active treatment in two preregistered randomized trials
(development sample, N=173; external validation sample, N=83). Participants received five
weekly group CBT sessions with identical psychoeducation and cognitive restructuring but
different behavioral modules: Realistic Planning and Timely Beginning (RPT) or Working Time
Restriction (WTR). Separate partial least-squares regression models used 483 baseline
demographic and self-report items to predict posttreatment Aitken Procrastination
Inventory–Revised (API-R) scores under each strategy. Predicted between-strategy differences
and Youden-index cutoffs generated recommendations: RPT, WTR, Either, or Neither. Because
treatment assignment was randomized, outcomes could be compared between participants whose
assigned treatment matched versus mismatched their model-derived recommendation.

Results: In the development trial, matched participants had lower posttreatment API-R scores
than mismatched participants (p=5.6×10−24; d=1.90) and higher likely-response rates
(p=1.8×10−15; RR=4.6). In the validation trial, each treatment-specific model explained 9% of
outcome variance. Matched participants again had lower API-R scores (p=.009; d=.53) and
higher response rates (p=.04; RR=1.3). Differences remained at six months (p=.033; d=.40).

Conclusion: Together, these findings indicate that personalization of procrastination treatment
can be achieved by modeling differential response to specific behavioral components rather than
entire treatment packages, supporting precision intervention in procrastination and beyond.
Further, explorative examination of predictors suggests that individuals may benefit from a
mechanism-informed, but not strictly mechanism-deterministic, precision framework.

articles_hidden.title: Consciousness Beyond the Brain: The Role of the Autonomic Nervous System in Non-ordinary States of Consciousness
articles_hidden.authors: Lana Porter; Valerie Bonnelle; Marieke Schölvinck; Martha N. Havenith
articles_hidden.abstract:
Non-ordinary states of consciousness (NOSCs), whether entered via psychedelics, breathwork, hypnosis or other means, show striking therapeutic promise by improving well-being and reducing psychopathology across diverse conditions. While the neuronal dynamics underpinning such therapeutic shifts in consciousness have to some extent been mapped, research has mainly focused on the central nervous system (CNS). In contrast, the contribution of the autonomic nervous system (ANS) to NOSCs remains largely unexplored. At the same time, growing evidence indicates that beyond simply regulating bodily functions, the ANS mediates a range of processes directly linked to the core effects of many NOSCs, from emotional regulation to interoception and cognitive function.

In this review, we delineate the potential role of the ANS in shaping NOSCs, and discuss pathways by which ANS responses may support the cortical dynamics associated with NOSCs. Based on these insights, we propose a framework whereby inducing physiological stress within a conducive context supports the emergence of NOSCs, and the coexistence of high arousal and relaxation, i.e. of both sympathetic and parasympathetic tone, serves a hallmark of peak NOSCs. Finally, we highlight opportunities for future research to pinpoint these dynamics further, and offer an outlook on how understanding the ANS dynamics linked to NOSCs can allow us to induce NOSCs more safely, optimize their therapeutic impact, and provide cost-effective yet powerful physiological tools to monitor and facilitate these states in real time.

articles_hidden.title: The role of childhood neurocognition in eating disorder state transitions: findings from the ABCD cohort
articles_hidden.authors: Jenni Leppanen; Karina Allen; Marja Kaila-Vanhatalo; Kate Tchanturia; Ian Kelleher
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Neurocognitive difficulties have been proposed to play a role in the development and progression of eating disorders (EDs). However, prospective evidence from general population samples is limited. This study examined whether childhood neurocognition predicted the development of threshold or sub-threshold ED over 6 years in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) cohort.
Method: We analysed data from 11,378 children aged 8 – 11 years from the ABCD Study. ED states were derived from parent-reported Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia data at baseline and annual follow-ups. Neurocognition was assessed with the NIH Toolbox Cognition battery at baseline. Multi-state models were used to estimate ED state transitions and the impact of childhood neurocognition. 
Results: Across the observation periods, the most probable state to stay in or transition to was the no ED state and the probability of transitioning from no ED to sub-threshold or threshold ED state was 0.5 – 1%. Better working memory performance was associated with a small but significantly lower probability of transitioning from sub-threshold ED to no ED. Better performance on the episodic memory task was associated with a small but significantly lower risk of transitioning from no ED to sub-threshold ED. 
Discussion: Childhood neurocognition showed limited influence on later ED state transitions in this general population sample. Working memory and episodic memory were the only cognitive domains associated with specific transitions, suggesting that these functions could be relevant to early ED risk and recovery and further investigation is warranted.

articles_hidden.title: Linking Trait Items of Self-Control to Broader Conceptualizations in Daily Life  Using Machine Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Anabel Büchner; Kai Tobias Horstmann; Marie Hennecke
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent research suggests that self-control in everyday life is composed of different components (frequency, intensity, and successful resolution of self-control conflicts), and that individuals seem to differ in their abilities to resolve different types of self-control conflicts (initiation, persistence, inhibition). To date, however, it is unclear how established trait measures capture individual differences regarding these different components and types of self-control. We apply machine learning techniques to experience sampling data (N = 491; 9,634 measurement occasions) and identify which items from various trait scales best predict the different components and types of self-control in daily life. Commonly used trait items indexed all components to some extent, but most strongly successful conflict resolution. Contrary to our expectations, we were unable to predict the frequency, intensity, or successful resolution of inhibition conflicts, despite various trait measures being primarily developed for this conflict type. By comparing the most important predictors, we found meaningful theoretical differences between the components and types. We conclude that applying a broader conceptualization of self-control offers novel opportunities for exploring diverse routes to successful goal attainment and discuss theoretical and methodological implications of the findings for future research on trait self-control.

articles_hidden.title: Bayesian Hierarchical Models for Longitudinal Meta-Analysis in Sports Science: A Practical Tutorial Using brms
articles_hidden.authors: Sandro Balbino Júnior; Ahlan Benezar Lima; Humberto M. Carvalho
articles_hidden.abstract: Meta-analysis in sports science has predominantly focused on cross-sectional comparisons, leaving the temporal structure of longitudinal evidence largely unexploited. This tutorial introduces Bayesian hierarchical longitudinal meta-analysis as a principled framework for synthesizing repeated-measures data and illustrates its implementation using the R package `brms`. We demonstrate a complete analytical workflow---from model specification and prior selection to convergence checks, posterior predictive checks, and reporting—using a simulated dataset based on pubertal stature growth in male youth athletes. The worked example highlights how polynomial growth models recover biologically meaningful parameters, such as age at peak height velocity, with full uncertainty quantification. Additionally, we compare three prior specifications using leave-one-out cross-validation to test robustness. Fully annotated code scripts are provided, providing researchers with the practical tools and methodological reasoning necessary to apply longitudinal Bayesian meta-analysis to their own work in sports science and related fields.

articles_hidden.title: Confidently Neutral: Cognitive States of Neutrality in Auditory Perceptual Decisions
articles_hidden.authors: Luzie Kallfaß; Mara Wolter; Carla Ludig; Christoph Korn; Verena Wagner; Yulia Oganian
articles_hidden.abstract:
Theories of perceptual decision-making attribute neutral decisions to internal states such as inattention or low confidence, detached from sensory properties of the stimulus. Consequently, forced-choice paradigms do not allow for neutral decision outcomes, even under ambiguity. In contrast, epistemology posits multiple distinct neutral states, notably mere indecision – an intermediate state associated with low confidence and continuous information gathering – and settled indecision – a final state reached by actively suspending judgment after deliberation. Here, we tested whether distinct neutral states can be identified in perceptual decision-making. We induced perceptual ambiguity in a speech discrimination task using German vowel minimal-pair words, e.g., satt/Saat (“full”/“seed”), acoustically manipulated to range from low to high ambiguity. On each trial, participants could categorize the stimulus as one of the two words, request its repetition (indicating mere indecision), or select a final neutral response (indicating settled indecision). In Experiment 1 (n = 36), repetition requests and final neutral responses occurred most frequently for ambiguous stimuli, reflecting stimulus acoustics. Repetition requests were often followed by final neutral responses, indicating sequential evidence accumulation. In Experiment 2 (n = 37), embedding targets in speech-shaped noise increased final neutral responses for less ambiguous targets, showing that settled indecision can be elicited by external noise. Experiment 3 (n = 38) showed comparable metacognitive confidence ratings for final neutral and categorized responses. Overall, our results support the existence of distinct neutral
states (mere and settled indecision) in perceptual decision-making and call for their integration in models of perceptual decisions under uncertainty.

articles_hidden.title: A twin study of genetic and environmental aetiologies of associations between sensory processing sensitivity and psychotic-like experiences
articles_hidden.authors: Marloes Mak; Angelica Ronald; Corina Greven; Tessa Marije van Leeuwen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Individual differences in Sensory Processing Sensitivity (SPS) indicate variation in depth of information processing, emotional and empathic reactivity, and sensitivity to subtle environmental details. Psychotic-like experiences (PLEs) are non-clinical psychotic symptoms (usually occasional, mild hallucinations and delusions). This study tested the associations between SPS and PLEs, and whether associations between PLEs and neuroticism and stressful life events are moderated by SPS.

Methods
A sample of 2888 adolescent twins, from the Twins Early Development Study, were assessed longitudinally at 16, 21 and 26 years.  The phenotypic and aetiological associations of SPS and PLEs were studied using twin model fitting. Additionally, the interaction between SPS and life events in determining PLEs was studied longitudinally. 

Results 
All tested PLEs were significantly associated with SPS. The largest point estimates were for associations between SPS and Paranoia, Hallucinations, and Cognitive Disorganization (Bs: 0.14 – 0.30). AE models with Cholesky decomposition showed that genetic influences on SPS accounted for 23%-71% of phenotypic correlations between SPS and PLEs Paranoia, Hallucinations and Cognitive Disorganisation, beyond Neuroticism. Longitudinally, SPS moderated the association between number of stressful life events and experienced PLEs (i.e., Paranoia, Hallucinations and Hedonia). 

Conclusions
This study is the first to demonstrate phenotypic and aetiological associations between SPS and PLEs. The results further indicate that the longitudinal association between stressful life events (another known PLE risk factors) and PLEs is genetically moderated by SPS.

Keywords
Sensory Processing Sensitivity; Psychotic-Like Experiences; Stressful Life Events; Twin Design; Longitudinal

articles_hidden.title: Ensemble clustering: A practical tutorial
articles_hidden.authors: Caroline X. Gao; Shengqi Wang; Ye Zhu; Myriam Ziou; Shu Mei Teo; Catherine L Smith; Derek Chiu; Aline Talhouk; Sue M. Cotton; Dominic Dwyer
articles_hidden.abstract: Cluster analysis is an explorative analytical method, serving as a critical tool in psychology, psychiatry and related fields to map heterogeneous data into meaningful subgroups. Despite their extensive historical use, traditional clustering techniques suffer from a lack of stability, robustness, and generalisability. These issues stem from the inherent difficulties of the clustering optimization problem as well as the stochastic nature of algorithm optimizers. To address these challenges, we demonstrate the use of methods utilising ensemble learning techniques to combine clustering results from different algorithms, model specifications, and/or sampled sub-datasets to form a single, more reliable consensus of clustering solutions. We detail ensemble clustering principles, variations in base clustering generation models, and consensus methods. Detailed introductions in existing R libraries and practical examples using R code are provided to guide users in both implementing and optimising ensemble clustering models. We then include simulation studies of real-world data to demonstrate the substantial benefit of ensemble clustering compared with single-run clustering models. The resources presented here will enable researchers to apply advanced clustering techniques to decompose heterogeneous and complex psychological data into stable subgroups.

articles_hidden.title: The relationship between mental time travel and aesthetic experience: a scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Yizhen Zhou; Hideaki Kawabata
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental time travel (MTT), the ability to project oneself backward to remember past experiences or forward to anticipate future events, shares neural correlates with aesthetic experiences within the default mode network. Previous research has demonstrated that mental imagery, a representational component of MTT, is deeply intertwined with aesthetic experience. However, a comprehensive overview of how retrospective (i.e., autobiographical/episodic memory) and prospective (i.e., episodic future thinking) components of MTT interact with aesthetic experiences is lacking. Guided by Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines, this scoping review identified 16 studies published between 2004–2026. Overall, evidence demonstrates a dynamic, bidirectional relationship between the retrospective component of MTT and aesthetic experiences: aesthetic appreciation facilitates episodic memory encoding and consolidation; furthermore, autobiographical memory and self-relevance appraisals drive aesthetic experiences. Empirical research on prospective MTT in aesthetic contexts remains limited.

articles_hidden.title: Do Youth Offending Labels Matter? The Impact of the Label “Young Serious Offender” on Public Attitudes Toward Youth Justice
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Yesberg; Clare-Ann Fortune; Hasi Kolongahapitiya
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on the impact of crime-first labels on public attitudes has focused almost exclusively on sexual offending. This pre-registered conceptual replication of Harris and Socia (2016) examined the effect of the label 'young serious offender' on support for punitive youth justice policies and beliefs about rehabilitation. Using an experimental design, 393 adult residents of New Zealand and Australia were randomly allocated to receive statements using either 'young serious offender' or the person-first alternative 'young people who have committed serious offences'. Contrary to our hypotheses, we found no evidence the label influenced attitudes relative to the person-first alternative, and no consistent moderation effects were observed. Exploratory analyses identified political orientation, ethnicity, and educational attainment as significant predictors of both punitive attitudes and belief in rehabilitation. These findings suggest crime-first labelling effects may only appear where strong stigma and well-established stereotypes already exist (e.g., sexual offending). However, this null result reflects only a single, one-off exposure in a survey context. The introduction of the Young Serious Offender designation in New Zealand embeds crime-first language into policy, with potentially cumulative effects that a one-off exposure cannot capture. Future research should use longitudinal designs to examine repeated exposure to labels over time.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation as a Digital, Individualized, and Adaptive Neurotechnology Platform
articles_hidden.authors: Anup Sharma; Manu Sharma; Hamed Ekhtiari
articles_hidden.abstract: Brain and mental health disorders are heterogeneous, dynamic, and increasingly managed through combinations of pharmacologic, psychotherapeutic, neuromodulatory, and digital interventions. Psychoeducation remains foundational though it is often delivered in static, standardized formats, in which fluctuations in cognition, affect, insight, and readiness to learn are not explicitly addressed. This chapter proposes Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation (NIPE) as a digital, individualized, and adaptive neurotechnology platform that reframes psychoeducation as a learning-driven intervention targeting mechanistic understanding, metacognition, and self-regulation. NIPE is conceptualized as a closed-loop learning system in which multimodal brain-behavior and contextual inputs are used to infer clinically meaningful functional states, such as arousal, fatigue, attentional stability, and affective load. These states guide responsive delivery of neuroscience-grounded explanations and skills, followed by explicit evaluation of learning-relevant responses and reinforcement processes that support consolidation and durable skill transfer beyond the platform itself. The chapter describes how adaptive personalization can be implemented through layered approaches, including rule-based logic to preserve interpretability and safety, data-driven machine learning to estimate functional learning states and optimize content delivery, and constrained generative interfaces to translate validated concepts into personalized language while maintaining clinical fidelity. Because NIPE sits at the interface of psychoeducation, digital therapeutics, and clinical decision support, trust, ethics, and equity are treated as core system requirements rather than downstream considerations, with emphasis on ongoing consent, privacy, transparency of adaptive processes, and alignment with clinical workflows. NIPE outputs are framed to support patients, clinicians, and health systems through low-burden learning summaries, interpretable clinician-facing dashboards, and group-level insights that extend beyond engagement metrics. Finally, the chapter outlines future directions for NIPE, including mechanistic studies of learning and metacognition, evaluation designs for adaptive interventions, and platform-level validation and governance. Together, NIPE is positioned as an infrastructure for brain-based learning support for patients and their stakeholders.

articles_hidden.title: Pilot Results of the Reintegrative Protocol in the Treatment of Binge Eating
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph Nicolosi; Christopher Rosik
articles_hidden.abstract: Experiencing a traumatic event, or a series of traumatic events, may increase the probability of subsequent development of binge eating and Binge Eating Disorder (BED). BED is the most common eating disorder in the United States, affecting some 2%-4% of people yearly. Due to the large prevalence of this disorder, as well as the burden BED puts on those living with it, effective treatment practices for treating BED are necessary. To date, there has been no research specifically examining the novel reintegrative protocol in a clinical setting as a treatment modality for BED. The purpose of this small, multiple-baseline pilot study was to explore the practicality and efficacy of the reintegrative protocol in treating BED by treating traumatic memories of individuals who engage in binge eating. Overall, the reintegrative protocol demonstrates promise as a tool for affect regulation and the treatment of BED. While implementing the protocol was feasible, the results varied among the 6 heterogeneous subjects and therefore, further research is required.

articles_hidden.title: Humanlike representation of social networks in large language models
articles_hidden.authors: Jae-Young Son; Daniel Carstensen; Serra Elizabeth Favila
articles_hidden.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have made great progress in their general reasoning capabilities, reasoning about social relationships has remained a challenge. In contrast, humans are naturally skilled at reasoning about how people are connected to one another, even in large, complex social networks. Recent research in cognitive science suggests that a key component of human social intelligence is the ability to represent social networks using multistep abstraction, which integrates knowledge of both direct and indirect social connections, and therefore supports inferences about network members’ social proximity to one another. Here, we test whether LLMs represent social networks using similar computational principles. In Study 1, we converted an existing human social navigation task into text and recorded LLM responses to the same problems humans were tasked with solving. LLMs’ behaviors closely mirrored those of human participants, and were best-explained by Katz communicability, a model of multistep abstraction that captures how humans represent and navigate social networks. In Study 2, we tested whether these multistep representations persisted in a task where they offered no benefit—and were in fact detrimental to task accuracy—and found that LLMs continued to show a multistep signature even in this context. These findings suggest that multistep abstraction may be a core property of how LLMs represent relational information, closely paralleling accounts of human cognitive maps.

articles_hidden.title: Impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on Canadian men and women with depressive and anxiety disorders: Time trend data from 9 waves of the iCARE Study
articles_hidden.authors: Marianne Berthiaume; Christina Bertachas; Mariam Atoui; Simon Bacon; Kim Lavoie
articles_hidden.abstract:
Importance: Psychosocial, employment and health impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic merit further examination among those with a mental health condition, as previous research shows these individuals were already vulnerable to these outcomes prior to this health emergency. 
Objective: To examine the 2-year psychosocial, employment, and health risk behaviour impacts of COVID-19 on Canadians adults with anxiety and/or depressive disorders, as a function of sex. 
Design, Setting and Participants: Nine cross-sectional online surveys from the iCARE Study were conducted between November 2020 and September 2022, weighted for age, sex and province. Participants were Canadian adults recruited through an online polling firm.
Main Outcomes and Measures: Rates of participants who reported significant psychosocial, employment, and health risk behaviour impacts as a result of COVID-19, and changes over a 2 year period. Formulation of the hypotheses preceded data collection. Measures included mental health status, psychosocial impacts of COVID-19 and changes in health risk behaviours. 
Results: Respondents (N = 27 142) were 52.6% being women with a mean age of 48.4 (SD 16.87) years. 24.33% reported being diagnosed with anxiety and/or depression disorders (N = 6411). Those with a mental health condition, versus those without, reported significantly greater emotional distress [ORadj (95% CI) = 3.84-5.57 (3.56-6.01)], interpersonal conflicts [3.39 (3.00-3.83)], employment loss [2.03 (1.82-2.27)], income reduction [1.90 (1.73-2.09)] and worse health behaviours (e.g., smoking [2.78 (2.52 to 3.06]), drug use [3.24 (2.96 to 3.54)]), and limited access to medical care [2.54 (2.32 to 2.78)]. Impacts on mental health, conflict, job/income and access to medical care decreased overtime (all p’s <.001), while difficulty affording food increased (p=0.02). Women with these disorders, compared to men, reported more emotional distress [OR (95% CI) = 1.17-1.39 (1.05-1.55)] and worse diet [1.36 (1.21-1.52)] and physical activity levels [1.24 (1.12-1.38)], but were less likely to report increased vaping [OR .67 (.57-.79)], alcohol [.86 (.76-.97)] and drug use [.79 (.70-.90)].
Conclusion and Relevance: Findings indicate that government initiatives aimed at mitigating the multidimensional impacts of a pandemic should prioritize individuals with mental health conditions, with women needing more psychosocial and health behaviour support, and men needing more substance use support.

articles_hidden.title: Leveraging Word Knowledge from Everyday Language
articles_hidden.authors: Layla Unger; Emma James
articles_hidden.abstract: Within the first few years of life, children go from nonverbal infants to fluent users of hundreds of words. This feat unfolds as children are immersed in a sea of words in conversations, stories and other language contexts. In principle, word contexts might support word learning because words similar in meaning tend to occur in similar contexts. Thus, a child who knows some fruit words and has heard them in the context of "juicy" might learn that a "juicy mango" is also a fruit even without ever seeing a mango. Indeed, cutting-edge large language models leverage just these context cues to form rich representations of words. Yet we do not know whether these cues are an important driver of real-world word learning. We quantified context cues in children’s everyday English language input and found that they did reliably predict real-world word learning, above and beyond other established predictors. These findings illuminate how everyday language scaffolds word learning.

articles_hidden.title: Complex systems methods in ageing research: An overview of emerging approaches
articles_hidden.authors: Gabriela Lunansky; Lotte P. Brinkhof; Ingrid A. van de Leemput; René J Melis; Marcel Olde Rikkert; Geeske Peeters; Rick Quax; Jeroen Uleman; Almar Andreas Leonardus Kok
articles_hidden.abstract:
The application of complex systems science is gaining traction in the field of ageing research. A complex system is a large collection of components whose dynamic interactions lead to 'emergent properties' that cannot be understood or predicted based on knowledge of the components in isolation. Here we conceptualise human ageing as resulting from integrated, multi-scale systems characterised by dynamic interactions within and between biological, behavioural, functional and environmental domains. 
Complexity science provides tools to study these joint dynamics, allowing researchers to address research questions that examine (1) interactions across levels or domains, (2) dynamic processes over time, or (3) emergent behaviour of the system as a whole, which is not reducible to individual components. Studying complex systems can benefit from these methodological tools, which are still underexplored in gerontology and geriatrics. With this article, we intend to inspire and support researchers in the field of ageing to explore the potential of complexity science methods for their own research. 
We explain four different methodological approaches to study complex systems: causal loop diagrams, system dynamics modelling, psychometric network analysis, and dynamical indicators of resilience and complexity. For each of these approaches, we explain their purpose and theoretical assumptions, provide examples from the scientific literature, and discuss their strengths and limitations. As it remains challenging to operationalise complexity-driven research questions and select appropriate methods from the growing range of available methodological approaches, particularly for researchers unfamiliar with them, we hope to have lowered this threshold.

articles_hidden.title: Mentalizing from self and friend perspectives: Relations between neural similarity, affective similarity and social anxiety symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Alicia Vallorani; Kathryn A. McNaughton; Marisa N. Lytle; Michael Hallquist; Elizabeth Redcay; Koraly Perez-Edgar
articles_hidden.abstract: Social interactions are dynamic and complex, relying on tracking variation in your own and your partner’s affective and mental states. Being “in-sync” neurally and building a shared consensus can mark successful social interactions. In addition, social anxiety can impact social experiences. We used a novel, naturalistic paradigm to investigate relations between inter-brain neural similarity within mentalizing regions, affective similarity and social anxiety symptoms. Undergraduate student friend pairs (N = 34, 85% White, 65% Women) engaged in a social interaction while videos previously captured from their individual perspectives were recorded. Participants watched clips of the social interaction from both their own perspective (their personal view of the social interaction) and their friend’s perspective (their friend’s personal view of the social interaction) while fMRI data were collected. They rated their affect after each clip. Inter-brain neural similarity was computed across three conditions: 1) Same-Stimuli: both participants viewed identical visual stimuli as in a traditional neural similarity paradigm, 2) Self-Perspective: both participants viewed the clip from their own perspective like the originally experienced social interaction and 3) Friend-Perspective: both participants viewed the clip from their friend’s perspective, a novel perspective. Participants self-reported their social anxiety symptoms and affective similarity captured affect rating concordance within dyads. In contrast to the Same-Stimuli condition, when participants viewed the clips like they originally experienced social interaction (Self-Perspective), greater affective similarity was associated with greater inter-brain neural similarity. When participants viewed the clips from a novel perspective (Friend-Perspective), participants lower in social anxiety symptoms exhibited greater inter-brain neural similarity with greater affective similarity; whereas, participants higher in social anxiety symptoms exhibited greater inter-brain neural similarity with less affective similarity. The results suggest stimuli from socially relevant perspectives, rather than identical stimuli, may reveal more nuanced brain-behavior dynamics, allowing for a better understanding of individual differences in socioemotional experience.

articles_hidden.title: The evolution of pain and associated anxiety, depression, and suicide was profoundly impacted by predation
articles_hidden.authors: Edgar T. Walters
articles_hidden.abstract: Predation is a powerful evolutionary selection pressure, but its roles in shaping human behavior are not understood. Predators often injure prey in unsuccessful attacks, and they selectively target injured and otherwise impaired prey. Injury commonly causes anxiety-like hypervigilance, which has been shown in squid to increase survival from predatory attack. It also induces persistent hyperactivity of primary nociceptors, which in mammals drives pain and anxiety. In social mammals and some eusocial insects, injury can elicit group antipredator defense and woundtending responses, usually from closely related kin. Accelerated evolution of affective pain is proposed to have occurred in social mammals to facilitate communication of need for support. This function probably evolved rapidly in hominins because of the abundance of large predators and the necessity of cooperative group defense for otherwise relatively defenseless individuals. Affective pain and its empathetic recognition by group members became increasingly useful as cooperative protection and care facilitated the recovery of temporarily incapacitated members to help the group. Such social functions may explain unusual human nociceptor properties that promote persistent pain. When hominin groups were small and predatory threat relentless, the value to the group of each member would have been high. Severe pain and depression could indicate to a member their incapacity and burden to the group, potentially motivating suicidal behavior, while ready access to predators would have made suicide easy. Thus, suicide motivated by intolerable pain and depression could have been under positive selection (genetic and cultural) in cooperative bands of hominins living alongside dangerous predators.

articles_hidden.title: Seeking and integrating social information under uncertainty: the role of high stakes and risky others
articles_hidden.authors: Caroline J Charpentier; Xiaodi Hu
articles_hidden.abstract: When making decisions under risk and ambiguity, we often have the opportunity to know what other people did and adjust our decisions. Yet, the cognitive mechanisms underlying how people actively seek social information, and how such information is integrated into choice, remain poorly understood. We addressed this question using a new social risk-ambiguity task in which participants first made baseline decisions under risk and ambiguity, then, in a social block, actively chose whether to view the decisions of two other players before deciding again. Across two large online samples (Ndiscovery=394, Nreplication=378), we found that social information-seeking increased with reward magnitude and reward probability, but was not affected by ambiguity. Individual differences further showed that participants who were more sensitive to reward probability during baseline choice were also more driven by reward probability when seeking information. Social information influenced both risky and ambiguous choices, even though participants weighed their own prior preferences more strongly. Critically, influence was asymmetric: the risky player exerted stronger influence than the safe player, with more risk/ambiguity-averse individuals exhibiting relatively weaker influence from the risky player. Computational modelling revealed a dissociation between two key processes captured by separable parameters: egocentric discounting (weight of individual vs social information) and asymmetry between risky and safe social influence. Together, these findings provide more integrated insights into the cognitive mechanisms underlying baseline choice, social information-seeking, and social influence under uncertainty, as well as the heterogeneity linking them.

articles_hidden.title: Social cure goes global: Socioeconomic and cultural factors shape social identifications’ effects on wellbeing across 56 countries.
articles_hidden.authors: Radhika Butalia; Tegan Cruwys; Jolanda Jetten; Catherine Haslam; Katrien Fransen; Stef Van Puyenbroeck; Rolf van Dick; Lies Bongaerts; Filip Boen
articles_hidden.abstract: Social identification has been robustly linked to wellbeing. However, most of this evidence relies on samples from White and WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich,  Democratic) nations. In this study, we tested the association between social identification and wellbeing in a global sample (46,156 participants in 56 countries), and assessed whether socioeconomic and cultural factors could explain variation between countries. Across this sample, social identification was positively associated with wellbeing, but these benefits were not uniform. Identification with family and friends (β = 0.24) showed stronger and more consistent associations with wellbeing than national identification (β = 0.07).
