Despite longstanding evidence distinguishing fragmentary (transient) and en bloc (permanent) blackouts, a measure distinguishing these two forms of blackout (the Alcohol-Induced Blackout Measure-2 [ABOM-2]) was only recently developed and has not been psychometrically evaluated among young adults with a history of alcohol-induced blackouts. The present study evaluated the psychometric properties of the ABOM-2, particularly its longitudinal measurement invariance and prospective predictive validity, among 169 heavy-drinking young adults (ages 18–30) with a history of blackout. Confirmatory factor analyses at baseline (T1) and one-month follow-up (T2) supported previous research showing the ABOM-2 items are best represented by two correlated factors. Both factors, en bloc and fragmentary, demonstrated convergent validity, showing significant associations with hazardous drinking, alcohol consumption, and alcohol-related consequences. In concurrent convergent and prospective predictive regression models that accounted for relevant covariates and included both types of blackouts, en bloc (but not fragmentary) blackouts significantly predicted hazardous drinking, alcohol consumption, and consequences across time. Longitudinal measurement invariance testing provided evidence for configural, metric, and scalar invariance across T1 and T2, supporting the measurement equivalence of ABOM-2 over time. Findings reinforce the distinction between en bloc and fragmentary blackouts, support the convergent and predictive validity of the ABOM-2, and highlight the clinical and research utility of the ABOM-2 as a reliable tool for assessing blackout across time. En bloc blackouts, in particular, serve as a robust marker of alcohol-related risk among young adults.

articles_hidden.title: The partner as reader: recognition, disclosure risk, and the unit of analysis in dyadic reflexive thematic analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Vince Jacques de Blauwe; Alina Gheorghita; Antonio Fidalgo
articles_hidden.abstract:
In dyadic qualitative research, an account may have an informed reader before it reaches any public audience: the person who shared the encounter. Conventional de-identification is generally calibrated to an external reader and may therefore leave unresolved recognition through shared memory, relational sequence, or a singular circumstance. This methodological case study examines that condition in a corpus of 150 immediate written micro-accounts from 30 university students following brief structured interactions in 15 stranger dyads. Reflexive thematic analysis generated four interpretive themes: calm-as-distance, vocabulary-as-bridge, masking under instruction, and provisional we-ness. A subsequent dialogue-informed dyad-level configurational reading extended, complicated, and bounded selected individual-level interpretations; it was not treated as independent corroboration.

The study develops the Partner-Recognition Framework for qualitative research in which both members of an encounter provide accounts. The framework specifies four prospective rules: name partner recognition in consent; declare dyadic provenance and the intended relationship between individual- and pair-level analysis; separate paired accounts by default in public reporting; and screen derived artefacts as data. The case also documents the evidential cost of partner-protective reporting and recursive disclosure risk, whereby protective documentation can create new linkage routes requiring further review. The framework is offered as a set of prospective design and reporting principles, not as a validated risk-assessment instrument, a guarantee of anonymity, or a substitute for case-specific ethical and legal review

articles_hidden.title: Directional Asymmetry in Reasoning About National and Religious Identity Is Category-Specific: Evidence From Palestine, Israel, and the United States
articles_hidden.authors: Mostafa Salari Rad; Jeremy Ginges
articles_hidden.abstract: Judgments about whether a person can gain or lose a group identity may depend both on which category is at stake and on the direction of transfer. For national identity, people judge that an outgroup-born child raised by the ingroup becomes one of us more readily than an ingroup-born child raised by the outgroup becomes one of them (Rad & Ginges, 2018). That work varied which outgroup was named but never which category, leaving open whether the asymmetry is a general property of reasoning about ingroups, is specific to nationality, or varies with how membership in a category is represented, which differs across populations. We tested these alternatives in settings where religion and nationality pick out nearly the same adversary, using switched-at-birth tasks with Muslim-Palestinians (N = 1,205), Americans (N = 989), and religious Israeli Jews (N = 280). The asymmetry appeared for national identity in all three samples and did not depend on the outgroup being the adversary. For religious identity it was absent among Palestinians and Americans, but present among Israeli Jews and not reliably different from nationality's. Across conditions and studies, directional asymmetry appeared only where membership was treated as substantially fixed at birth, and where it appeared it was carried almost entirely by judgments of what ingroup upbringing confers rather than of what birth transmits. The asymmetry is therefore neither a general feature of group boundaries nor a property of nationality in particular, but emerges where membership is understood as substantially fixed at birth.

articles_hidden.title: Individual differences in visual imagery vividness predict neural responses to language-induced visual expectations
articles_hidden.authors: Ana Chkhaidze; Lera Boroditsky; Sean Trott; Anastasia Kiyonaga; Seana Coulson
articles_hidden.abstract: Grounded accounts of meaning propose that language comprehension recruits sensorimotor systems to represent described content. However, people differ markedly in how vividly they can picture objects and scenes in the mind's eye, raising the question of whether perceptual simulation is recruited similarly across individuals. We addressed this question using the sentence-picture verification task, in which pictures are verified more quickly when their shape matches rather than mismatches the state implied by a preceding sentence, a match effect taken to index perceptual simulation. In preregistered Experiment 1 (N = 110), matching pictures were verified faster and more accurately than mismatching pictures, yet the magnitude of this effect did not vary with imagery vividness. We reasoned that similar behavior might arise from different processes, so in Experiment 2 we recorded picture-locked event-related potentials (ERPs) from 34 participants performing the verification task. Shape mismatch elicited an early right-posterior response at 150-190 ms and a later, broader posterior response at 300-500 ms. Crucially, imagery vividness interacted with the shape match effect in the early window only: stronger imagers showed a pronounced right-posterior negativity, whereas verbal thinking tendency did not, indicating specificity to visual imagery. Together, results suggest that comparable behavioral outcomes may arise through partly different paths to meaning: an early, visually specific route recruited more strongly by vivid imagers, and a later conceptual route shared more broadly across the imagery spectrum. Language comprehension may draw on both perceptual simulation and linguistic associations, with the relative contribution of each depending in part on the comprehender.

articles_hidden.title: Mindscapes of Second Language Acquisition: A New Perspective on the Cognitive Inquiry of Language
articles_hidden.authors: Junya Fukuta
articles_hidden.abstract:
This volume repositions second language acquisition (SLA) not as a peripheral concern, but as a central domain of cognitive science. It establishes the epistemological foundations required for SLA to function as a genuinely cognitive science, and on this basis develops a new Causal-Mechanistic Systems Approach. Through a series of specific models, the book offers fresh resolutions to long-standing theoretical debates in the field.

A distinctive feature of the volume is its attempt to bridge classical cognitivism and complex systems theory while advancing a new form of realist cognitivism. It also brings probabilistic inference, embodiment, and linguistic relativity together within a single integrated explanatory framework.

Departing from approaches that treat pedagogical outcomes in isolation, the book situates SLA within a broader account of cognition and the human mind. In doing so, it connects questions traditionally addressed in second language research with debates across cognitive science, linguistics, and the philosophy of mind. This ambitious and interdisciplinary volume will be essential reading for researchers in SLA, cognitive scientists, linguists, and graduate students seeking a deeper understanding of language, cognition, and the architecture of the human mind.

articles_hidden.title: What is attention for?  A theory of attention as control  over information sampling
articles_hidden.authors: Heleen A Slagter; Thomas Parr
articles_hidden.abstract:
Goal-directed attention shapes what we perceive, learn, and ultimately how we act in the world. Yet, despite its central role in cognition, what attention fundamentally is remains debated, with dominant accounts treating it either as a filter over sensory processing or tightly linked to goal-directed action. Here, we propose a unified account in which goal-directed attention is understood as control over how information is sampled within the framework of active inference. In this perspective, goal-directed attention does not simply modulate sensory processing, nor can it be equated to, or seen as the covert shadow of goal-directed action. Rather, attention governs information seeking, determining what is brought into evidence, and thereby what the organism perceives, learns from, and uses to guide action. Mechanistically, we propose that alternative ways of weighting information are themselves evaluated as candidate courses of action, and selected according to their expected informativeness and usefulness. 
	A conceptualization of goal-directed attention as control over information sampling renders attention inherently inferential, prospective, and agentic, as the organism must evaluate alternative epistemic futures on the basis of what would come to be known if information were sampled in one way rather than another. It also explains attention's sensitivity to salience, prior experience, value, and context, because which way of sampling information is selected is jointly shaped by both what is informative and what matters to the organism. More generally, our review shows that our account can parsimoniously explain a wide range of attentional phenomena, and that influences traditionally attributed to distinct sources of control, such as goals, salience, and selection history, can be understood as different constraints on a single inferential process through which organisms determine how information should be acquired in the service of adaptive behaviour. We discuss this proposal in relation to influential perception- and action-based theories of attention, and explore its implications for understanding the relationship between covert and overt attention, attentional agency, habit formation, and attentional dysfunction. More broadly, we argue that progress in understanding attention requires moving beyond describing the factors that influence attentional selection toward a mechanistic account of how organisms determine what to know next.

articles_hidden.title: A Practical Causal Mediation Workflow for Psychologists: From Concepts to Implementation
articles_hidden.authors: Joshua D Wenger; Zoe Baker; Vasant G Honavar
articles_hidden.abstract: Mediation analysis is widely used across psychology to support claims about psychological mechanisms. Such claims often carry causal interpretations that depend on assumptions that are frequently left unstated, and may not be justified under traditional mediation approaches. Despite substantial advances in mediation best practices emerging from the field of causal inference, uptake of these approaches has remained low, possibly due to the highly technical literature and lack of practical implementation guidance. This paper addresses that gap by integrating developments in causal mediation into an accessible, fully demonstrated workflow for applied researchers without prior knowledge of causal inference. We identify two major limitations of traditional mediation approaches: vulnerability to mediator–outcome confounding and reliance on a product-of-coefficients approach that cannot account for predictor–mediator interactions and certain nonlinear models more generally. We then present concrete solutions to each that can be applied throughout the research workflow with limited additional work: before data collection (design-based solutions), during mediation effect estimation, and after analysis to assess robustness (sensitivity analysis). In doing so, we introduce key causal inference frameworks (directed acyclic graphs and potential outcomes) to facilitate understanding of these problems, bridge conceptual reasoning and practical solutions, and equip readers to reason about these issues within their own study contexts. Finally, we provide a fully worked example, including R code that readers can adapt for their own use. Overall, the proposed workflow requires only modest extensions to standard practice but can substantially improve the validity of causal claims drawn from mediation analysis.

articles_hidden.title: Shame- and Fear-based Autobiographical Memories and Their Identity Centrality and Intrusiveness in Young Adults Exposed to Childhood Maltreatment
articles_hidden.authors: Ellen Iredale; Xenia Bunk; Jasmine Stringer; louise johns; Carmen Chan; Alex Lau-Zhu
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Exposure to childhood maltreatment is an established risk factor for adult psychopathology, but the underpinning mechanisms remain unclear. Developmental theory suggests that alterations in cognitive processes, such as autobiographical memory, play an important role.  
Aim: We examined whether autobiographical shame vs fear memories differ in intrusiveness and identity centrality in young adults with high exposure to childhood maltreatment compared to low exposure peers. Furthermore, we investigated whether such memory characteristics could reflect markers of latent vulnerability to psychopathology, with implications for early intervention efforts.  
Methods: In a cross-sectional design, we examined shame- and fear-based autobiographical memories in a UK community sample of young adults aged 18 to 25 (N = 127), with high vs low exposure to childhood maltreatment. Participants completed an online survey including questions on adverse experiences, current psychological symptoms and an autobiographical memory task involving recall of specific childhood events most strongly associated with shame and fear, followed by ratings of memory intrusiveness and centrality.  
Results: Intrusiveness and identity centrality of shame and fear memories were rated as significantly higher in young adults exposed to high levels of maltreatment than their low-maltreatment peers. Centrality (but not intrusiveness) ratings remained significantly associated with maltreatment after accounting for concurrent psychopathology. However, there was no evidence that the association between maltreatment and memory characteristics differed between shame- and fear-based memories. This may indicate that the observed memory alterations may not reflect shame-specific mechanisms and suggest that the conceptual distinction between shame- and fear-related autobiographical memory processes may be less clear-cut. 
Conclusion: The present work suggests that autobiographical memory – irrespective of emotional category (shame vs fear) – may be one mechanism through which childhood maltreatment increases risk for later psychopathology. While memory intrusiveness may reflect ongoing psychopathology, its centrality to identity may reflect a latent vulnerability to future psychopathology. Pending further work with longitudinal designs, autobiographical memory could offer a mechanistic focus for early interventions in maltreatment-exposed youth.

articles_hidden.title: Boghossian et al.’s (2026) critique of humanistic scholarship is itself bad scholarship and should be corrected or retracted
articles_hidden.authors: Patrick E. Savage
articles_hidden.abstract: Boghossian et al.’s (2026) “Report on the State of Scholarship in the Humanities and the Humanistic Social Sciences” argues that humanistic scholarship has experienced “a deterioration in scholarly standards fueled by the substitution of political criteria for properly scholarly criteria”. I argue that their report itself represents low scholarly standards. Specifically: 1) it is primarily based on unpublished, unverifiable data; 2) the limited data that have been published (largely from unvalidated LLM categorisations) do not support the main claims of a “deterioriation in scholary standards”; and 3) the report unjustifiably generalises from a narrow set of examples (e.g., the cancelation of a panel on sex and gender by the American Anthropological Association) to make sweeping conclusions about global humanities scholarship. I describe counter-examples from past and present research in the humanities and the sciences by myself and others to show that biased and low-quality scholarship is not a new or unique problem for progressive humanistic research. While I agree with the authors that critical evaluation of the quality of academic scholarship (both humanistic and scientific) is urgently needed in today’s global political climate, the report’s strongest conclusions are not justified by their data and thus are not of sufficient quality to achieve their intended goal of helping university leaders to make policy decisions. I recommend it be corrected or retracted to resolve these issues.

articles_hidden.title: Language supports the emergence of abstract relational reasoning in early childhood
articles_hidden.authors: Emilie Serraille; Jean-Rémy Hochmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Young children demonstrate sensitivity to abstract relations such as same and different, yet they typically fail analogical reasoning tasks such as the Relational Match-to-Sample (RMTS) until four to five years of age. We investigate whether this developmental discontinuity reflects general task demands or a qualitative change in the representational format of thought. Specifically, we contrast accounts according to which young children have the competence to solve RMTS but fall victim of an induction problem, with accounts proposing that early cognition lacks the discrete representations of relations necessary to solve RMTS. Across three experiments involving 3- to 6-year-old children, we progressively reduced the inductive demands of RMTS tasks by priming relational content and constraining the hypothesis space. Although these manipulations improved performance, success consistently depended on children’s knowledge of the relational terms “same” and “different.” Children lacking evidence of relational vocabulary continued to perform at chance despite succeeding in simpler relational tasks. These findings suggest that early relational cognition does not rely on discrete relational symbols and that lexical acquisition plays a critical role in enabling abstract relational reasoning. More broadly, the results favor the hypothesis that developmental changes in language contribute to transformations in the format, structure and flexibility of human thought.

articles_hidden.title: UK-Adaptation of the Dutch PET@home Toolkit for Clients Receiving Home Care with Pets (SAFEpet@home): A Participatory Adaptation Study
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Reniers; Ine J.N. Declercq; Marie-Jose Enders-Slegers; Karin Hediger; Elizabeth Ormerod; Ruslan Leontjevas
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Pets can contribute to the wellbeing of people receiving home care but may also present practical challenges for clients, family caregivers, and professional caregivers. The Dutch PET@home Toolkit was developed to support stakeholders in addressing pet-related issues in home care. Differences in care practices and support infrastructure mean that the toolkit cannot simply be transferred to other national contexts.
Objective: To adapt the Dutch PET@home Toolkit for use in the United Kingdom.
Design: Participatory adaptation study using qualitative interviews and focus groups.
Setting(s): Interviews and focus groups were conducted online with participants based in the United Kingdom.
Participants: Twelve participants with backgrounds in social care, veterinary practice, animal welfare, and related fields contributed through individual interviews, focus groups, and/or member checking.
Methods: The Dutch PET@home materials were translated into English and reviewed with UK-based stakeholders. Information relevant to adaptation was identified through a pragmatic and iterative analysis of interviews and focus groups. Suggested adaptations were incorporated into the materials and reviewed within the research team. Revised materials were subsequently returned to participants for member checking and review of UK English.
Results: The adaptation resulted in the SAFEpet@home Toolkit. Key changes included greater emphasis on collaboration with veterinary practices, replacement of the Five Freedoms with the Five Domains Model, increased diversity in visual materials and represented companion animal species, and inclusion of UK-specific organisations and support resources. Other adaptations addressed practical issues such as planning for multiple pets and veterinary decision-making.
Conclusions: The Dutch PET@home Toolkit was adapted to reflect UK care practices, animal welfare guidance, and support infrastructure while retaining the core principles of the original toolkit. The findings suggest that a participatory adaptation process is a feasible approach for adapting toolkits to different national contexts.

articles_hidden.title: The Dutch D70: Psychometric validation of the Dark Factor of Personality
articles_hidden.authors: Ann De Buck; Lieven Pauwels
articles_hidden.abstract: The Dark Factor of Personality (D) represents a common dispositional core underlying socially and morally aversive traits (Moshagen et al., 2018, 2020). This study provides the first psychometric evaluation of the Dutch 70-item D factor scale (Dutch D70) across two independent samples: an online community sample (n = 978) and a student sample (n = 1,806). Using confirmatory factor analysis, we compared a unidimensional model, a hierarchical second-order model, and a bifactor model. In both samples, the bifactor structure demonstrated the best overall fit. It indicated a dominant general Dark Factor accounting for the vast majority of the common variance with high reliability. The specific residual factors contributed minimal unique variance. Multi-group analyses supported full scalar invariance across self-reported sex, showing that the scale functions equivalently for men and women. Construct and nomological validity were supported through consistent associations of D with lower empathic concern and higher levels of low morality and ethnocentrism. Significant relations between D and self-reported out-group aggression further supported criterion-related validity. Overall, the findings show that the Dutch D70 is a reliable and valid instrument for assessing a strong general Dark Factor, with structural and validity evidence replicated across both community and student samples.

articles_hidden.title: Stable tendencies in spontaneous working memory usage during flexible behaviour
articles_hidden.authors: Levi Kumle; Amy Xiangjin Li; Joel Kovoor; Amelia G. Rock; Emily Hesselink; Ellen Jones; Meadhbh Brosnan; Anna C Nobre; Dejan Draschkow
articles_hidden.abstract: Unlike standard working memory (WM) tasks, real-world settings allow individuals to spontaneously adapt how much information to use from WM before resampling the environment. Here, we considered whether individuals exhibit distinct, trait-like tendencies in their spontaneous use of WM. Across three studies (N = 220) using an Object Copying Task, we show that some participants consistently exhibited greater WM usage than others. These tendencies were reliable, stable across time, and predicted individuals’ task efficiency and responses to changing task demands. Finally, spontaneous WM usage could only partially be explained by established measures of WM capacity and attentional control – two plausible predictors of natural WM usage. In summary, we find stable tendencies in individuals’ spontaneous WM usage, despite the variable nature of self-structured natural behaviour. Our results position inter-individual variability as an important dimension in understanding natural, memory-guided behaviour, highlighting the need to investigate its broader determinants and behavioural consequences.

articles_hidden.title: The Neural Bases of Prediction in Music and Speech: An Integrative Theoretical Approach to Understanding Content and Timing Interactions
articles_hidden.authors: Lu Lucuța; Anne Kösem; Peter E. Keller; Anna Fiveash
articles_hidden.abstract: Predictions of content (“what”) and timing (“when”) have been widely investigated in both music and speech research. Considering that music and speech serve distinct communicative functions, predictions of content and timing, as well as their interplay, are likely to exhibit domain-specific characteristics. However, because these domains have largely been studied in isolation, the neural bases of content–timing interactions remain poorly understood. This review sets multiple objectives. The first is to provide an overview of how the neural correlates of content and timing predictions in music and speech have been investigated through the lenses of Predictive Coding and Dynamic Attending Theory. The second is to evaluate the extent to which these frameworks account for the interaction between content and timing predictions, particularly at a neurophysiological level. The third is to highlight points of convergence between the two frameworks that are often difficult to identify due to differences in nomenclature and research design. The fourth is to propose an integrative perspective through which methodological strengths from both research traditions can be complementarily implemented to further our understanding of the neural bases of content and timing predictions in music and speech, by considering different decisions that must be taken when investigating prediction in music and speech (stimulus, analysis, and interpretation decisions). Reconciling key aspects of these theoretical frameworks across multiple levels of description (i.e., computational, algorithmic, implementational) within music and speech processing can provide insights into prediction as a fundamental aspect of cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding and Avoiding Construct Redundancy Fallacies in Environmental Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Taciano L Milfont; Gordon Hodson
articles_hidden.abstract: Construct proliferation and measurement redundancy can undermine conceptual clarity and cumulative scientific progress. We examine these challenges in environmental psychology, a rapidly growing field characterised by an expanding number of constructs and measures. After reviewing the historical problem of construct redundancy fallacies in psychological science, we illustrate its relevance to environmental psychology with two examples based on re-analysis of published data. We first examine multiple connection-to-nature constructs and measures that may represent alternative operationalisations of the same underlying latent construct. We then consider strong associations among environmentalism-related constructs typically regarded as theoretically distinct. Building on this evidence, we advance consideration of a generalised common factor (g-environmentalism) underlying diverse environmentalism-related measures. We conclude with recommendations for improving conceptual clarity, measurement practices, parsimony, and cumulative progress in environmental psychology.

articles_hidden.title: Out-of-Context and In-Context Environmental Effects on Exploratory Reinforcement Learning and Decision-Making
articles_hidden.authors: Mianzhi Hu; Emma Dennin; Ben D. Ulicnik; Darrell A. Worthy

articles_hidden.title: Developing a Neuroimaging Training Framework and Certificate Program
articles_hidden.authors: Dianne Karen Patterson; Thomas Hicks; Aneta Kielar
articles_hidden.abstract: As neuroimaging workflows grow increasingly reliant on complex computational ecosystems, cloud and cluster computing, and open science standards, academic training programs must evolve to provide relevant instruction and practice. This paper describes the design, implementation, and evolution of a fully asynchronous neuroimaging education framework at the University of Arizona. Designed to support the rapidly expanding computational ecosystems demanded by modern neuroimaging workflows, the curriculum targets a diverse trainee cohort; including graduate and undergraduate students, research staff, and faculty. In addition to teaching experimental design, data processing, and statistical analysis, the program provides practical competencies in modern computational skills, such as the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) specification, Unix command-line navigation, High-Performance Computing (HPC), notebooks (JupyterLab), basic programming (MATLAB, Bash), and containerization (Docker/Apptainer). A key contribution of the framework is its focus on pedagogical adaptability: we've found that many modern learners seek flexibility, in support of active laboratory research, over certification. To this end, our framework provides online, a la carte lessons and individual course access in addition to a complete neuroimaging certificate path. The granularity of the offerings facilitates expanding and updating materials to accommodate community requirements and feedback. Recognizing the challenges that Artificial Intelligence (AI) presents to traditional testing, we are exploring new assessment techniques that are both more resilient to AI's disruptions and incorporate AI into the evaluation process. Our AI-ready framework replaces easily exploitable multiple-choice questions with interactive matching questions and traditional testing with structured generative AI workflows, while retaining hands-on practicals. Ultimately, this case study provides a template for institutions seeking to deliver targeted, cutting-edge, on-demand training in computational neuroimaging and demonstrates how curricular flexibility can reach a broad audience but still be tailored to individual learners.

articles_hidden.title: “What we found was…” Syntactic prominence cues to information structure affect semantic prediction.
articles_hidden.authors: Eleonora Beier; Adrian Zhou; Fernanda Ferreira
articles_hidden.abstract: While predicting the content of upcoming words facilitates comprehension, it is often what cannot be predicted that conveys the most novel, important information. We address the cognitive mechanisms underlying the interplay between predictions for upcoming content and expectations about its novelty. In Experiment 1, we used eye-tracking to measure reading times to sentences containing a target word that was either predictable or unpredictable (but plausible). Expected novelty was manipulated through syntactic prominence: the target was either narrowly focused through a wh- cleft (“What he made was…”; high prominence), marked as presupposed through a subordinate clause (“After he made…”; low prominence), or presented through a “neutral” structure (“He made…”; intermediate prominence). We found that the facilitatory effect of predictability on reading times was eliminated for words in high prominence, while it was enhanced for words in low prominence. In Experiment 2, we addressed whether this interaction was due to a direct effect of prominence cues on semantic pre-activation, or an indirect effect on ease of integration of unpredictable content, using the visual world paradigm with auditory stimuli. Compared to the neutral baseline condition, we found that while hearing the focusing construction, listeners made fewer fixations towards the predictable item and more towards the unpredictable alternative; while hearing the subordinate clause, they made fewer fixations towards both predictable and unpredictable items. Overall, we show that syntactic prominence affects semantic prediction through multiple cognitive mechanisms: wh- clefts lead listeners to expect the unexpected, while subordinate clauses lead to shallow processing and less prediction.

articles_hidden.title: The respiratory cycle shapes perceived and self-generated time
articles_hidden.authors: Carlotta Lega; Maaike Weevers; Federica Biondi; Luigi Cattaneo
articles_hidden.abstract: Bodily rhythms are increasingly recognized as active organizers of brain function. Respiration, in particular, rhythmically modulates cortical excitability, perceptual sensitivity, memory, and action well beyond its homeostatic role. Whether breathing also shapes the brain's representation and generation of time, however, remains poorly understood. Here, we asked whether respiratory phase modulates two complementary domains of human timing, temporal perception and temporal production. Across two experiments in healthy adults (N = 40 each), respiration was continuously recorded and instantaneous respiratory phase reconstructed using Hilbert-transform-based analyses. In Experiment 1, participants performed an auditory temporal bisection task, judging intervals as “short” or “long” relative to previously learned anchors. Stimulus presentation was prospectively triggered at different phases of the respiratory cycle. Temporal judgments varied systematically with respiratory phase, particularly for perceptually ambiguous intervals: identical durations were judged as longer around peak inhalation/early expiration and shorter near peak exhalation. This modulation was specific to respiratory phase during stimulus presentation and was absent when phase was measured at the subsequent manual response, supporting a perceptual rather than response-related locus. In Experiment 2, participants synchronized finger taps to auditory metronomes at three tempi (75, 100, and 125 bpm) and subsequently continued tapping at the same tempo without external pacing. During self-paced continuation, the respiratory phases associated with slowest tapping clustered consistently across participants, particularly at the slowest tempo, with shorter inter-tap intervals occurring around inspiration. No corresponding respiratory modulation emerged during externally paced synchronization. Together, these findings suggest that respiration rhythmically shapes both perceived and self-generated time, consistent with a transient acceleration of internal timing around inspiration. Thus, the brain’s sense of time may fluctuate with each breath, suggesting that temporal processing is dynamically embedded within the ongoing physiological rhythms of the body.

articles_hidden.title: Environmental Exposures and Brain Health Outcomes in Healthy Ageing: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Kelly E Perry; Breanna Watterson; Jenna Louise Merenstein
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Air pollution and built environment features are increasingly associated with negative health outcomes, yet their relation to brain health in older adults without dementia remains unclear.

Methods: To synthesise the extant literature, we conducted a systematic review, searching MEDLINE (PubMed) and Web of Science (Core Collection) from inception to February 23, 2026. Eligible studies assessed a natural or built environmental exposure against brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) measures in cognitively healthy older adults (ages 65+ without dementia). Reviewers screened and extracted summary data from published reports in Covidence; no individual patient data were sought. The main outcome was brain health; findings were synthesised narratively using an effect-direction approach, as heterogeneous exposures, outcomes, and effect metrics precluded pooling.

Findings: Of 2,496 records screened, 26 studies met eligibility, comprising >84,000 older adults across 10 countries: United States, South Korea, United Kingdom, France, Spain, Sweden, Netherlands, Taiwan, Germany, and Japan. Thirteen studies were cross-sectional and 13 were cohort studies (eight observational and five longitudinal). Higher air pollution exposure—particularly PM2·5, NO2, and PM10—was associated with altered brain structure: smaller total, grey matter, and white matter volumes, greater white matter hyperintensities, cortical thinning, and medial temporal and hippocampal atrophy; greenspace was generally protective. 13 studies met criteria for high methodological quality and low risk of bias, though outcome assessment was a recurring source of bias (12 of 26 studies), and four of the five longitudinal studies did not meet criterion for follow-up adequacy.

Interpretation: This novel review synthesises compelling evidence that brain structure is susceptible to air pollution in healthy ageing, supporting the notion that this modifiable environmental exposure may serve as a potential target for physicians and policymakers aiming to protect brain health in the fastest growing segment of the global population.

articles_hidden.title: Executive Function and Affective State Recognition Show Distinct Associations with Empathic Choice Across Socioeconomic Contexts
articles_hidden.authors: Fiorella Macchiavello; Huepe David; Valentina Vallejo-Correa; F. Rojas-Thomas; José Javier Bórquez Henríquez; Consuelo Ruiz; Luis Sebastian Contreras-Huerta
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract: Empathy research has traditionally emphasised the capacities and dispositions that enable people to understand and respond to others’ affective states. Motivational accounts, however, have highlighted that empathy also depends on whether individuals choose to engage with those states when engagement is optional. Building on this distinction, we examined how social-specific affective state recognition and domain-general executive function relate to empathic choice, and whether these associations vary with socioeconomic vulnerability (SV). 96 Chilean adults participated (50 High SV; 46 comparison). High SV participants showed lower affective state recognition and executive function, yet the groups did not differ in mean empathic choice. Across participants, better affective state recognition was associated with less frequent empathic choice, whereas dispositional empathy was positively associated with choice. Executive function was associated with more frequent empathic choice in High SV but not comparison participants, and this association differed significantly between groups. In contrast, the association between affective state recognition and empathic choice did not differ by socioeconomic group. Better affective state recognition was also associated with greater relative cognitive effort during empathic engagement. These findings show that distinct cognitive capacities relate differently to empathic motivation and that their behavioural relevance can depend on socioeconomic context.
Keywords: empathy; executive function; motivation; affective state recognition; empathic choice; socioeconomic vulnerability.

articles_hidden.title: The developmental dynamics of bilingual spelling:  Longitudinal and intervention evidence for language-specific orthographic differentiation
articles_hidden.authors: Manon Jones; Catherine Alice Clark; Gwennant Evans; Joseph Benjamin Russell Smith; Carly Deluca; James Hodgetts; Ferrida Ponce; Cadi Sion; Samuel David Jones; Cameron Downing
articles_hidden.abstract: Spelling in bilingual children requires navigating two orthographic systems that may compete as well as cooperate. Although bilingual language research demonstrates extensive cross-language co-activation, far less is known about how such dynamics shape spelling development. We investigated whether cross-linguistic influence in spelling – indexed by the extent to which children’s misspellings conformed to English-consistent versus Welsh-consistent phoneme–grapheme mappings – predicted literacy development in Welsh–English bilingual children. Across three studies involving 524 children aged approximately 7–11 years, we quantified the extent to which misspellings reflected sublexical mappings characteristic of English or Welsh orthography. In Study 1, longitudinal analyses of children in control groups showed that greater phonological plausibility under English-consistent mappings at baseline predicted greater growth in English spelling accuracy, whereas greater plausibility under Welsh-consistent mappings predicted slower growth. In Study 2, a Welsh-medium literacy intervention did not affect English spelling accuracy but strengthened Welsh-consistent mappings and improved English-consistent mappings among children with the weakest baseline skills. In Study 3, an English-medium intervention strengthened English-consistent mappings but did not alter Welsh-consistent mappings. Together, these findings suggest that bilingual spelling development involves increasing differentiation of language-specific sublexical mappings through experience. This differentiation appears to be shaped by instructional context and orthographic depth, such that increasing sensitivity to target-language mappings supports spelling growth, whereas persistent influence of non-target mappings may constrain it.

articles_hidden.title: Gratitude Towards Our Past Self and General Gratitude Enhance Self-Continuity
articles_hidden.authors: Zoe Fowler; Kyle Fiore Law; Liane Young; Madeleine Gross; Jonathan Schooler; Stylianos Syropoulos
articles_hidden.abstract: Does gratitude for the past strengthen our connection to our past and future selves? Across three pre-registered studies (N=1,779 US participants), we explored the relationship between gratitude and self-continuity–our sense of self-similarity across time. In Study 1, higher general gratitude and past-self gratitude (PSG) were associated with increased self-continuity 10 years into the past and future, with the association between gratitude and future self-continuity (FSC) significant when controlling for demographic variables and the alternative temporal dimension of self-continuity. Study 2 replicated these results in a representative US sample, finding that gratitude is linked to FSC up to 25 years ahead. Study 3 demonstrates that expressing PSG causally increases past and future self-continuity, effects not observed for gratitude towards others. Our findings suggest that individuals with higher general gratitude feel more connected to their intertemporal selves, and that promoting PSG could strengthen self-continuity, with the potential to benefit future-oriented decision-making.

articles_hidden.title: Trauma Exposure Changes Substance Use Expectancies and Affects Subsequent Use among Early Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Herry Patel; Fiona A Ralston; Cheyenne Yochum; Jack Waddell; Emily C. Kemp; Isabel R. Aks; William E. Pelham; Sandra Brown
articles_hidden.abstract: We examined changes in substance use (SU) expectancies following potentially traumatic events (PTEs) in a community-based cohort of early adolescents for three common substances used by teens (alcohol, cannabis, and nicotine) how those changes affected SU itself. We leveraged data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (N=11,868, 48% female, 52% White), containing annual assessments of PTEs, SU expectancies, and SU itself from ages 10 to 14 years old. Using multilevel models to estimate between- and within-person effects, we tested whether PTEs predict negative and positive SU expectancies concurrently and prospectively and whether those expectancies forecast subsequent use. At the between-person level, PTEs were associated with increased negative and positive SU expectancies and subsequently associated with greater SU, directly and indirectly via positive expectancies concurrently and prospectively. At the within-person level, PTEs were associated with increased negative and positive SU expectancies concurrently but not prospectively. PTEs were associated with increases in SU directly and indirectly via positive expectancies and decreases in cannabis and nicotine use only via negative expectancies. But prospectively, PTEs were only associated with greater SU directly and not indirectly via positive or negative expectancies. Closer in time to each other, PTEs heighten the saliency of both positive and negative expectancies; however, over time, the effect of PTEs on expectancies diminishes. Current findings highlight a temporal window for optimal intervention to prevent SU following PTEs by assessing and targeting SU expectancies.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing Common-Cause Implications of Reflective Models:  A Simulation Study of the Tetrad Fit Index
articles_hidden.authors: Ellie Bastos Degobi; Víthor Rosa Franco; Marcos Jiménez
articles_hidden.abstract:
Conventional factor-analytic fit indices such as the CFI, TLI, RMSEA, and SRMR summarize 
discrepancies between observed and model-implied association structures, but they do not 
directly target the vanishing-tetrad constraints entailed by pure linear common-factor models. We 
evaluated a revised Tetrad Fit Index (TFI), which quantifies discrepancy between tetrads 
computed from the observed correlation matrix and from a purified model-implied correlation 
matrix. Across two simulation scenarios, we manipulated items per factor (8 or 16), 
factor-loading magnitude (low or medium), and sample size (200, 500, or 1,000). In the 
multidimensional scenario, the TFI selected the data-generating model in at least 99.1% of 
replications when compared with underfactored or overfactored alternatives. CFI, TLI, RMSEA, 
and SRMR performed well against the underfactored model but were substantially less accurate 
against the overfactored model. In the bifactor scenario, TFI accuracy ranged from 67.4% to 
99.3%, whereas conventional indices rarely selected the generating correlated-factor model. The 
TFI was only weakly to moderately associated with the other indices, which were highly 
intercorrelated. An empirical illustration with the Antinatalism Scale showed that the TFI 
favored the one-factor solution selected in the original study, whereas conventional indices 
favored a four-factor alternative. These findings support the TFI as a complementary index for 
comparing reflective factor models when researchers wish to evaluate common-cause covariance 
implications in addition to conventional global fit.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Diagnosis: Shared and Distinct Cognitive Mechanisms Across Developmental Coordination Disorder, Autism, ADHD, and Dyslexia
articles_hidden.authors: Joanna Greer; Lucy H Eddy
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) is a neurodevelopmental condition affecting sensorimotor skills in around 5% of the population. Increasingly, research recognises that DCD also impacts cognition and executive functioning (EF). Despite this, cognition in DCD is rarely studied alongside the neurodevelopmental conditions with which it most commonly co-occurs (autism, ADHD, and Dyslexia), despite each also showing cognitive challenges. Much of the literature also relies on binary diagnosed/typically developing comparisons, which cannot capture natural variability within and across these conditions. Methods: This cross-sectional online study used a trait-based approach to explore shared and distinct cognitive profiles across these conditions. Participants (342 adults aged 18–76 years) completed trait questionnaires for autism, ADHD, DCD, and Dyslexia, four cognitive measures (related to executive function and everyday memory), and two mental health and wellbeing questionnaires. Results: K-means cluster analysis and exploratory factor analysis both identified a profile in which DCD traits aligned closely with ADHD and Dyslexia traits, while autism traits remained relatively distinct. Linear regressions showed that DCD traits made small but consistent independent contributions to EF outcomes after accounting for ADHD, autism, and mental health, although ADHD traits typically explained more variance. Critically, difficulties rarely stemmed from a single trait profile - they were more often predicted by a combination of trait profiles. Conclusion: These findings suggest that the cognitive profile of DCD is best understood alongside ADHD and Dyslexia, with executive functioning difficulties frequently mapping onto multiple trait profiles. This has two implications for support: (i) DCD diagnostic criteria do not include cognitive difficulties, thus a diagnosis-led model risks missing additional support needs; and (ii) individuals whose difficulties span multiple trait profiles but do meet diagnostic thresholds, risk being excluded from support altogether.

articles_hidden.title: Adaptation and Validation of the Real Relationship Inventory–Therapist Form into Brazilian Portuguese
articles_hidden.authors: Lucas Remião Sampaio; Eduarda Rossatto de Bona; Manuela Bizzi Schvartzman; Amanda Pacini Teixeira C. Preta; Marcela Alves Sanseverino; Mirian Porciúncula Moreira Cuchiara; Christian Haag Kristensen
articles_hidden.abstract: The real relationship is a relevant component of the therapeutic relationship, yet validated instruments for assessing this construct remain scarce across cultural contexts. This study aimed to translate, culturally adapt, and validate the Real Relationship Inventory–Therapist Form (RRI-T) for use in Brazilian Portuguese, based on data from online psychotherapy. Participants were 142 therapists from different Brazilian states. The study included procedures for cross-cultural adaptation, content validity analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, internal consistency assessment, and convergent validity analysis with the Working Alliance Inventory–Short Revised–Therapist Version (WAI-SR-T). Results indicated satisfactory internal consistency for the total scale and for the realism and genuineness dimensions. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the theoretical two-factor model, with adequate fit indices. Moderate to strong positive correlations were observed between the RRI-T and the WAI-SR-T, suggesting partial convergence between related but distinct constructs. These findings provide satisfactory evidence of validity and reliability for the Brazilian Portuguese version of the RRI-T, particularly in the context of online psychotherapy.

articles_hidden.title: Protective Parenthood Factors in the Context of Sex Chromosome Trisomy: Supporting Social Behavioral Development through Reflective Functioning and Parental Behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Nienke Bouw; Hanna Swaab; Sophie van Rijn
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose. Children with Sex Chromosome Trisomies (SCT) are at elevated risk for early social and behavioral difficulties, which can place additional demands on parents. This prospective study examined behavioral development in young children with SCT, alongside parental reflective functioning and observed caregiving, to inform early family-centered support.
Methods. Participants included 107 children with SCT (1-7 years; M = 3.76, SD = 1.92) and 102 population-based controls (58 girls, 44 boys; M = 3.60, SD = 1.62). The SCT group comprised 33 girls with 47,XXX, 50 boys with 47,XXY, and 24 boys with 47,XYY. Most participants were White (83.7%), with others reporting Black/African American, Asian, Latino/Hispanic, Brazilian, or mixed ethnicity. Child social behavioral functioning was assessed via parent-report questionnaires (CBCL, SRS-2) and structured observations (ASIEP-3), while parental reflective functioning and behavior were measured with the Parent Development Interview and an observed Teaching Task.
Results. Children with SCT exhibited persistent social and behavioral vulnerabilities. Parental reflective functioning was comparable to controls, but parents of SCT children showed lower sensitivity and emotional regulation (η² = .06). Better parental regulation and positive affect predicted improved child outcomes (R² = .08 / 07). 
Conclusion. Early interventions should support parents in providing sensitive, well-regulated caregiving to promote resilience.

articles_hidden.title: Vocabulary depth, vocabulary breadth, and speechreading as predictors of reading comprehension and inference accuracy in deaf adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Fiona Elizabeth Kyle; Roxy Cosma; Kyi Aye
articles_hidden.abstract: The current study examined the contributions of vocabulary breadth, vocabulary depth, and speechreading to reading ability in 37 severely and profoundly deaf adolescents aged 14 to 16 years. Participants completed assessments of nonverbal cognitive ability, vocabulary breadth, vocabulary depth, speechreading, word reading, sentence comprehension, and passage comprehension. Vocabulary depth was the most consistent predictor across all reading outcomes, whereas vocabulary breadth was not significantly associated with any reading measure. Nonverbal cognitive ability, vocabulary depth, and speechreading together accounted for 77% of the variance in word reading accuracy and 86% of the variance in sentence-level comprehension. Vocabulary depth and nonverbal cognitive ability were significant predictors of passage comprehension (explaining 67% of variance), as well as performance on both literal and inferential comprehension questions. These findings underscore the importance of rich and precise word knowledge for reading development and suggest that interventions targeting vocabulary depth may enhance reading comprehension in deaf adolescents.

articles_hidden.title: Protocol of the CHILL 2.0 Study:  Optimizing, Explaining, and Sustaining Neuroticism Change
articles_hidden.authors: Wiebke Bleidorn; Rosalie Andrae; Peter Haehner; Christopher James Hopwood; Lina Hungerbuehler; Robert Tobias; Amanda Jo Wright
articles_hidden.abstract: This article describes the protocol of the Changing How I Live Life (CHILL) 2.0 project, a large-scale smartphone-based intervention program designed to optimize neuroticism-change interventions, test mechanisms of personality change, and examine the long-term consequences of intervention-induced neuroticism change. Building on findings from CHILL 1.0, CHILL 2.0 employs a fractional factorial randomized design. In this design, 1,020 participants are assigned to combinations of six theoretically derived strategy blocks comprising 16 evidence-informed intervention strategies and one attention-matched placebo control group. Participants complete repeated assessments of personality traits, neurotic affects, behaviors, and cognitions (ABCs), consequential life outcomes, peer reports, and mobile sensing before, during, and after a 6-week smartphone intervention, with follow-up extending to 1 year. An independent zero-intervention comparison cohort provides benchmark estimates of natural personality change, while a randomized booster substudy examines whether brief booster sessions enhance the long-term maintenance of intervention effects. By integrating intervention optimization, intensive longitudinal assessment, rigorous comparison groups, and long-term follow-up within a single research program, CHILL 2.0 is designed to identify the active ingredients of neuroticism interventions, test competing theories of personality change, and inform the development of more effective and personalized interventions to promote emotional stability.

articles_hidden.title: Construct Continuity With Limited Cross-Modal Agreement: Attention Networks in Immersive Virtual Reality
articles_hidden.authors: David Levi Tekampe; Anxhela Sulaj; Angelica Mendes; Philip Samuel Santangelo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Immersive virtual reality (VR) is increasingly used in cognitive assessment, yet it remains unclear whether established attention paradigms
retain their interpretability when translated from desktop presentation to head-mounted delivery. The present study examined whether atten-
tional effects measured with the Attention Network Test-Revised (ANT-R) are preserved in immersive VR when task-defining properties are
held constant across modalities. Seventy-nine adults (N = 79) completed a within-subject comparison of a desktop ANT-R and a task-matched
immersive VR implementation (ANT-VR; Meta Quest 3). Across modalities, stimuli, cueing logic, trial timing, conflict manipulations, and
scoring were matched. Trial-level reaction time (RT) and accuracy data were analysed using pre-specified mixed-effects models, and sec-
ondary psychometric analyses examined cross-modal agreement of participant-level effect scores. Canonical ANT-R effects were reproduced
across both modalities, especially in RT, including alerting benefits, orienting and validity effects, flanker conflict, location conflict, and dual-
conflict (flanker-by-location) integration. However, VR was associated with slower responses and slightly lower accuracy than desktop ad-
ministration, and modality moderated selected orienting-related and conflict-related contrasts. Secondary agreement analyses showed selec-
tive participant-level agreement between desktop and VR, with the strongest cross-modal agreement observed for flanker conflict, whereas
equivalence was not supported. These findings indicate that immersive VR preserves the major canonical ANT-R contrast pattern under task-
matched implementation while shifting baseline performance and moderating selected effect magnitudes. Immersive VR therefore supports
construct continuity of ANT-R performance but should be treated as a distinct measurement context rather than as psychometrically inter-
changeable with desktop administration.

articles_hidden.title: On the importance of effort perception in stroke care: From evidence to an ideal care pathway – An opinion paper
articles_hidden.authors: Maëlle Charonitis; Fabienne Collette; Benjamin Pageaux
articles_hidden.abstract:
Post-stroke rehabilitation has traditionally relied on objective assessments of motor and cognitive abilities. However, one crucial factor remains underestimated in current practice: the perception of effort, that is, the conscious experience of task intensity and difficulty. Effort perception is strongly influenced by internal states such as fatigue and pain, two symptoms frequently reported after stroke, even without major neurological deficits. While these symptoms are often treated separately, they converge into a shared experience: heightened perceived effort.
Recent literature suggests that both physical and mental fatigue, along with pain, increase perceived effort by impacting available resources and motivation to engage and persist in cognitive and physical tasks. This modulation can directly affect patient engagement and adherence to rehabilitation. When effort is perceived as disproportionate—even for a simple task—it may lead to reduced participation or withdrawal from the care plan. Conversely, a better understanding of effort perception could pave the way for personalized interventions that consider not only patients’ actual capacities but also their subjective experiences.
It is therefore urgent to consider the perception of effort as a clinical indicator in its own right—one that sits at the intersection of body, brain and lived experience. By integrating this dimension, research could better explain why some patients disengage from post-stroke care, despite good recovery potential and clinical practice could refine motivational strategies and therapeutic adherence models. The stakes are twofold: improving the understanding of the mechanisms underlying effort perception and harnessing it as a lever for optimizing post-stroke care trajectories.

articles_hidden.title: PTSD risk detection from trauma narratives using natural language processing
articles_hidden.authors: Giuliano Groer; Laurin Plank; Armin Zlomuzica
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Natural language processing shows promise for detection of trauma-related
disorders through the analysis of trauma-related narratives. We developed a classifier
detecting high or low PTSD symptoms from "PTSD Checklist for DSM-5" (PCL-5) scores
using semantic embeddings derived from autobiographical narratives of participants’ most
traumatic life events.
Methods: Participants (N=150) provided narratives about a traumatic, negative,
and neutral life event, and completing the PCL-5 and the "Depression, Anxiety, and Stress
Scale" (DASS-21). Semantic embedding models were used to represent narrative content
numerically. These semantic representations were used to train classification models via
nested cross-validation procedures, and model performance was evaluated using
permutation testing.
Results: The best performing classifier family trained on trauma narratives
achieved significant PTSD symptom detection performance (pooled AUC = .734, p < .002)
and significantly outperformed a word-frequency baseline (pooled AUC difference = .152,
95% CI [.070, .202]). They significantly outperformed classifiers trained on negative or
neutral narratives, which themselves did not achieve significant detection, highlighting the
unique role of traumatic memories in PTSD symptom detection. Classifiers trained on
trauma narratives showed no significant detection of DASS-21 subscales, despite strong
correlations of PCL-5 and DASS-21 values.
Conclusion: Our findings support the potential of language-based assessment of
trauma narratives for the detection of concurrent PTSD symptomatology.

articles_hidden.title: Forecasting next-day urge to drink without craving’s own history: an individualized analysis of responsive EMA in residential alcohol-use-disorder recovery
articles_hidden.authors: Bilal Khan; Dennis McChargue; Kimberly Tyler; Arthur Andrews; Lucy E. Napper; Therese Wang; Tzeyu Michaud; Kaeli Samson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs) for substance-use recovery need decision inputs that anticipate risk, yet deployed systems rely largely on static rules. A published 30-day responsive ecological momentary assessment (rEMA) study followed adults recovering from severe alcohol use disorder in residential treatment. It collected five daily self-report items: urge to drink, affect intensity, stress, alcohol use, and importance of Alcoholics Anonymous engagement. Adherence and interest in prompt-based support were high. Whether these sparse reports carry a short-horizon forecasting signal was untested.

Methods: We ran a retrospective, individualized forecasting analysis of that cohort (61 enrolled; 53 analytic). Each forecast answers one question: issued daily at 15:30, will the participant’s next 24 hours contain any reported urge to drink (a positive day), or remain urge-free (a negative day)? Rolling-origin ordinary least squares models were fit within each participant, on data available at forecast time, after a burn-in of 10 days. Three pre-specified feature sets decompose the signal: FULL (all five items plus time structure), CONTEXT (urge history withheld), and AR (urge history alone). Forecasts were scored against a per-participant base-rate baseline, with participant-level bootstrap intervals and Wilcoxon tests.

Results: We scored 1,013 participant-days. The cohort summary curves gave mean AUCs of 0.66 (95% CI 0.589 to 0.730) for CONTEXT and 0.62 (0.560 to 0.673) for FULL. Per-participant AUCs exceeded chance in both arms (p = 0.0018 and 0.0077). AR’s cohort summary curve gave 0.56 (0.504 to 0.630); its per-participant AUCs did not exceed chance (p = 0.24). At the operating point, CONTEXT raised recall to 0.619 against the baseline’s 0.366; the false-positive rate did not differ (0.351 versus 0.355). No between-arm difference was significant within participants.

Conclusion: In this cohort, next-day urge to drink was forecastable above chance from sparse rEMA, even with the urge item’s own history withheld. We found no evidence that this history adds signal beyond the other items. These results indicate which items a JITAI trigger model should monitor, groundwork for prospective validation. We do not model drinking or relapse.

articles_hidden.title: Factors Influencing Attitudes Towards Help-Seeking Behavior In Individuals Identifying As Affected By Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Giovanni Foglia; Wendy Ross
articles_hidden.abstract: This mixed method study examined factors influencing attitudes towards help-seeking behavior in individuals identifying as affected by Depersonalization/Derealization disorder (DDD). Participants (N= 140) completed online questionnaires, including the Cambridge Depersonalization Scale, the Attitudes Towards Help-Seeking Professional Psychological Help scale, and the Self-Stigma of Seeking Help scale.58.9% of participants lacked a formal DDD diagnosis. While participants demonstrated positive attitudes towards help-seeking behaviour, this was coupled with high levels of self-stigma. However, there was no significant difference in scores between those with a formal diagnosis and those without, suggesting that structural rather than psychological factors may lie behind the underdiagnosis of DDD. Free text answers indicated that for 45% of participants, the reasons for not having a diagnosis were related to lack of knowledge or belief from medical professionals, indicating that targeted training may be more effective than psychological support.

articles_hidden.title: Before There Is a Tool: Using Early-Stage Co-Design to Examine the Legitimacy of Digital Pathways for Youth Social Prescribing
articles_hidden.authors: Simone Minett; Nikki Rickard
articles_hidden.abstract: Young people experience high levels of loneliness and social disconnection, yet they often make limited use of formal mental health services. Social prescribing aims to support wellbeing through connection to community-based activities, including arts and cultural participation. In practice, however, prevailing social prescribing models are commonly organised around practitioner-mediated pathways that may be poorly aligned with how many young people seek and negotiate support. This Commentary offers a critical reflection on an early-stage youth social prescribing project that explored the possibility of an AI-enabled digital pathway for young people as a complement to existing models. Rather than assuming the value or necessity of such an approach, the project treated the proposed digital pathway as provisional and used exploratory co-design, informed by participatory action research principles, to support reflection on its purpose, role, and boundaries. Drawing on our experience of this process and relevant published literature, we argue that early-stage co-design should attend not only to technological functionality but also to questions of legitimacy, discovery, identity and social fit, feasibility, readiness, trust, and system positioning. We offer eight practice-oriented recommendations for using early-stage co-design to support informed judgement about whether, how, and under what conditions digital pathways to offline social connection for young people should proceed within health and community systems, before tools are built.

articles_hidden.title: Locating Gambling Severity Within Polysubstance Involvement: The Specific Role of Methamphetamine in 9,421 Adults Entering Treatment
articles_hidden.authors: Georgia Murphy; Matthew Browne; Alex M T Russell
articles_hidden.abstract: Gambling problems are common among people entering alcohol and other drug (AOD) treatment, yet they are easily missed and the substance-use patterns that mark them are poorly understood. Population research ties gambling to alcohol, a framing that may not hold in treatment populations where involvement is severe and mixed, and evidence points more consistently to stimulants. Using intake data from 9,421 adults entering Australian AOD treatment who reported past-year gambling, we asked whether gambling severity (PGSI) tracks broader non-alcohol polysubstance involvement, particular substances within it, or alcohol. Confirmatory factor analysis of ten WHO-ASSIST severity indicators identified a single non-alcohol polysubstance dimension, with alcohol loading only weakly and standing apart. Gambling severity was modelled on that dimension, substance-specific severity, and alcohol severity together, using ordinal logistic regression. The clearest and most specific association was with high-severity methamphetamine use (OR ≈ 3.7), which held across gambling-severity thresholds in non-proportional odds models. The polysubstance dimension was independently but more modestly associated; high-severity alcohol was not once other involvement was accounted for. Patterns beyond methamphetamine largely reflected general polysubstance load rather than distinct effects. Gambling severity in this cohort was not primarily alcohol-centred, and was not explained uniformly by polysubstance involvement. It concentrated around high-severity methamphetamine use within a broader non-alcohol context. Routine gambling screening remains warranted, with particular attention to clients presenting with high-severity methamphetamine use and complex polysubstance profiles.

articles.title: Closed for the holidays: why the annual cycle of protest is institutional, not thermal
articles.authors: Syed Mustafa Quadri
articles.abstract: Protest is not spread evenly through the year, and the standard explanation is climatic: people take to the streets when the weather permits. Using 984,026 ACLED demonstration events across 159 countries and 28 years, merged with ERA5 temperature climatology, we show that the annual cycle is institutional rather than thermal. Each hemisphere reaches its annual minimum during its own local summer, in opposite calendar months, a pattern that survives every leave-one-year-out test in both hemispheres. That minimum is not heat. For 66 countries we code school holidays from their published start and end dates and derive month indicators by a fixed rule, so which break counts as the long one is decided by its duration rather than by our expectations about its temperature. Breaks suppress protest by 17.6 percent when they fall in a country's hottest months, 8.7 degrees Celsius above its own annual mean, by 15.8 percent when they fall in its coldest, 8.9 degrees below, and by 11.8 percent when they carry no thermal contrast whatever, 0.1 degrees. In the twelve countries whose annual temperature range averages 2.7 degrees, where there is almost no thermal cycle for a calendar to be confused with, breaks still cut protest by 13.9 percent. Rotating each country's calendar by a random number of months destroys the effect in all 200 draws. Temperature does carry an independent association, which we report rather than dismiss: per comparable unit it is about a third the size of the break effect, and its sign is negative, so warmer months see less protest, not more. The break effect is roughly twice as large in richer and more open countries as in poorer and more closed ones, although income and democracy cannot be separated from one another. A composition check supports the mechanism: student identified protest, whose institutional calendar is documented and unambiguous, is two and a half times more seasonal than protest in general and shows the two term shape. We also report a negative result that bears on how such work should be done. The northern annual peak is February and is stable across all 27 year-drops and all 10 country-drops, but the southern peak is not identifiable: it moves between March, May, October and November depending on the window chosen, because six countries carry 91 percent of the southern temperate sample and a single episode, the Chilean uprising of October 2019, shifts the annual peak by seven months. A five-year window yields an apparently stable southern peak that a 28-year window does not support. The annual rhythm of protest tracks institutions in session; claims about hemispheric peak alignment do not currently have the data to stand on.

articles.title: Varieties of democratic vulnerability: a comparative study of checks and balances and popular acceptance of transgressions
articles.authors: Honorata Mazepus; Magnus Feldmann; Giovanni D'Agostino
articles.abstract:
The recent wave of democratic backsliding has demonstrated that liberal democracies are vulnerable to subversion by authoritarian leaders. Research showed that democratically elected leaders remove checks and balances that constrain their power. One of the explanations why leaders can violate democratic rules focuses on the response of citizens who trade off democracy for partisan and policy gains. This article investigates cross-country differences in vulnerabilities to democratic backsliding by comparing democratic priority profiles of citizens and the patterns of approval for transgressions of democratic rules. 
We use observational evidence from online surveys with large quota-based samples of citizens in a two-party presidential system (USA, N > 1700), a multi-party parliamentary system based on proportional representation with some semi-presidential features (Poland, N >1800), and a consociational parliamentary system based on proportional representation (Netherlands, N = > 2100). To complement observational evidence, we test experimentally some of these aggregate-level differences: next to partisanship and policy gains, we also manipulate different democratic transgressions (protest rights and decree powers) and measure their effects on government approval in the three countries. 
Our results show that citizens of different countries have different democratic priority profiles and differ in their disapproval of specific transgressions. Although overall transgressions are not rewarded, and citizens are mostly vigilant and disapproving of violating democratic rules, we find both observational and experimental evidence indicating that liberal democracies can have different vulnerabilities that relate to the democratic attitudes of citizens.

articles.title: Specification, Heterogeneity and Functional Form in the Determinants of Small-Firm Profitability
articles.authors: Angelo Leogrande; Mauro Di Molfetta; Valeria Nortarnicola; Maria Giovanna Trotta; Antonio Volpe Plantamura
articles.abstract: Studies of small-firm profitability estimate financial structure as the focal regressor and treat cost composition as an unexamined control. This paper reverses the emphasis and places both blocks in one equation, estimated on 91,756 firm-year observations covering 14,913 unlisted Italian firms across three regulatory regimes. Three methods interrogate different assumptions on the same sample: panel estimation across fourteen specifications, unsupervised partitioning selected on eleven validity criteria, and machine-learning regression applied to the same firm-demeaned data. The capitalisation coefficient is not identified. It moves from +0.177 under two-way fixed effects to between −0.12 and −0.28 under five instrument sets, all of which fail because profitability persists at 0.271, so any lagged financial ratio embeds past profit. The labour-share coefficient is stable across estimators, groups and functional forms, and the paper tests whether that stability is arithmetic, since return on assets and the labour share are consecutive lines of one statement. It is not: value added over total assets varies by a factor of 2.8 across the four operating archetypes recovered from the data, while the coefficient varies by 1.07. The accounting identity explains part of the magnitude and none of the stability.

articles.title: Documentation Gap Analysis: Independent Audit of TGA COVID-19 Vaccine Safety Monitoring Plan
articles.authors: Paul Rekaris
articles.abstract:
This independent audit evaluates the TGA COVID-19 Vaccine Safety Monitoring Plan (February 2021). The Plan operationalised National Cabinet's commitment to enhanced pharmacovigilance accompanying provisional approval, covering 68.4 million doses, 91.2% of Australia's rollout. Enhanced monitoring claims cannot be independently verified when the underlying processes are undocumented. This audit tests whether that verification is possible.

The audit finds a systematic failure to demonstrate the enhanced monitoring underpinning Australia's largest provisional medicine rollout. Only 3 of 19 audited outputs (16%) are fully documented; 16 (84%) are partially or not documented. This is despite the TGA's own OAIC-directed searches surfacing 2,218+ pages of potentially relevant material in September 2024, none identified as Plan-implementation documentation. The TGA reports 148 signals investigated and 57 regulatory actions taken (the signal count was updated to 150 in the subsequent Question on Notice 559). No audit trail links signals to actions, and 91 signals have no documented disposition in the record. The OAIC found that the implementation records "cannot be found or do not exist".

Senior TGA officials told the Senate (9 October 2025) that monitoring occurred through "day-to-day processes," without systematic tracking against Plan objectives. The TGA cannot demonstrate documented implementation of its own Safety Monitoring Plan. This is a potential failure of regulatory accountability for the largest provisional medicine rollout in Australia's history.

The audit's open-source methodology applies ISO 19011:2018, ANAO guidance, and OSINT principles to public and FOI records, providing evidence for independent investigation and pharmacovigilance reform aligned with international standards and recognised good practice, including ICH E2E and CIOMS. It is published under CC BY 4.0: open access and independently replicable.

The audit repository, containing the supporting evidence, primary sources, methodology, version history, and replication resources, is maintained at: https://github.com/paulrekaris/TGA-COVID19-Vaccine-Safety-Monitoring-Audit

Updated versions of this paper are available on SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6333058

Version 6 note: This revision adds substantial documentary and regulatory analysis, including a new Appendix mapping the national enhanced-monitoring commitment, February 2021 Plan, provisional-registration framework, sponsor obligations and Commonwealth accountability requirements. It also updates FOI/OAIC, Senate and TGA evidence and refines regulatory framing, assessment scope and implementation-tracking analysis. Audit ratings and overall conclusions are unchanged.

articles.title: Captured by the Ballot: Non-Partisan Judicial Elections and Democratic Erosion in Mexico
articles.authors: Brett Ryan Bessen
