articles.abstract: Public tolerance for democratic erosion is often attributed to voter partisanship. Voters are thought to overlook undemocratic maneuvers to support the partisan in-group. Yet, backsliders  often disavow traditional parties and frame their reforms as non-partisan. I examine the role of voter partisanship in non-partisan elections, showing how elite manipulation of the information environment can generate partisan outcomes that facilitate backsliding—even when citizens prefer non-partisan outcomes on average. I examine Mexico’s 2025 judicial elections, pairing a conjoint experiment with an analysis of the electoral results. While the conjoint indicates that voters preferred independent judges, the electoral results indicate that government-aligned candidates on illicitly circulated voter guides (acordeones) received the most support, contributing to the partisan capture of the Supreme Court. Elite manipulation of the information environment and electoral incentives—rather than partisan preferences among the eligible electorate—were primary contributors to the court’s partisan capture.

articles.title: Rethinking Socialism in the Era of Human Genomics
articles.authors: Jorge Antonio Benitez
articles.abstract: This article examines twentieth-century socialist regimes as large-scale social experiments in the light of new insights from the sequencing of human genomes. It contends that extreme collectivization, while driven by ideological, political, and economic factors, may also have partially underestimated patterns of human behavior shaped by evolutionary and gene-environment dynamics. Historical cases show that institutional models lessening property rights and sense of agency required coercion and subsequent reform. Based on findings from genome-wide studies and behavioral genetics, this paper emphasizes that human social traits are polygenic, probabilistic, and context-dependent, yet not infinitely malleable. It views behavioral patterns as statistical distributions driven by gene-cultural dynamics placing political extremism as a key factor in institutional long-term stability. In this framework, extreme privatization and extreme collectivization can be considered equally wrongful.

articles.title: Cognitive Expectations of Homophily in Village Social Networks
articles.authors: Eric Martin Feltham; Nicholas Christakis
articles.abstract:
Homophily, the tendency for individuals to associate with similar others, has long been
treated as a central principle of social organization. Yet people may overestimate its
importance in reasoning about their social networks. Here, we investigate individuals’
cognitive expectations of homophily and compare these expectations to actual homophily
among 10,072 adults in 82 isolated Honduras villages. We elicited subjects’ beliefs about
whether pairs of people in their village social networks were socially tied. We show that
people deploy cognitive heuristics that substantially overestimate homophily, including
based on wealth, ethnicity, gender, and religion. We also find that people exploit network
structure when predicting ties between others, independent of expectations about
homophily. Understanding cognitive homophily has implications for models of network
formation, interventions targeting social behavior and information diffusion, and the
maintenance of social inequality.

articles.title: ESG Implementation in Small and Medium Cosmetics Industries: Certifications, Barriers, and Theoretical Implications in the Brazilian Context
articles.authors: Orlando Nastri Neto; Murilo Dotti Garcia
articles.abstract: The world's fourth-largest cosmetics industry operates largely through small and medium-sized enterprises. In Brazil, these SMEs account for the largest share of sectoral production and are also the least prepared to meet the growing environmental, social, and governance (ESG) demands that increasingly condition access to international markets, supply chains, and capital. This article examines that mismatch. Drawing on an integrative literature review, we combine Legitimacy Theory (Suchman, 1995), Stakeholder Theory (Freeman, 1984), and the Resource-Based View (Barney, 1991) to analyze how certifications such as Ecocert/COSMOS, Leaping Bunny, B Corp, SA8000, GRI, and EcoVadis function as instruments of legitimation, and why most Brazilian cosmetics SMEs fail to obtain them. We identify six interdependent barrier dimensions and propose the concept of “ESG legitimation capacity” as a theoretical proposition for future empirical research. The main contribution is showing that the problem is not a lack of ESG awareness, but a structural resource gap that no single voluntary compliance instrument can solve on its own.

articles.title: The Retreat from Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion: Language Change on Large U.S. Foundation Websites, 2019–2025
articles.authors: Chad M. Topaz; Benham Cobb; Frances Lu; Aniya Smith; Nathan Zekarias
articles.abstract: Following the murder of George Floyd in 2020, many U.S. organizations, including large private foundations, publicly foregrounded language related to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). Beginning in 2023, a series of legal and political developments shifted the institutional environment: the Supreme Court’s ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023), state-level anti-DEI legislation, and Executive Order 14151 (2025). Using the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine, we construct a longitudinal corpus of archived web pages from thirteen large U.S. private foundations with established DEI vocabulary and track the frequency of sixty-seven DEI-related terms from 2019 to 2025. Among eight foundations with paired 2023 and 2025 data, six reduced their DEI word intensity; most terms present in the paired corpus declined, with race-related terms contributing the largest share of the drop. The aggregate decline on the full sixty-seven-term index is marginal (exact Wilcoxon p = .074, one-sided); evidence is stronger on the dictionary’s definitional core, the diversity-equity-inclusion triad and its variants (p = .031). The decline concentrates in the 2024–2025 window containing the January 2025 executive orders: eight of nine foundations fell (p = .020), with scattered movement earlier. Qualitative comparison of archived pages illustrates three pathways of retreat: elimination of equity framing, substitution of technical for justice-oriented vocabulary, and reduced prominence through site redesign. These patterns suggest institutional isomorphism operating in reverse—convergent abandonment amid shared political pressure—though our descriptive design cannot identify the mechanism. The findings establish an empirical baseline for tracking organizational communication about equity under political pressure.

articles.title: A Party for People Like Me. Voter-Party Linkages and Dynamic Group Identities.
articles.authors: Tarik Abou-Chadi; Markus Kollberg; Francesco Raffaelli
articles.abstract: We introduce a theory of dynamic identity-based linkages between parties and voters. Social groups are associated with political parties. When people identify with a group and that groups is seen as associated with a political party, they become more likely to view a party as a party for people like me, which should increase party support. As salient identities can vary over time, these linkages are dynamic and can change party support. We test this framework using a three-wave panel survey experiment in the UK. Increasing the salience of working-class (wave 2) and rural identities (wave 3) makes people more likely to regard the party most associated with these groups (Labour and the Green Party) as a party for people like me. It also increases party support. We contribute a framework for party-voter linkages that goes beyond programmatic competition and provide a micro-foundation for the growing literature on group appeals.

articles.title: Digital Influencers, Gambling Perceptions, Behavior and Harm: What Do We Know? A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Anass El Mokhtari
articles.abstract:
Background: Digital influencers (DIs), including celebrities, social media influencers, tipsters, and gambling livestreamers, have become a prominent vehicle for online gambling promotion. This scoping review mapped the empirical evidence on how DI gambling content relates to gambling perceptions, behavior, and harm, with attention to livestreams and to groups at heightened vulnerability.

Methods: Guided by JBI methodology and reported following PRISMA-ScR, four databases and Google Scholar were searched for primary empirical studies published in English or Dutch between January 2016 and June 2026.

Results: Ten studies were included, all published since 2021, five quantitative and five qualitative, with seven conducted in Spain or Australia. DI content was widely perceived to increase the appeal and social acceptability of gambling, and tipster content was further linked to beliefs about skill and control. Evidence on behavior was more limited and largely self-reported. Only three studies applied validated harm instruments on outcomes, and only two addressed livestreams. Reported vulnerability concentrated in adolescents, women, and higher-risk gamblers, but followed largely from the populations sampled.

Conclusions: The evidence is concentrated on perceptions, limited for behavior and thin for gambling harm. All studies were observational, so selection and reverse causation cannot be excluded. Prospective research is needed for further insights, particularly on livestreams.

articles.title: DE LA MAREA ROSA A SOMOS MÉXICO: EL ESFUERZO PARA CREAR UN PARTIDO
articles.authors: RICARDO DE LA PEÑA MENA
articles.abstract: El texto analiza el surgimiento de la organización política Somos México (derivada de la Marea Rosa y opositora a la autodenominada Cuarta Transformación). Examina el contexto histórico de las reformas electorales impulsadas por Andrés Manuel López Obrador (Planes A, B y C) y el proceso de obtención de su registro como partido político nacional ante el INE en 2026, enfrentando impugnaciones jurídicas y observaciones sobre su denominación y emblema.

articles.title: Private Government Behind the Gates: Homeowners’ Associations, Institutional Lock-In, and the Democratic Commons
articles.authors: George Skouras
articles.abstract:
Common-interest developments house tens of millions of Americans and increasingly assign homeowners’ associations functions once performed by municipalities. This Article examines physically gated communities as a particularly visible subset of that broader system. It argues that mandatory private residential governance can provide valued services while also creating problems of accountability, amendment, public access, and regional coordination. The Article combines doctrinal analysis, institutional theory, and descriptive housing data; because no national dataset precisely enumerates gated communities, its population estimates are presented as 
The Article also presents a stylized voting model showing how amendment provisions measured against all eligible owners can create institutional lock-in when participation is low. The model is illustrative rather than predictive: its central result follows from the interaction among the denominator, the approval threshold, turnout, and support among participating owners. The Article then evaluates state and local reforms, including judicial threshold-reduction procedures, quorum-sensitive voting rules, transparency protections, and prospective infrastructure conditions. Its contribution is to connect property theory, commons governance, local-government law, and democratic accountability without treating either privatization or municipal control as categorically superior.

articles.title: When voters take a stance: How voting on issues influences support for parties
articles.authors: Davide Morisi
articles.abstract: What are the consequences of referendums for voting for parties? Despite increased use of direct democratic instruments around the world, this question has been essentially ignored. I argue that referendums lead to a realignment between voters and parties that is consistent with a bidimensional model of proximity voting. The analysis of nine referendums that took place in seven countries between 2015 and 2025 confirm the predictions showing that, after each consulta-tion, a sizeable share of cross-pressured voters who cast a referendum vote against party recom-mendations “follow the issue”, switching to a party that is in line with their issue positions. Ideological proximity with parties, however, moderates vote switching. In highly salient consultations, this pattern persists over time. Further experimental evidence confirms the causal link between issue-based considerations and voting. These findings have relevant implications for how direct democracy impacts a fundamental aspect of democratic representation, namely voting for parties.

articles.title: ICT, Sustainable Development and Job Polarization: Evidence from ECOWAS
articles.authors: Dennis Nchor
articles.abstract: This paper assesses the contribution of information and communication technology (ICT) to sustainable development and job polarization in the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). Panel pooled mean group models are used to assess the role of ICT in sustainable development whereas changes in employment shares of the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO08) occupations are used to investigate the changing employment distribution in the labor markets in the region. The results show that all measures of ICT had a positive and significant impact on sustainable development. The paper also finds that the West African countries are lagging in terms of ICT adoption and ICT infrastructure. The pace of adoption is slower compared to developed countries thus minimizing the pace of job polarization. The results obtained found no u-shaped employment distribution in the countries to indicate job polarization. Significantly however, there is a decline in the share of employment of the agriculture, forestry and fishery sectors. The decline in the share of employment is however offset by rising employment shares of most middle-skilled occupations in the region.

articles.title: When the Diagnosis Breaks the Home: Paternal Abandonment and Maternal Endurance in Families of Children with Disabilities in Bangladesh
articles.authors: Syed Jabir Hossain
articles.abstract: In Bangladesh, literature shows that a child with a disability is considered to profoundly reorient family life around the mother, who becomes the primary and often only caregiver. A smaller but growing body of research has also documented the financial hardship, institutional barriers, and religiously-inflected stigma that already accompany this caregiving role. An examination of a dimension that is not closely studied in the context of Bangladesh, a child’s disability in marriage dissolution of the parents, extends that literature. In keeping with the secondary qualitative methodology that Cheong et al. (2023) propose, the study analyses eight past news narratives (2016-2026) in Bangladeshi media, which are publicly available. In these narratives, family members speak for themselves about raising a disabled child. Discourse analysis reveals three themes. First, mothers globally carry the structural weight of caring for the family, regardless of the father’s involvement. Second, some discourse suggests the child’s disability is sometimes ‘responsible’ for the father’s exit, which can occur before and/or after birth. Third, despair for the future collides with maternal agency, best seen through the mother who established her own school after being turned away from every single one. The analysis does not imply a causal link between disability and divorce. It shows how this link is narrated in the Bangladeshi public sphere. The analysis offers the narrated link as a focused question for future primary, interview-based research. As an exploratory secondary analysis, this piece recognises the limitation of the data being drawn from credible journalistic sources rather than high-quality interviews.

articles.title: Radiografía de la Accesibilidad Digital Municipal en Chile 2026
articles.authors: Jaime Elorrieta
articles.abstract:
La digitalización de los servicios municipales en Chile promete acercar el Estado a la
ciudadanía, pero revela una barrera crítica: la exclusión por diseño. Hoy, el acceso a la
información pública digital no es universal. Este informe expone los resultados de una
auditoría de accesibilidad web bajo estándares WCAG 2.1, aplicada a veinte plataformas
municipales de las regiones Metropolitana y del Maule. El estudio delimitó su alcance a
versiones de escritorio ya que esto permite establecer una línea base sobre la calidad del
código estructural. El objetivo fue medir empíricamente las barreras que aíslan a personas con
discapacidad visual y motriz, sugiriendo replicar esta metodología en futuros estudios
móviles.Los hallazgos revelan que la exclusión digital es sistémica y no obedece estrictamente a una
falta de presupuesto. Se detectó un severo bloqueo a la navegación motriz: el 50% de la
muestra no puede operarse mediante teclado, impidiendo el acceso a personas con
discapacidad motriz severa o usuarios de lectores de pantalla. Esta exclusión se agudiza en la
Región del Maule, donde el 60% reprueba esta métrica. A esto se suma una profunda brecha de
diseño visual, con 573 errores críticos de contraste lumínico que invisibilizan los textos para
personas con baja visión. Aunque el Maule presenta un 62% más de errores que la
Metropolitana, comunas de altos ingresos como Providencia y Las Condes también
reprobaron, demostrando que se prioriza la estética corporativa por sobre la legibilidad
universal.Finalmente, existen graves deficiencias en la gestión de contenidos. Destaca una invisibilidad
de la información operativa y transversal, al sumar más de 440 imágenes sin textos
alternativos (ALT), censurando el contenido gráfico para usuarios con ceguera. Además, se
advierte un fenómeno de accesibilidad performativa: el 20% de la muestra usa widgets o
botones flotantes que generan una falsa ilusión de inclusión. En la práctica, estas
herramientas institucionales no solucionan el código base excluyente generando nuevos
conflictos de interfaz para quienes dependen de tecnologías de asistencia.

articles.title: El Encuadre de la Responsabilidad Ciudadana: Comunicación Digital del Servel en la Elección Presidencial y Parlamentaria 2025
articles.authors: Jaime Elorrieta
articles.abstract:
Los organismos electorales enfrentan un desafío comunicacional distinto al de los partidos o candidaturas: deben informar y movilizar al electorado sin abandonar su mandato de neutralidad. Este informe examina cómo el Servicio Electoral de Chile (Servel) resolvió ese desafío en su publicidad digital durante la elección presidencial y parlamentaria de 2025, a partir del análisis de 101 anuncios publicados en Google Ads y Meta Ads.
Los resultados muestran que la comunicación del Servel es abrumadoramente práctica: el 85,1% de los anuncios se centra en información procedimental —dónde votar, qué documentos llevar, cómo revisar el rol de vocal de mesa— por sobre la apelación emocional, cívica o sancionatoria. Contra lo esperable, el tono no escala hacia la urgencia a medida que se acerca la elección; en cambio, mensajes puntuales como el llamado al deber cívico o la alerta contra la desinformación aparecen concentrados en momentos específi cos de la campaña, no en un crescendo progresivo. La advertencia sobre multas por no votar, pese a ser un rasgo central del sistema electoral chileno, ocupa un lugar marginal (3% de la muestra) en la comunicación digital del organismo.

articles.title: Juicio didáctico-matemático sobre el output de la IA generativa: revisión integrativa crítica de la evidencia empírica en educación matemática
articles.authors: Hector Enrique Banquez Buendia
articles.abstract:
Objetivo. Sintetizar críticamente la evidencia sobre cómo docentes, futuros docentes y estudiantes juzgan outputs matemáticos y didácticos de IA generativa, y formular un constructo de competencia profesional con anclaje disciplinar.

Método. Revisión integrativa crítica de literatura empírica publicada entre noviembre de 2022 y agosto de 2026, desarrollada mediante procedimientos sistemáticos de búsqueda, cribado, apreciación y codificación, con reporte orientado por PRISMA 2020. El corpus se constituyó en dos fases: una búsqueda inicial en ocho fuentes, de la que se retuvieron 13 estudios tras aplicar los criterios definitivos, y una actualización en ERIC, SciELO y Dialnet que incorporó 19 estudios. El corpus final reunió 32 estudios únicos: 18 con participantes humanos y 14 de evaluación sistemática de outputs. Se distinguieron las unidades de análisis, los roles del evaluador y las unidades de evidencia independiente, controlando posibles solapamientos entre publicaciones.

Resultados. Se identificaron diez convergencias transversales, seis de grado alto y cuatro moderado. El hallazgo central muestra que el juicio tiende a concentrarse en la dimensión que la tarea hace visible y deja la otra menos examinada. La dirección observada de esta asimetría varía según el rol y la experiencia: en tareas de diseño predomina la atención didáctica, mientras en algunos escenarios de tutoría predomina la corrección matemática. Una segunda convergencia indica que la exposición a un error no garantiza su reconocimiento y que la calibración de la confianza condiciona el ejercicio del juicio.

Conclusiones. Se propone el Juicio Didáctico-Matemático sobre el Output de IA (JDMO), compuesto por cinco operaciones con indicadores observables: lectura analítica, verificación matemática, valoración de la pertinencia didáctica, curaduría del prompting y transformación y decisión. La calibración actúa como condición transversal. El constructo formaliza la mediación profesional necesaria entre el output generado y su incorporación educativa.

articles.title: Donor Responses to Civil Society Repression
articles.authors: Andrew Heiss; Suparna Chaudhry
articles.abstract: This chapter examines donor responses to the global crackdown on civil society, where governments use legal measures to repress NGOs. Donors, including bilateral and multilateral agencies, respond variably; bilateral aid often decreases following anti-NGO laws, while multilateral aid remains stable. Private donors' responses depend on factors like social trust and NGO transparency. NGOs adapt by diversifying funding, forming affiliates, or shifting to community-based support. As the space for civil society continues to shrink, coordinated international efforts are essential to counteract these repressive trends and uphold civil society's role in democratic governance.

articles.title: Evaluating the Theory of the AnthroShift:  How are Climate Shocks Related to Civic Engagement and Support for Climate Science in the US?
articles.authors: Dana R Fisher; Arman Azedi
articles.abstract: Since the theory of the AnthroShift was introduced in 2019, it has been increasingly seen as a theoretical lens through which to analyze social responses to climate change. This paper builds on this small but growing literature to assess the AnthroShift at the individual level.  We analyze a new dataset collected from a national sample of adults in the US to understand how experiencing climate shocks is associated with climate-change supportive attitudes and behaviors.  Specifically, we look at how self-reported experiences with climate shocks are associated with heightened levels of civic engagement and support for the science that documents climate change.  This paper is separated into three sections.  First, we review the theory of the AnthroShift, which explains how risk pivots can drive environmental behaviors, and connect it with the growing research that assesses the social effects of climate shocks.  Next, we describe our data, which were collected from a nationally representative sample of adults in the US in fall 2025 (n=1,068).  Third, we present the results of our analysis that document how individuals’ experience with climate shocks is strongly associated with civic and political engagement and support for climate science.  The paper concludes by discussing the implications of our findings for the relationship between climate shocks, attitudes, and behaviors, as well as for our understanding of the society-environment relationship and the sociological theory of the AnthroShift.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (VI): The Social Foundations, Core Demands, and Future Trajectory of Han Nationalism
articles.authors: ZY Liu
articles.abstract:
After 2020, discussions related to Han nationalism in Chinese online space have increased markedly and have gradually become an important topic for understanding contemporary Chinese ethnic identification, historical narratives, and social contradictions. As the final article in this series of studies, the present paper attempts, from the angles of demographic change, resource allocation, ethnic policy, and national identification, to analyze the social background of the emergence and development of Han nationalism. The article argues that Han nationalism does not simply originate from historical sentiment, but is a form of identity-political expression formed in the process of change in Chinese social structure. With the decline in birth rates, adjustments in the mode of economic growth, and increases in social competitive pressure, some groups have begun to reopen discussion of the fairness of ethnic policy, the boundaries of the national community, and the relations of responsibility and interest among different groups. The article further organizes the principal demands advanced by some Han nationalists, including the abolition of preferential policies based on ethnic identity, renewed discussion of relations of autonomy and fiscal transfer in ethnic regions, and the improvement of social security for lower- and middle-strata groups. At the same time, the article analyzes the possible positive effects of Han nationalism—for example, pushing long-neglected questions into public discussion, emphasizing the principle of civic equality, and strengthening the sense of social responsibility of the majority group. Yet the article also points out that this body of thought possesses potential risks such as ethnicizing complex social problems, neglecting intra-ethnic class differences, and intensifying logics of group competition.
This article does not attempt simply to affirm or negate Han nationalism; rather, it hopes, by organizing its internal logic and social background, to provide an exploratory analytical framework for understanding changes in Chinese ethnic identification after 2020.

articles.title: When Full Employment Is No Longer Necessary
articles.authors: Hong-Ming Chen
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence may reduce the economic necessity of some forms of cognitive labour faster than employment and social institutions can reorganize the time, identity and roles that work currently structures. Rather than forecasting mass unemployment, we ask what should be tested if that transition arrives unevenly or abruptly: how people are received after occupational loss, how newly available time becomes genuinely self-directed, whether AI can make heterogeneous, voluntary arrangements administratively feasible without turning personalization into obligation, whether unmet human needs can support voluntary new roles, and what it costs to keep the human last mile human. Employment organizes more than income, so occupational displacement is an institutional problem as well as an economic one. We set out a sequence — receive, stabilize, recover, choose — in which recovery is a legitimate state rather than a delay before activation, and in which voluntary reconnection is one possible exit among many. The central proposition is offered as a hypothesis rather than a finding: full employment may have functioned partly as a technology of standardization, while AI could make heterogeneity administratively affordable. Because the same capacity could also produce a more efficient workfare machine, we propose personalization without compulsory optimization as a governing constraint. AI may make matching cheap without making human contact cheap.

articles.title: When Are Asymmetric Fixed-Effects Models Within-Person Tests of Reversibility? Heterogeneous Responses and Bidirectional Support
articles.authors: Jiwon Lee
articles.abstract: Asymmetric fixed-effects models are increasingly used in sociological research to test whether an effect reverses when a time-varying predictor changes direction. Because these models rely on within-person change, directional asymmetry is often interpreted as evidence of within-person irreversibility. This study shows that this interpretation requires an additional cross-person homogeneity assumption. I reparameterize Allison’s (2019) cumulative asymmetric fixed-effects model exactly as a model of current state and total movement, revealing that the specification pools current-state responses across individuals. When those responses are heterogeneous and systematically related to who moves upward versus downward, pooled asymmetry can arise even when every individual’s response is perfectly reversible. I derive this mover-composition result and characterize what remains identifiable when individual state responses are unrestricted. A common path response—the additional response associated with accumulated movement conditional on current state—can then be identified only from within-person bidirectional movement, provided that the resulting variation is not absorbed by period effects. Monte Carlo simulations and a reanalysis of Allison’s wage example illustrate the resulting assumption–support–precision trade-off and show that relevant support depends on the structure of observed trajectories, not simply on the number of directional transitions.

articles.title: A Moment or a Movement? The Effects of Spatial Exposure to the 2017 Women’s March on Political Attitudes and Behavior
articles.authors: Colette Marcellin
articles.abstract: How do social movements affect the public in a polarized era? I examine how the 2017 Women’s March—the largest single-day protest in US history—affected Americans who were exposed to the march in their local communities. I theorize that crowd size moved residents’ political attitudes and behavior in a liberal direction, particularly among Republicans. Using an instrumental variables approach, I find that crowd size increased Republican women’s disapproval of Trump and both Republican women and Republican men’s Democratic vote choice in the 2018 midterm elections. This paper has important implications for understanding the effects of protests that reach a range of communities and focus on identity.

articles.title: Discussions of Race in Online Right-Wing Communities: A Cross-platform Computational Analysis of Reddit, Telegram, and Truth Social Using BERT and Structural Topic Modeling
articles.authors: Qin Li; Jack Gabriel Risien Wippell; Jasmine Hunt; Robert Bond; Joseph Tien; Nicole Yadon
articles.abstract: Race has long been a divisive fault line in American public discourse. Yet, political and societal changes have catalyzed the emergence of alternative collective identities, particularly in digital environments where alternative narratives can flourish. We examine right-wing social media spaces as forums in which racial discourse (specifically, that related to Black identities) is produced and contested through conversation, focusing on three platforms—Reddit, Truth Social, and Telegram—during Summer 2022. Structural topic modeling reveals six prominent themes: comparisons of the Black Lives Matter and January 6th protests; persistent discussions of race, crime, and violence; perceived racism within the Democratic party; broad discussion about ``wokeness''; race and health issues (abortion and infectious disease); and racial identity. While their relative prominence and framing vary, these themes appear across all three platforms. This indicates that racial narratives do not vary substantially across platforms. By extending the scope of social media platforms studied and foregrounding everyday conversations about race, this study advances academic understanding of how racial identities are both (re-)constructed and (re-)enforced online. In doing so, this study offers insights for political psychologists concerned with identity and its social underpinnings, as well as for scholars of race, political communication, culture, and collective behavior.

articles.title: Social Cohesion in Iraq: Leveraging Religious, Political, and Tribal Authorities for Conflict Transformation
articles.authors: Mae Anna Chokr; Ali Al-Ahmad; Abbas Aroua
articles.abstract: How can we foster social cohesion by engaging with informal religious and political authorities in conflict contexts, such as present-day Iraq? This report answers this question by outlining a conflict transformation approach developed by Cordoba Peace Institute – Geneva (CPI), and in Samarra, Talafar, and Iraq as a whole, between 2018 and 2023. The methodology used was a combination of: 1) a ‘safe mediation space’ approach and diapraxis, 2) collaboration between insider and outsider mediators, and 3) leveraging formal and informal sources of influence, including religious, political, and tribal. The report aims to learn from the experiences of case studies to guide practitioners applying such methods in other similar contexts.

articles.title: How Much Labelled Data Is Enough? A Simulation Study of Prompting Strategies for Unbiased and Reliable LLM-Based Annotation Workflows in Social Sciences
articles.authors: Qixiang Fang
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in (computational) social science to annotate text at scale. Typically, this approach requires researchers to provide (enough) gold labels, develop and evaluate candidate prompts, and decide on the most promising prompt. Meanwhile, many questions arise and remain unanswered: How much labelled data is enough? How should prompt evaluation be conducted? In particular, how can researchers prevent overfitting, an important consideration many social scientists are unfamiliar with. To address these questions, this paper reports a simulation study of prompt evaluation workflows for LLM-based text annotation. I compare intentionally biased yet often employed all-data reuse and validation-only baseline strategies with two defensible workflows: a two-way development/evaluation split and a three-way Explore--Select--Evaluate (ESE) workflow. Across 360 simulation scenarios and 360,000 workflow-level simulation results, all-data reuse and validation-only workflows produced positive reporting bias, especially under adaptive prompt development. In contrast, both two-way and ESE workflows had near-zero mean reporting bias and close-to-95% coverage. However, ESE did not generally select stronger prompts. In fixed-candidate settings, two-way selection outperformed ESE because ESE retained less data for formal prompt comparison without gaining any benefit from exploration. In adaptive settings, ESE reduced regret only modestly under some split ratios, while two-way workflows usually selected prompts with higher absolute true performance. The results suggest that a held-out evaluation set is essential, but that a separate Select stage should be used selectively rather than treated as universally optimal.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (III): From Banner Affiliation to Ethnicity—The Reconstruction of Modern Manchu Identity and Online Narratives of Manchu–Han Conflict
articles.authors: ZY Liu
articles.abstract: This article examines the formation of modern Manchu identity and its relationship to Manchu–Han tensions within the context of Han nationalist discourse on the Chinese internet in the 2020s. It begins by analyzing the Qing Eight Banner system, arguing that the banners were not a single-ethnicity organization in the modern sense, but a political and social system composed of multiple identity groups including Manchu, Mongol, Han-martial (Hanjun), and bondservant (baoyi) populations. After the fall of the Qing, the former banner affiliation was gradually reorganized within the modern ethnic classification system, producing the Manchu identity of today. The article further discusses the process of reconstituting modern Manchu identity since the 1980s, contending that this process involves both historical continuity and the influence of ethnic policy, local administrative factors, and practical interests. When ethnic identity becomes linked to the allocation of public resources, social policy, and historical narrative, it may shift from cultural identification toward an identity of social interest. The article maintains that contemporary Manchu–Han contradictions are not purely ethnic conflicts, but the product of the combined operation of historical memory, identity recognition, class differences, and material interests. Reducing the binding between ethnic identity and the distribution of public goods, thereby allowing ethnic identity to return more fully to the domain of cultural identification, may be an important direction for alleviating related tensions.

articles.title: Dynamic Democratic Consent: A System Dynamics Framework for Public Trust, Political Communication, and Policy Feedback
articles.authors: Muhammad Sukri Bin Ramli
articles.abstract: Political communication is often analyzed through event-based models that give lim ited attention to feedback, delay, saturation, and changing public trust. This conceptual paper proposes the Dynamic Democratic Consent framework, integrating selected princi ples from Edward Bernays’ account of public relations with the S-E-E-D behavior modes of Snowball growth, Equilibrium seeking, Elastic adjustment, and feedback-loop Dominance. The framework extends the conventional resource categories of manpower, mindpower, and money by treating algorithmic media infrastructure as a conditional fourth dimension. It maps an eight-stage communication-planning process onto reinforcing and balancing feed back structures, perception delays, demographic capacity, and institutional trust. Simulated reference modes illustrate how political-support momentum may encounter electoral satura tion, how delayed perception and corrective response may produce oscillatory adjustment, and how divergence between communication and policy delivery may weaken institutional trust and contract effective support capacity. A four-stage diagnostic process is proposed for describing trajectories, identifying feedback structures, designing policy interventions, and examining potential behavioral shifts. The framework is exploratory rather than predictive. Empirical estimation, comparative case testing, sensitivity analysis, and ethical evaluation are required before it can support applied political analysis.

articles.title: Towards a Typology of Islamic Higher Education in Europe: A Comparative Analysis of Institutional Models
articles.authors: Cemal YILMAZ
articles.abstract: This article examines the emergence and institutional diversity of Islamic higher education in Europe and develops a comparative typology of its principal institutional models. While existing scholarship has focused primarily on individual countries, institutions, or debates concerning imam training, a systematic comparative framework for understanding the broader landscape of Islamic higher education remains underdeveloped. Using a comparative institutional analysis of developments in the Netherlands, Germany, Belgium, Austria, England, France, Spain, and Italy, the study examines historical trajectories, state–religion relations, institutional structures, accreditation systems, leadership formation, and sources of legitimacy. The findings demonstrate that Islamic higher education in Europe has not developed through a single institutional pathway. Instead, five ideal-type models can be identified: the Independent Islamic University Model, the State-Integrated Islamic Theology Model, the Seminary-Based Model, the Hybrid Partnership Model, and the Emerging and Transitional Model. The study contributes to the literature by providing a comparative framework for analyzing institutional diversity and by proposing a typology that facilitates future research on Islamic higher education, Muslim institutionalization, and religious leadership in Europe.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (I): Examining the Narrative Contest between Han Nationalism and State Nationalism through the Withdrawal of the Film The Battle of Penghu
articles.authors: ZY Liu
articles.abstract: Taking the withdrawal of the 2026 film The Battle of Penghu as a point of entry, this article explores the rise of Han nationalist ideology within Chinese society in the 2020s, and the increasingly prominent divergences in orientation between it and the officially led “Chinese nationalism (state nationalism).” The article analyzes the institutional roots of Han nationalism during a period of economic zero-sum competition, its contestation of historical narratives in the sphere of popular culture, and its comprehensive deconstruction of the official discursive system on core issues such as the definition of the nation, historical orthodoxy, and territorial legality.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (II): Cultural Products, Historical Memory, and the Narrative Conflicts of Zhonghua Nationalism
articles.authors: ZY Liu
articles.abstract: This paper examines how the narrative of Zhonghua nationalism exerts influence over cultural production in contemporary China and analyzes its structural ramifications. Within film and television, specific historical themes are constrained from entering mainstream cultural production; in video games, certain historical factions are minimized or rendered entirely absent from narratives; in online literature, market mechanisms reflect historical preferences distinct from official state narratives through reader subscription behavior; in historical publications, ethnicity-inflected linguistic expressions from the past undergo textual revision; and within the Hanfu movement, Han culture is not directly suppressed but rather subsumed and repackaged within the overarching framework of "Zhonghua culture."

articles.title: Everyday Talk and Child Development: A Conceptual Framework for the Informal Conversation Deficit Hypothesis A Theoretical Paper Proposing an Untested Hypothesis and Research Agenda
articles.authors: Craig Davidon
articles.abstract: Over recent decades, documented shifts in family and community routines — including declining rates of children walking to school, smaller household sizes, and increasingly structured extracurricular scheduling — have measurably reduced the settings in which children once encountered casual, unscripted conversation with a range of adults and peers. This paper proposes the term informal conversation deficit to describe a hypothesized reduction, alongside these routine changes, in children's everyday practice with varied social speech. The framework is motivated by the author's own long-standing personal observations, made over approximately five decades, of apparent declines in children's verbal and nonverbal (for example, body-language-based) social communication. These observations are offered as motivating context only: the paper presents no empirical data of its own, and every causal relationship it proposes is a hypothesis rather than an established finding. Drawing on Vygotsky's (1978) account of private speech, Romeo and colleagues' (2018) finding that conversational turns are associated with language-related brain function, and the ongoing debate over socioeconomic disparities in children's verbal environments, the paper considers how reduced frequency and variety of conversational practice may plausibly be linked to slower pragmatic language development and, in turn, to difficulty articulating internal states such as fear, frustration, or unmet needs. It is hypothesized that resulting frustration may sometimes present as behavior that resembles or compounds features of neurodevelopmental conditions, without being caused by them. The paper closes with explicit limitations and a proposed longitudinal study — using LENA audio-recording metrics — designed to test, for the first time within this framework, the relationship between conversational-turn exposure and children's emotional self-regulation

articles.title: Between Disintermediation and Inertia: Preprints and the Digital Transformation of the Scientific Knowledge Order
articles.authors: Christian Koß; Frank Marcinkowski
articles.abstract: Informed by work on the digital transformation of traditional knowledge orders, this study examines how researchers use preprints relative to journal publication, and how they perceive preprints’ credibility, benefits, and risks. Evidence comes from a cross-disciplinary survey of 1,403 researchers affiliated with German universities who had previously served as corresponding authors on Web of Science-indexed publications. Corresponding authors indexed in Web of Science are not representative of the scientific community as a whole, and participation was low relative to the number invited, so the estimates describe the respondent sample rather than population prevalence. Unlike studies that recruit through preprint servers, however, this frame also reaches researchers who have never posted a preprint. We investigate five dimensions: (1) adoption rates and disciplinary variations, (2) publication practices, (3) audience orientation and reported feedback, (4) motivations for preprint use, and (5) scientific perceptions of preprints’ implications for research integrity and credibility. Our findings reveal disciplinary differences: 48.6% of natural scientists had uploaded a preprint compared with 18.6% of humanities scholars. Among adopters, reported motivations emphasized access, open science, and speed. Respondents also expressed concerns about credibility and premature public reporting. Intended audiences and reported feedback were concentrated within the scientific community, with little frequent feedback reported from journalists, policymakers, industry, or citizens. Most users posted preprints alongside the journal publication process, although 21.6% included having no intention to publish elsewhere among the circumstances in which they usually posted. These findings describe preprints as a widely used but unevenly adopted publication mode that commonly coexists with formal peer review, with implications for scientific policy and research integrity.

articles.title: Cognitive Degradation: The Reconfiguration of the Labor Process and Knowledge Authority in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence
articles.authors: 王本杰
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly entering knowledge-intensive work, including programming, writing, design, analysis, and management. Unlike earlier forms of automation that were often concentrated on physical operations or clearly defined executional tasks, generative AI can produce text, code, classifications, and proposals within the workflow itself. Its significance therefore lies not simply in the displacement of particular tasks, but in the possibility that activities once associated with professional judgment become increasingly mediated by corporate technological systems. This paper examines that possibility through the concept of “cognitive degradation.” Drawing on Marx’s analysis of machinery and fixed capital, Braverman’s account of labor-process control and deskilling (Braverman, 1974), and Burawoy’s emphasis on worker agency and consent (Burawoy, 1978; 1979), the paper defines cognitive degradation narrowly. It occurs when AI takes over cognitive tasks previously performed by workers, workers’ effective authority over the criteria and application of judgment declines, and that shift is stabilized through organizational rules, technological systems, or labor institutions. The concept therefore should not be treated as synonymous with deskilling, declining productivity, or algorithmic management. To explore the mechanism, the paper examines three ideal types rather than three directly comparable causal cases: boundary-setting in the Writers Guild of America (WGA), internalization in AI-assisted software development, and institutional mediation through German co-determination. The cases show that AI can increase productivity without necessarily reducing workers’ skills, while still altering how knowledge and judgment are organized. The paper argues that the central issue in AI-mediated labor is therefore not whether machines replace workers, but whether workers retain meaningful authority over the definition, evaluation, and application of knowledge. The paper further proposes that sustained changes in such authority may affect occupational autonomy, skill formation, and bargaining power. Claims about macro-level class restructuring, however, remain propositions for future empirical research rather than conclusions established by the cases examined here.

articles.title: Mapping film commissions in Brazil: Intermediary organizations and institutionalization dynamics in challenging creative ecosystems
articles.authors: Débora Póvoa
articles.abstract: This article presents a panorama of film commissions in Brazil, describing their diverse intermediary roles, tracing their distinct institutionalization paths and reflecting on how trends toward institutional isomorphism or divergence unfold in this emerging field within the Brazilian cultural and creative industries (CCIs). Based on qualitative interviews with 15 film commission representatives, it reveals that these organizations act as strategic intermediaries within local audiovisual ecosystems and follow diverse institutionalization trajectories, with some operating independently with minimal resources and others benefitting from more robust budgets and institutional structures. As relatively new players navigating the uncertainties of Brazil’s cultural and creative landscape, film commissions exhibit a degree of isomorphism in following similar institutional templates, performing analogous logistical functions, and exchanging best practices in consultancies and sector events. Yet, divergence also occurs, particularly due to local and regional inequalities in cultural funding and industry development, which fundamentally shape how each of them operates. Despite their increasing prominence in creative ecosystems worldwide, film commissions remain under-researched, particularly in the Global South. This study fills in this gap by examining the case of Brazil and offering a more nuanced understanding of cultural intermediation and the dynamics of institutional homogeneity and diversity, especially in contexts characterized by significant local and regional variation in the development, size, and funding of the CCIs.

articles.title: A study on the influence of social movements on political representation focusing on the minimum wage case in the mid- 2010s American states
articles.authors: Jihun Yeo
articles.abstract: This study examines how the social movement can contribute to improving political representation with the case of the minimum wage legislation in American states after 2012. The contribution of this research is that it’s an empirical analysis of how social movement affects the legislative process, especially in the agenda-setting stage and how social discourse takes part in this process, given the lack of research concerning determinants of the state legislation of the higher minimum wage, especially focusing on the influence of the social movement on the legislation. I analyze the impact of the social movement, measured by the media exposure frequency, on public opinion, the proposal of bills and the legislation with the national-level time serial and the state-level data. I investigate the impact of the social discourse on public opinion and the legislative process to illuminate the underlying mechanism where the social movement affects the political outcome. The social movement contributes to the improvement of political representation by spreading the social discourse, setting the agenda in civic and political society and triggering partisan politics for institutional change.

articles.title: Value-Based Adaptive Reuse: Design and Initial Testing of a Serious-Game Prototype
articles.authors: Fatemeh Hedieh Arfa
articles.abstract: Adaptive reuse of heritage buildings requires stakeholders, and more specifically, architects to navigate interdependent questions of heritage significance, contemporary function, environmental performance, community benefit, financial feasibility, and approval of other stakeholders (developers, investors, and regulators). Process models can structure these questions, yet conventional validation methods reveal only part of how practitioners move between them under constraint. This paper presents the design and pilot testing of Architect's Design Challenge, a tabletop serious-game prototype developed to explore professional decision-making in adaptive reuse and to examine the practical legibility of the Effective Adaptive Reuse of Heritage Buildings (EARHB) process model. Players progress through six stations, allocate limited resources, select action cards, respond to stakeholder requirements, and construct a design proposition using four predefined project-value categories represented by coloured components. Two formative test rounds, involving students and architects, were organised around introduction, gameplay, and debriefing. The tests indicated that the prototype could stimulate explicit discussion of priorities, sequencing, resource allocation, and trade-offs. They also revealed a central design tension: abstraction supported strategic play but sometimes weakened correspondence with professional practice, particularly for expert players. The study contributes a transparent mapping between research constructs and game mechanics, identifies requirements for future validation, and shows how serious gaming could make selected moments of value recognition, translation into design choices, negotiation, and revision observable within a simulated decision pathway. The evidence is exploratory. It does not establish learning effects, behavioural validity, or transfer to real projects.

articles.title: The Cultural Integration of Wellbeing Practices (CIWP) Framework: Conditions of Possibility Through Design
articles.authors: Carolina Andrea Cárdenas Fernández
articles.abstract:
The gap between knowing about wellbeing and practicing it constitutes a central challenge for research in design and public health. This article proposes the Cultural Integration of Wellbeing Practices (CIWP) Framework, a conceptual framework developed through Research through Design that articulates five dimensions—connection with meaningful values, situated opportunities, appropriation, everyday sustainability, and social legitimacy—to understand the conditions that support the incorporation of evidence-based wellbeing practices into everyday life and, eventually, into culture. Through a retrospective reading of the Wellbeing Practices in Waiting Spaces (WPWS) Framework, the article shows how these conditions can be translated into concrete design decisions through a situated activation mechanism, operationalized through three interdependent components—spatiotemporal conditions, human capacities, and visual mediation devices—and five design principles. The crosswalk indicates that WPWS provides direct operational expression to three of the five CIWP dimensions—situated opportunities, appropriation, and everyday sustainability—while connection with meaningful values and social legitimacy remain open dimensions that require processes beyond the visual mediation device itself. CIWP is offered as a transferable conceptual architecture—not as a fixed configuration—whose value will be tested through future operationalizations in contexts other than waiting spaces.

Keywords: cultural integration of wellbeing practices; conditions of possibility; salutogenesis; interdisciplinarity for wellbeing; design for wellbeing promotion; Trauma-informed design; Research through Design; situated activation.

articles.title: Understanding children’s housing in Australia: a data framework
articles.authors: Amy Clair; Emma Baker; Lynne Giles; Claire Morey; Megan Robinson
articles.abstract: This project examines the available data on children’s housing and wellbeing and current policy in Australia to highlight how housing affects children’s health and development. It provides policymakers with a guide to the different housing situations children face, identifies significant knowledge gaps and related risks, and proposes priorities for policy-relevant data collection and evidence development. The impacts of Australia’s housing crisis on children have received less attention than for other population groups. Accessible data collections rarely focus on them. Yet households with children are particularly affected by poor quality and insecure housing, and children’s physical vulnerability and dependence on caregivers increases the related risks to their wellbeing. This underscores the need for stronger data insights to support earlier intervention, better targeting and more accountable policy for children.

articles.title: CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES FOR DEVELOPING UPCYCLED COSMETIC INGREDIENTS IN BRAZIL: A PERSPECTIVE FOR SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES
articles.authors: Murilo Dotti Garcia; Orlando Nastri Neto
articles.abstract: The use of plant by-products to develop cosmetic ingredients has gained considerable momentum globally, driven by growing demand for sustainability and the increasing expectation that ingredients deliver scientifically proven efficacy. Brazil offers particularly favourable conditions for this trend, since the country combines unparalleled biodiversity with a world-scale agribusiness chain that generates vast volumes of largely underused by-products. This article examines the main challenges and opportunities facing Brazilian small and medium cosmetic enterprises (SMEs) as they develop ingredients from these by-products, focusing on regulatory, technical, scientific and market dimensions. Drawing on an integrative review of recent scientific and sectoral literature and on an analysis of the national context, it argues that SMEs, despite capital and infrastructure constraints, hold genuine advantages in agility and proximity to regional production chains. It concludes that conditions are favourable for smaller companies willing to invest in technical capacity, strategic partnerships and differentiation grounded in scientific evidence.

articles.title: Toward an Intersectional Occupational Health Framework: Psychosocial Conditions as Allocated Exposures
articles.authors: Iara Teixeira
articles.abstract: Occupational health research treats psychosocial working conditions either as features of a job or as traits that help workers cope. This article proposes the Intersectional Occupational Health (IOH) framework, which instead treats these conditions as exposures that labor regimes allocate to differently positioned workers. Drawing on vulnerability theory and the sociology of work, the framework argues that a worker's psychosocial profile records where that worker has been placed, since who meets high-strain conditions, and for how long, is set by law, immigration rules, and welfare systems. On this reading, the uneven spread of these conditions measures a process that produces vulnerability rather than a tally of how well workers cope. The framework follows the path from social position to health outcome, and it treats a sound intervention as one that redistributes exposure rather than one that raises the average. Two cases, domestic work in Southern Europe and platform delivery in Germany, ground a set of recommendations for governments, ranging from household labor inspection to an enforceable presumption of employment.

articles.title: From humanitarian design to design for social innovation: a comparative experiment activating reflexivity on coloniality and power dynamics.
articles.authors: Riccardo Torta; Marco Andrea Finardi; Abigail Turinayo; Victor Muwonge Semaganda; Marco Gobetti
articles.abstract:
This meta-research originates from two experiences of the first two authors, who respectively worked on a Humanitarian Design (HD) project in Uganda with Design Without Borders and on a Design for Social Innovation (DSI) project in Italy with Polimi DESIS Lab. Similar tensions emerged from both contexts regarding the relationship between the design teams and the communities engaged, highlighting the risk of perpetuating systemic oppression and epistemic injustice. To explore these imbalances, the teams were engaged in two sets of sessions, activating reflexivity on social structures embedded in their practices, to uncover potential dynamics rooted in coloniality and power.

Where the Ugandan HD project served as a testbed for the approach and three reflexive tools, the sessions within the Italian project confirmed the initial proposition, showing the potentially broad impact of the application of reflexivity on oppressive dynamics within DSI projects. This experiment uncovered the risks entailed by engaging with local communities, raised issues about urbanity and rurality, different forms of knowledge and models of development, challenging the conception of modernity and recognising these foundational elements of coloniality even in a European context.

Considering the exploratory nature of this research, the intent is to provide grounding for future critical inquiries within the wider DSI community, demonstrating the need to rethink current design practices from a liberatory and relational perspective.

articles.title: Statistischer Quartalsbericht 4/2022
articles.authors: Amt für Statistik und Wahlen Stadt Leipzig
articles.abstract: Regelmäßige vierteljährliche Veröffentlichung: Textbeiträge zu ausgewählten Themen (Teil 1) und statistische Daten (Teil 2)

articles.title: Spirit Becoming Matter: A Thematic Analysis of Creation Stories
articles.authors: Pamela Venerdrow Lucas; Michelle Fauver
articles.abstract:
Objective
This qualitative study examined the creation stories from a cross-section of cultures and traditions to determine whether there are important similarities. 
Methods
Thematic analysis was conducted with 15 creation stories from 11 traditions. Initial coding was reviewed to develop themes, which were then recursively applied to the stories to find further examples and refine definitions. The resulting 13 themes were then clustered into 4 categories. 
Results
The diverse stories shared significant commonalities in their processes, elements, and implications. The first category is consciousness, which includes the themes of creator being, humans as co-creators, thought/mind, and one source. The second category is the elements, which includes the themes of water, light, and earth. The third category is opposites and similars, with no further subcategories. The fourth category is energy, which includes the themes of energy/vibration, breath, void, and time.
Conclusions
Surprising similarities across cultures point toward a model of reality in which consciousness is primary, preceding, and giving rise to physical form. All matter started as energy, and each part contains elements of the whole. The findings suggest that the divine, or universal consciousness, is contained in all matter, that consciousness may be eternal, and that the continuum of consciousness facilitates communication between humans, the divine, and all manifest forms.

articles.title: Are we nursing the technologies? An ethnographic study of nurses’ tech work and its implications for well-being
articles.authors: Paulien D'Huyvetter; Ellen Algera; Daantje Derks; Pascale Marie Le Blanc; Iris Wallenburg; Rik Wehrens
articles.abstract: Healthcare systems across the world face persistent nursing shortages. Although technological innovations are widely promoted as solutions to rising workloads and staff shortages, they also generate additional, largely invisible forms of work. We examine nurses’ tech work: the unanticipated work nurses perform to keep hospital technologies functioning. Drawing on insights from Science and Technology Studies and Work and Organizational Psychology, we investigate the types of tech work nurses perform and their implications for nurses’ well-being. Based on ethnographically grounded observations, interviews, and focus groups conducted in a Dutch academic hospital, we identify eight types of tech work in nursing. For each type, we show tech work can negatively affect nurses’ well-being through hindrance demands and reduced perceptions of meaningfulness, particularly when combined with other demanding tasks. Our findings suggest that the challenge is not the deployment of more technologies, but their design and implementation in ways that minimize burdensome tech work and better support nurses’ care practices.

articles.title: The Politics of Consolidation: Authoritarian Drift and Economic Ambition in Post-Election Tanzania
articles.authors: Rutashubanyuma Nestory
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Tanzania’s political trajectory in August 2026 is increasingly defined by a striking contradiction: ambitious economic modernization is unfolding alongside a marked contraction of political space. Following the contested October 2025 general election, President Samia Suluhu Hassan’s administration appears increasingly focused on restoring political control while facing unresolved questions concerning electoral legitimacy, accountability and constitutional reform (BBC, 2026; Xinhua, 2026a; Xinhua, 2026b). The resignation of Vice President Emmanuel Nchimbi on 25 August 2026 (BBC, 2026; KBC Digital, 2026), restrictions on opposition political activity (The Citizen, 2026b; Daily News, 2026a), and the prosecution of opposition leader Tundu Lissu (The Citizen, 2026a; Mwananchi, 2026) have intensified concerns about the direction of Tanzania’s political order. At the same time, major infrastructure achievements, particularly the Julius Nyerere Hydropower Project, provide the government with a powerful narrative of developmental competence (Xinhua, 2026c).
This paper situates these developments within the comparative literature on democratic backsliding, electoral authoritarianism, political legitimacy, institutional change and developmental states. Drawing on Bermeo’s (2016) analysis of democratic backsliding, Schedler’s (2013) conception of electoral authoritarianism, Beetham’s (1991) theory of political legitimacy, and Doner, Ritchie, and Slater’s (2005) analysis of developmental states, it argues that Tanzania is exhibiting features of political consolidation in which executive control and developmental performance increasingly operate as mutually reinforcing sources of regime stability. The paper does not suggest that Tanzania has become a fully authoritarian state. Rather, it identifies an authoritarian drift in which restrictions on political competition and civic space coexist with continued electoral institutions and ambitious economic modernization. The central argument is that economic performance may strengthen short-term regime legitimacy, but it cannot permanently substitute for credible elections, accountable institutions, judicial independence and meaningful political inclusion. The widening gap between developmental ambition and political openness consequently represents both a democratic challenge and a long-term governance and investment risk.

articles.title: Does Democratic and Economic Benchmarking Matter for Affective Polarization? A Survey Experiment in Poland
articles.authors: Maciej Sychowiec
articles.abstract: This article examines whether international benchmarking, cross-national comparisons of a country’s democratic or economic performance, intensifies affective polarization among citizens. While prior research has shown that international economic comparisons shape electoral behavior, little is known about how such external evaluations influence emotional hostility between partisan groups. Drawing on a survey experiment conducted as part of the 2023 Polish National Election Study, the study tests whether exposure to negative international assessments increases affective polarization. The results reveal a striking asymmetry. Exposure to democratic benchmarking, information signaling Poland’s decline on democratic indicators relative to regional peers, significantly increases affective polarization, whereas economic benchmarking produces no comparable effect. These effects are conditional. Democratic benchmarking polarizes primarily among citizens with negative evaluations of the outgoing government, while leaving strong government supporters unaffected. The findings suggest that benchmarking is most polarizing when it concerns identity-relevant and normatively charged domains in which responsibility can be credibly attributed to domestic political actors. Overall, the study shows that international reputational cues can deepen partisan divides, reinforcing emotional boundaries between political camps rather than fostering a common ground for evaluating national performance.

articles.title: Perceived Benefits of a Cosmetology-Based Self-Care Program for Family Caregivers of Older Adults with Cognitive Decline: An Exploratory Qualitative Study
articles.authors: Riko Nakayama; Hana Sakurai; Fumiko Miyamae; Mutsuko Okamura; Chiaki Ura; Tsuyoshi Okamura; Tomoko Wakui
articles.abstract:
Background: Family caregivers of older adults with cognitive decline often have limited opportunities for self-care. Objective: This study explored the perceived benefits of a cosmetology-based self-care program for family caregivers of community-dwelling older adults with cognitive decline. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted with family caregivers in a community setting in Tokyo, Japan. Participants attended a cosmetology-based session that included light physical activity, skincare, and makeup. Data were collected using free-response questionnaire and focus group interviews and analyzed using inductive content analysis.
Results: Eight family caregivers were included in the analysis. Inductive qualitative content analysis identified three main categories: (1) emotional relief and enjoyment through shared experience, (2) heightened self-awareness and reorientation toward the self, and (3) emerging motivation for self-care and reframing of caregiving. Participants described relaxation, recognition of accumulated fatigue and neglected personal needs, and reassurance and connection through interactions with other caregivers.

articles.title: Institutional Voice Laundering: Multimodal Risks and a Benchmark for Civic Fidelity
articles.authors: Yukai Zeng
articles.abstract: Public institutions are increasingly being designed in forms that Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems can process easily, sometimes before those forms are equally clear to citizens. People increasingly encounter ministries, hospitals, regulators, and courts through AI-mediated summaries, translations, voice interfaces, and visual reformulations, often before seeing the original communication itself. This paper argues that such mediation can weaken important features of institutional communication. Public messages that were originally attributable and open to scrutiny may be recast as apparently neutral assistance, while losing cues about jurisdiction, uncertainty, evidence, and avenues for appeal, even when the output appears fluent and useful. To frame this problem, two linked concepts are introduced here: (1) the machine-readable institution and dual legibility; and (2) a Civic Fidelity Index to assess how much civic meaning is preserved when institutional communication is transformed by AI. This problem is fundamentally multimodal, because many failures arise not from text paraphrase alone but from the way information is reformulated across text, speech, images, and interface elements. We identify research directions around multimodal fidelity, reversible mediation, cross-lingual robustness, and no-laundering standards for accountable AI.

articles.title: NEXUS-HC: A Framework for Technology Foresight in Strategic Communications
articles.authors: Yukai Zeng
articles.abstract:
This conference paper introduces NEXUS-HC (Navigational Examination and Understanding System for Hype Cycle Analysis), a decision-oriented framework for technology foresight in strategic communications. The framework adapts the familiar hype-cycle concept for contested, next-generation information environments shaped by automation, synthetic media, algorithmic information operations, AI avatars, and emerging influence technologies. It standardises technology assessment through a lightweight cross-impact rubric and links assessment outcomes to five portfolio postures: Monitor, Pilot, Adopt, Govern/Harden, or Counter. NEXUS-HC is designed to help strategic communications teams compare emerging technologies, record evidence and confidence levels, set reassessment triggers, and brief leaders using a transparent and auditable decision record.

This is the published conference proceedings paper from the Proceedings of the 25th European Conference on Cyber Warfare & Security (ECCWS 2026). The official version of record is available at https://doi.org/10.34190/eccws.25.1.4709.

articles_hidden.title: Time Discounting, Relative Risk Aversion, and Educational Inequalities
articles_hidden.authors: Herman Gerbert van de Werfhorst
articles_hidden.abstract: Using recently collected survey data merged with register data from the Netherlands, this study examines the predictive value of personal concerns with avoiding downward mobility and time discounting preferences for later school careers. Following implications of relative risk aversion theory and time discounting theory, the results show that children from low-income households need to have both a concern to avoid downward mobility and a higher willingness to wait for longer-term returns in order to make it to the higher tracks. Starting from the premise that, given earlier performance, it would be rational to go on to the highest possible track to avoid downward mobility, the Dutch early-tracking system assumes that students oversee a long educational future to optimize their educational investment. This assumption is less valid for low-income students, which could explain why early tracking increases socioeconomic inequalities in school careers.

articles_hidden.title: Changes in homeownership and entry into parenthood in the Nordic countries
articles_hidden.authors: INVEST Flagship; Jessica Nisén; Lars Dommermuth; Sofi Ohlsson-Wijk1; Peter Fallesen
articles_hidden.abstract: Since 2010, fertility levels have declined unexpectedly in all Nordic countries, with record lows being reached in recent years. The reasons for these declines are unclear, except that fewer people are becoming parents. The aim of this study was to investigate whether changes in housing tenure played a role in the declined entry into parenthood. We expected that changes in housing tenure, particularly a decline in homeownership related to housing affordability challenges among young adults, may have contributed to this decline. Using harmonized Nordic individual-level register data, we assessed to what extent changes in housing tenure, changes in fertility behavior within tenure groups, or both, contributed to the decline. Discrete-time event history models and multivariate decomposition were applied. According to our results, homeownership among young adults declined in the 2010s in Denmark and Finland – but not in Sweden or Norway. The decline in first births was only partially attributable to compositional change in housing tenure along with other socioeconomic factors in Denmark, Finland and Sweden. Entry into parenthood declined among women, regardless of their tenure status, in all four countries during the 2010s, suggesting the importance of behavioral changes. However, the decline was more pronounced among renters than homeowners.

articles_hidden.title: Context-Dependent Resource Conversion: Estimands and Decompositions in the Capability-Ecological Dynamic Model
articles_hidden.authors: Subir Hait
articles_hidden.abstract: Social-science models often summarize the association or effect of a resource with one coefficient or average treatment effect, even when the return to that resource varies across actors, relationships, institutions, and time. This article develops the Capability-Ecological Dynamic Model (CEDM), an estimand-centered middle-range framework for context-dependent resource conversion. Building on capability theory, capital and social-capital theory, stratification, multilevel sociology, heterogeneous-effect methodology, experimental development economics, and transportability, CEDM distinguishes resource possession from access, mobilization, and realized conversion into functionings. It defines an observed conversion surface and the local conversion return, then formalizes conversion modification, ecological shaping, cross-capital complementarity or substitution, conversion instability, context comparison, and dynamic path dependence. Formal results establish aggregate masking; an exact symmetric conversion-structure/composition decomposition; a multilevel decomposition of conversion-return variance; a pseudometric for comparing conversion-return functions; and the logical independence of substantive conversion stability from inferential robustness. Social capital is treated as role-dependent: network structure, accessible resources, mobilized resources, and realized conversion are distinct objects, and social capital may be a focal resource, a modifier of another resource's return, or a contextual property depending on the estimand. Causal interpretation is separated from descriptive conversion and requires a defensible intervention and identification strategy. A reproducible multilevel simulation with 150 contexts and 40 actors per context illustrates the framework: the seeded sample has a pooled mean conversion return of 0.0105, 61.6% of realized conversion-return variance lies between contexts, and 80.3% of that between-context component is associated with ecological support in the specified linear projection. CEDM does not replace established theories or estimators; its proposed contribution is a common estimand-centered language for studying when, where, and through which social conditions resources acquire heterogeneous returns.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-Asset Shock Diffusion: A Reproducible Test of Residual Underreaction, Shock Coherence, and Trading Economics
articles_hidden.authors: Alina Khaybullina
articles_hidden.abstract:
This paper examines whether differences in the speed with which traded assets respond to a common market shock can predict subsequent relative returns.
